questions.stem: The complement of a $28^\circ$ angle measures ___ degrees and its supplement measures ___ degrees. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: Complement: $90 - 28 = 62^\circ$. Supplement: $180 - 28 = 152^\circ$. The supplement is always $90^\circ$ more than the complement.

questions.stem: Which pairs of angles must be supplementary? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A linear pair always adds to $180^\circ$, and $90 + 90 = 180$. Vertical angles are equal, not necessarily supplementary (two $40^\circ$ vertical angles add to $80^\circ$), and adjacent angles can have any sum.

questions.stem: Two lines cross. One angle measures $(3x + 10)^\circ$ and the angle vertical to it measures $(5x - 30)^\circ$. Put the steps for finding all four angles in order.
questions.explanation: Vertical angles are congruent, so $3x + 10 = 5x - 30$, giving $40 = 2x$ and $x = 20$. The vertical pair measures $70^\circ$ each; the other two angles form linear pairs with them, so they are $110^\circ$ each. The four angles around the point add to $360^\circ$.

questions.stem: In the right-hand panel of the picture, the $120^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ angles are supplementary. Why are they not a linear pair?

image.alt: Three panels: adjacent complementary angles of 35 and 55 degrees; a linear pair of 60 and 120 degrees; and two separate angles of 120 and 60 degrees.

choices: Their measures do not add to $180^\circ$.
Supplementary angles can never form a linear pair.
questions.explanation: A linear pair must be adjacent, sharing a vertex and a side, with the outer sides forming a line. These two angles are in different places, so they are only supplementary. Their sum is $180^\circ$, the $60^\circ$ angle is acute, and every linear pair is in fact supplementary.

questions.stem: This is the perpendicular bisector construction for $\overline{AB}$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Segment AB with equal compass arcs from A and from B crossing above and below it, a dashed line through the two crossings, and a right-angle box where the dashed line meets AB.

questions.explanation: 1 lies on one of the arcs drawn with the compass. 2 is where an arc from $A$ and an arc from $B$ cross; it is the same distance from $A$ and $B$. 3 is where the new line meets $\overline{AB}$, the midpoint. 4 lies on the dashed line through the two crossings, the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for constructing the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$ in order.
choices: Open the compass to more than half of $AB$
With the point on $A$, draw arcs above and below $\overline{AB}$
With the same opening and the point on $B$, draw arcs crossing the first two
Draw the line through the two crossing points
questions.explanation: The opening must be set first (more than half of $AB$, or the arcs won't meet). The arcs from $B$ must cross arcs already drawn from $A$, and the line can only be drawn once both crossing points exist.

questions.stem: Match each construction to the reason it works.
choices: Two triangles are congruent by SSS
The compass holds the same distance
All three sides are radii of length AB
Six equilateral triangles meet at the center
questions.explanation: The angle bisector gives $\triangle BXZ \cong \triangle BYZ$ by SSS. Copying a segment just transfers the compass opening. In Euclid's equilateral triangle, $AC$ and $BC$ are radii of circles with radius $AB$. Stepping the radius around a circle works because the hexagon is six equilateral triangles with sides equal to the radius.

questions.stem: To construct a regular hexagon in a circle of radius $5$ cm, you keep the compass opening at ___ cm while stepping around the circle. The hexagon's perimeter is ___ cm. Give only the numbers.

image.alt: A circle with center O and radius r; six points stepped around it with the compass set to r form a regular hexagon split into six equilateral triangles.

questions.explanation: The compass stays at the radius, $5$ cm. Each side of the hexagon is a side of an equilateral triangle whose other sides are radii, so each side is $5$ cm and the perimeter is $6 \times 5 = 30$ cm.

questions.stem: Which of these can be done exactly with compass and straightedge alone? Select all that apply.
choices: Mark a segment exactly 3.7 cm long
questions.explanation: Angle bisection and the regular hexagon are standard constructions. Trisecting an arbitrary angle was proved impossible in the 1800s, and the straightedge has no scale, so with no given unit length there is no way to measure out 3.7 cm (if a 1 cm segment were given, 3.7 cm could be constructed from it).

questions.stem: Points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ on a line have coordinates $9$, $-5$ and $2$. Which statement is true?
choices: None of the points is between the other two
questions.explanation: In order, $-5 < 2 < 9$, so $Z$ (at 2) is in the middle. Check: $YZ + ZX = 7 + 7 = 14 = YX$. Of three distinct points on a line, exactly one is between the other two, so the last choice is impossible.

questions.stem: Three collinear points have $AB = 7$, $BC = 3$ and $AC = 4$. Which point is between the other two?
questions.explanation: The middle point's two distances add to the third. $AC + CB = 4 + 3 = 7 = AB$, so $C$ is between $A$ and $B$. ($AB + BC = 10 \ne 4$ and $BA + AC = 11 \ne 3$.)

questions.stem: Which of these sets are convex? Select all that apply.
choices: A line with one point removed
questions.explanation: A ray contains the segment between any two of its points, and a half-plane is convex by the Plane Separation Postulate. The segment joining two points of a circle passes through the inside, which is not on the curve, and on a line with a gap, the segment joining points on either side of the gap needs the missing point.

questions.stem: Sets $S$ and $T$ are both convex. What can you say about their intersection (the points in both)?
choices: It is convex only if $S$ and $T$ have the same shape
It is convex only if one set contains the other
questions.explanation: If $P$ and $Q$ are in both sets, then $\overline{PQ}$ is in $S$ (because $S$ is convex) and in $T$ (because $T$ is convex), so it is in the intersection. That is why interiors of angles and triangles, which are intersections of half-planes, are convex.

questions.stem: Line $\ell$ is $y = 3x - 2$. Where does the segment from $P(1, 4)$ to $Q(2, 1)$ cross $\ell$?
questions.explanation: With $d = y - (3x - 2)$: $d_P = 4 - 1 = 3$ and $d_Q = 1 - 4 = -3$. Opposite signs, so the segment crosses $\ell$, at $t = \tfrac{3}{3 - (-3)} = \tfrac12$ of the way from $P$: the midpoint $(1.5, 2.5)$. Check: $3(1.5) - 2 = 2.5$. The point $(1.25, 1.75)$ is on $\ell$ but not on $\overline{PQ}$, and $(2, 4)$ is on $\ell$ but not on $\overline{PQ}$ (the segment reaches $x = 2$ only at $Q(2, 1)$).

questions.stem: Line $\ell$ is $y = x + 1$. For $P(2, 5)$, $y - (x + 1) =$ ___. For $Q(4, 1)$, $y - (x + 1) =$ ___. So $P$ and $Q$ lie on ___ sides of $\ell$.
questions.explanation: $P$: $5 - 3 = 2$. $Q$: $1 - 5 = -4$. The values have opposite signs ($P$ is above the line, $Q$ below), so the points are on opposite sides and $\overline{PQ}$ must cross $\ell$.

questions.stem: Which describes the interior of $\angle ABC$?
choices: The points on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{BA}$ as $C$ or on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ as $A$
The points on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{BA}$ as $C$ and on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ as $A$
The points closer to $B$ than to $A$ or $C$
questions.explanation: The interior is the intersection of two half-planes, so a point must pass both tests ("and"). With "or" you would also get points on the far side of one of the lines. The points of $\overline{AC}$ between $A$ and $C$ are in the interior, but they are only a small part of it.

questions.stem: $B = (0, 0)$, $A = (0, 4)$ and $C = (5, 0)$. Which point is in the interior of $\angle ABC$?
questions.explanation: The interior is on $C$'s side of the $y$-axis ($x > 0$) and on $A$'s side of the $x$-axis ($y > 0$): the open first quadrant. Only $(2, 3)$ passes both tests. $(3, 0)$ is on the side $\overrightarrow{BC}$ itself, which is not interior.

questions.stem: Line $\ell$ crosses $\overline{AB}$ between $A$ and $B$ and passes through no vertex of $\triangle ABC$. Put the steps of the proof that $\ell$ crosses another side in order.
choices: $\overline{AB}$ meets $\ell$, so $A$ and $B$ are on opposite sides of $\ell$
$C$ is not on $\ell$, so $C$ is on the same side as $A$ or as $B$
Suppose $C$ is on the same side as $A$; then $C$ and $B$ are on opposite sides
So $\overline{BC}$ meets $\ell$ by the Plane Separation Postulate
questions.explanation: First locate $A$ and $B$ (opposite sides, since a segment within one half-plane can't meet $\ell$). Then place $C$ in one of the two half-planes, take a case, and conclude with the postulate. The other case ($C$ on $B$'s side) gives a crossing of $\overline{AC}$ the same way.

questions.stem: Match each name to its statement.
choices: A line entering a triangle through one side leaves through another side
A ray from the vertex into an angle's interior meets a segment joining the two sides
A line splits the rest of the plane into two convex half-planes
B is on segment AC, with AB + BC = AC
Two points determine exactly one line
questions.explanation: Pasch's axiom is about a line and a triangle; the Crossbar Theorem is about a ray inside an angle; the Plane Separation Postulate defines half-planes; betweenness is the relation behind segments and rays. "Two points determine a line" is the first incidence postulate of Lesson 1.

questions.stem: In the false proof that every triangle is isosceles, which step is the one that fails?
choices: $PB = PC$ because $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{BC}$
questions.explanation: The congruences and $PB = PC$ are all correct. The last step assumes $E$ is between $A$ and $B$ and $F$ is between $A$ and $C$. In an accurate drawing of a non-isosceles triangle, one foot lands on an extension of a side, so one of the sums is really a difference, such as $AB = AE - EB$.

questions.stem: In an accurate drawing for the false proof, with a triangle where $AB < AC$, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Left, the false drawing with P inside the triangle and E and F on the sides. Right, an accurate drawing where P is below BC, outside the triangle, E is on line AB beyond B and F is on side AC.

choices: Both $E$ and $F$ lie on the sides of the triangle
questions.explanation: Steps 1 to 3 of the argument are valid, so $AE = AF$ still holds. But $P$ is outside the triangle (on the circle through $A$, $B$ and $C$), and only one of the feet, here $F$, is on a side; $E$ is on $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ beyond $B$.

questions.stem: A line in a plane separates the points of the plane not on it into two ___. A plane separates the points of space not on it into two ___.
questions.explanation: That is the Plane Separation Postulate and its version in space. The line (or plane) is the edge and belongs to neither part.

questions.stem: Line $\ell$ in the plane of $\triangle ABC$ crosses side $\overline{AB}$ between $A$ and $B$ and passes through no vertex. How many sides of the triangle does $\ell$ cross in all?
questions.explanation: By Pasch's axiom it crosses one more side, and the proof shows it cannot cross the third: $A$ and $B$ are on opposite sides of $\ell$, and $C$ is on the same side as one of them, so the segment joining $C$ to that vertex stays in one half-plane. Exactly 2 sides.

questions.stem: Seven points are marked, no three collinear. How many lines pass through two of them?
questions.explanation: One line per pair: $\binom{7}{2} = \tfrac{7 \cdot 6}{2} = 21$. 42 counts ordered pairs, so each line twice, and 35 is $\binom{7}{3}$, the number of triples.

questions.stem: Nine points are marked. Five lie on one line, and no other three of the points are collinear. How many lines pass through at least two of the points?
questions.explanation: Without the collinear points there would be $\binom{9}{2} = 36$ lines. The five collinear points make $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ pairs, all giving one line, so remove 10 and add that line back once: $36 - 10 + 1 = 27$. 26 forgets to add it back.

questions.stem: Eight points in space are placed so that no four are coplanar. They determine ___ planes and ___ lines.
questions.explanation: Each plane comes from a triple: $\binom{8}{3} = \tfrac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{6} = 56$. Each line comes from a pair: $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ (no three are collinear, since three collinear points plus any fourth would be coplanar).

questions.stem: Five lines are drawn in general position. Into how many regions do they divide the plane?
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{25 + 5 + 2}{2} = 16$. Step by step: 1 region, then each new line adds as many regions as its position number: $1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 16$. 32 is the false $2^n$ pattern, and 11 is the count for four lines.

questions.stem: Seven lines in general position cross at ___ points and divide the plane into ___ regions, of which ___ are bounded.
questions.explanation: Crossings: $\binom{7}{2} = 21$. Regions: $\tfrac{49 + 7 + 2}{2} = 29$. Unbounded regions: $2 \cdot 7 = 14$, so bounded: $29 - 14 = 15$, which matches $\binom{6}{2} = 15$.

questions.stem: How many lines in general position are needed to divide the plane into exactly 56 regions?
questions.explanation: Solve $\tfrac{n^2 + n + 2}{2} = 56$: $n^2 + n - 110 = 0$, so $(n + 11)(n - 10) = 0$ and $n = 10$. Check: $\tfrac{100 + 10 + 2}{2} = 56$. Nine lines give 46 and eleven give 67.

questions.stem: Put these counts in order from smallest to largest.
choices: Crossing points of 6 lines in general position
Planes through 6 points in space, no four coplanar
Lines through 7 points, no three collinear
Regions made by 6 lines in general position

questions.stem: Three lines pass through one point. How many pairs of vertical angles are formed?
questions.explanation: The lines make 6 rays. Of the $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ pairs of rays, 3 are opposite (straight angles), leaving 12 angles, which come in $n(n - 1) = 3 \cdot 2 = 6$ vertical pairs. 12 is the number of angles, not pairs.

questions.stem: Five lines pass through one point with equal angles between neighboring rays. The smallest angle measures ___ degrees, and there are ___ pairs of vertical angles. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: Ten rays split $360^\circ$ into ten equal angles of $36^\circ$ (that is, $\tfrac{180^\circ}{5}$). Vertical pairs: $n(n - 1) = 5 \cdot 4 = 20$.

questions.stem: Match each count to its formula.
left: Lines through $n$ points, no three collinear
Planes through $n$ points in space, no four coplanar
Regions made by $n$ lines in general position
Bounded regions made by $n$ lines in general position
questions.explanation: Lines and planes are $\binom{n}{2}$ and $\binom{n}{3}$. Regions are $1 + n + \binom{n}{2} = \tfrac{n^2 + n + 2}{2}$; removing the $2n$ unbounded ones leaves $\binom{n-1}{2} = \tfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}$. Doubling ($2^n$) matches only up to two lines.

questions.stem: Seven points on a circle are joined by every possible chord, and no three chords pass through one interior point. How many regions are inside the circle?
questions.explanation: $1 + \binom{7}{2} + \binom{7}{4} = 1 + 21 + 35 = 57$. The doubling pattern would predict 64, but it already failed at six points (31, not 32).

questions.stem: Which changes make $n$ lines (with $n \ge 3$) divide the plane into fewer than $\frac{n^2 + n + 2}{2}$ regions? Select all that apply.
choices: Two of the lines are parallel
Three of the lines pass through one point
The lines are drawn in a different order
questions.explanation: Each line adds one region per piece, and its pieces come from crossings. Parallel lines lose a crossing, and three lines through one point merge crossings, so both give fewer regions. Lines are already infinite, and the order of drawing doesn't change the final picture.

questions.stem: Three parallel lines are crossed by two transversals, which meet each other at a point not on any of the parallel lines. Into how many regions is the plane divided?
questions.explanation: The parallels make 4 strips. The first transversal crosses 3 lines, so it is cut into 4 pieces and adds 4 regions: 8. The second crosses the 3 parallels and the first transversal, 4 points, so it adds 5: 13. (16 is the general-position count for five lines.)

questions.stem: The picture shows 4 lines in general position. How many of its 11 regions are unbounded, and why?

image.alt: Four lines crossing at six points and cutting the plane into eleven numbered regions: three small enclosed ones and eight that reach the edge of the picture.

choices: 8, because a large circle around the crossings is cut by each line twice
4, because each line makes one unbounded region
3, because the bounded regions are triangles
6, because there are six crossing points
questions.explanation: A big circle around all the crossings meets each line twice, in $2 \cdot 4 = 8$ points, which cut the circle into 8 arcs, one per unbounded region. That leaves $11 - 8 = 3$ bounded regions.

questions.stem: An interpretation of the undefined terms of an axiomatic system in which every axiom is true is called a ___ of the system.
questions.explanation: A model gives the undefined terms a meaning that makes all the axioms true. Every theorem is then true in the model too, and the existence of a model shows the axioms are consistent.

questions.stem: Match each goal to the method that achieves it.
left: Show axiom X is independent of the others
Show statement S is a theorem
Show statement S is not a theorem
choices: Find one model where every axiom is true
Find a model where the other axioms hold and X fails
Find a model where every axiom holds and S fails
Check many examples and find no contradiction
questions.explanation: Consistency needs one model of all the axioms. Independence and "not a theorem" both need a model in which the axioms (or the other axioms) hold but the statement fails, because a proof would force the statement to hold in every model. A theorem can only be shown by a proof. Failing to find a contradiction proves nothing.

questions.stem: Given Euclid's other postulates, which of these statements are equivalent to the parallel postulate? Select all that apply.
choices: Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel to the line.
The angles of every triangle add to $180^\circ$.
questions.explanation: Playfair's axiom, the $180^\circ$ triangle sum and the existence of a rectangle are each equivalent to the fifth postulate, so each fails in hyperbolic geometry. Vertical angles are congruent in every geometry discussed here: the proof uses only linear pairs, not parallels.

questions.stem: Each panel pictures one of Euclid's postulates. Name the postulate shown in each numbered panel.

image.alt: Four panels. Panel 1: a segment joining two points. Panel 2: a segment with dashed extensions and arrows at both ends. Panel 3: a circle with its center and one radius drawn. Panel 4: two right angles in different positions.

choices: Postulate 1: a line can be drawn between any two points
Postulate 2: a segment can be extended
Postulate 3: a circle can be drawn with any center and radius
Postulate 4: all right angles are equal
questions.explanation: The first three postulates describe what a straightedge and compass can do: join two points, extend a segment, and draw a circle. The fourth says all right angles are equal, wherever they are. The parallel postulate would need two lines and a transversal.

questions.stem: In the four-point geometry (four points; each pair of points on exactly one line; each line has exactly two points), how many lines pass through each point? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: A point is paired with each of the other 3 points, and each pair has its own line, so 3 lines pass through each point. (Check: 4 points × 3 lines each counts every line twice, once at each end, so there are $\tfrac{4 \cdot 3}{2} = 6$ lines.)

questions.stem: Name the numbered point and circles on this sphere.

image.alt: A sphere with a point at the top, a small circle near the top, a large circle around the middle, and a tilted large circle passing through the top and bottom points. Hidden back halves are dashed.

choices: Line of latitude (not a great circle)
questions.explanation: Great circles have the sphere's center as their center: the equator and every circle through both poles. A line of latitude near the top is a smaller circle whose center is above the sphere's center, so it is not a great circle and not a shortest path.

questions.stem: Match each geometry to its parallels and triangle angle sums.
choices: Exactly one parallel; angle sum equal to 180°
Infinitely many parallels; angle sum less than 180°
No parallels; angle sum more than 180°
No parallels; angle sum less than 180°
questions.explanation: The number of parallels through an outside point controls the angle sum: one parallel gives exactly $180^\circ$, many give less, none gives more.

questions.stem: On a sphere, with great circles as the lines, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Some triangles have three right angles.
Any two points lie on exactly one line.
questions.explanation: Two great circles always cross (at two opposite points), each great circle is $2\pi R$ long, and the pole-to-equator triangle has three right angles. But two opposite points, such as the poles, lie on infinitely many great circles, so the last statement fails.

questions.stem: A spherical triangle has angles $100^\circ$, $80^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Its spherical excess is ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $E = 100 + 80 + 60 - 180 = 60^\circ$, which is $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ radians. On a sphere of radius $R$ the triangle's area would be $R^2 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{3}$.

questions.stem: Put these events in the history of the parallel postulate in order, earliest first.
choices: Euclid's Elements states the fifth postulate
Saccheri tries to prove it by contradiction
Lobachevsky and Bolyai publish hyperbolic geometry
Beltrami's models show hyperbolic geometry is as consistent as Euclidean geometry
Einstein's general relativity describes gravity with curved spacetime
questions.explanation: Euclid wrote about 300 BCE; Saccheri published in 1733; Lobachevsky (1829) and Bolyai (1832) published hyperbolic geometry; Beltrami's models came in 1868; general relativity in 1915.

questions.stem: Two friends each arrive at a random time between 12:00 and 1:00 and wait 15 minutes. The square shows all pairs of arrival times ($x$ for friend X, $y$ for friend Y). What does each numbered region or line mean?

image.alt: A 60 by 60 square of arrival times with a band around the dashed diagonal, an upper-left corner triangle and a lower-right corner triangle.

choices: They arrive at the same moment
questions.explanation: In the upper-left triangle $y > x + 15$: Y comes more than 15 minutes after X, so X has already left. The lower-right triangle is the reverse. The band $|x - y| \le 15$ is where they meet, and the diagonal $y = x$ is where they arrive together.

questions.stem: Match each random experiment to the measure you should use to find its probabilities.
left: The moment you arrive during a 10-minute wait for a bus
The point where a dart lands on a board
The arrival times of two people in the same hour
A random point inside a cube
questions.explanation: One random time is a point on a segment (length). A dart's landing spot is a point in a flat region (area). Two random times together form a point in a square (area). A point in a solid uses volume. Counting outcomes doesn't work because there are infinitely many.

questions.stem: A point is chosen at random inside a circle of radius 6. The probability that it lies within 2 units of the center is ___. Give an exact fraction.
questions.explanation: The favorable region is a circle of radius 2: $P = \dfrac{\pi \cdot 2^2}{\pi \cdot 6^2} = \dfrac{4}{36} = \dfrac19$. Comparing radii ($\tfrac26 = \tfrac13$) is the common mistake: area, not radius, is the measure.

questions.stem: A circle of radius 5 is inscribed in a $10 \times 10$ square, and a point is chosen at random in the square. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The probability it lands inside the circle is $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
The probability it lands outside the circle is $1 - \tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
The probability it lands within 2.5 of the center is one quarter of the probability it lands inside the circle.
The probability it lands inside the circle is $\tfrac12$, because the radius is half the side.
questions.explanation: $P(\text{circle}) = \tfrac{25\pi}{100} = \tfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785$, so the outside has $1 - \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. A circle of radius 2.5 has area $6.25\pi$, a quarter of $25\pi$ (half the radius gives a quarter of the area). The last statement compares lengths instead of areas.

questions.stem: Two people arrive at random times in the same $T$-minute window and each waits $w$ minutes. Put the steps for finding the probability that they meet in order.
choices: Let $x$ and $y$ be the two arrival times.
Draw the $T \times T$ square of all possible points $(x, y)$.
Mark the band $|x - y| \le w$ where they meet.
Find the area of the two corner triangles outside the band.
Divide that area by $T^2$ and subtract the result from 1.
questions.explanation: The method turns two random times into one random point in a square. The corner triangles (legs $T - w$) are where they miss each other, so $P = 1 - \tfrac{(T - w)^2}{T^2}$.

questions.stem: Which projective plane axiom means there are no parallel lines?
choices: P2: any two distinct lines meet in exactly one point.
P1: any two distinct points are on exactly one line.
P3: there are four points, no three on one line.
Playfair's axiom: through an outside point there is exactly one parallel.
questions.explanation: Parallel lines are lines that don't meet. P2 says every two lines meet, so there are none. P1 is about points, P3 rules out tiny models, and Playfair's axiom belongs to affine planes, which do have parallels.

questions.stem: Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ with the three lines $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ satisfy P1 and P2. Why is this not a projective plane?
choices: It fails P3: it doesn't have four points with no three on a line.
Lines $AB$ and $BC$ meet in two points.
questions.explanation: Each pair of the three lines meets at one corner, so P2 holds, and each pair of points has one line, so P1 holds. But there are only three points, so P3 fails. P3 exists precisely to rule out degenerate models like this one. (Lines $AB$ and $CA$ do meet, at $A$.)

questions.stem: The Fano plane has points $A$ to $G$ and lines $ADB$, $BEC$, $CFA$, $AGE$, $BGF$, $CGD$, $DEF$. Which set of three points is a line?
questions.explanation: $CGD$ is on the list (it is the median from $C$). $A$, $B$, $C$ are the triangle's corners, which lie on three different lines. $D$ and $G$ share only line $CGD$, and $B$ and $E$ share only $BEC$.

questions.stem: A projective plane of order 4 has ___ points. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: A plane of order $n$ has $n^2 + n + 1$ points: $16 + 4 + 1 = 21$. (Each line has $n + 1 = 5$ points.)

questions.stem: In the usual picture of the Fano plane, the circle $DEF$ crosses the median $BF$ at a spot with no dot. What is that crossing in the geometry?
choices: An eighth point of the plane
Nothing: it is not a point of the geometry
questions.explanation: The geometry has only the seven points $A$ to $G$. Lines $DEF$ and $BGF$ already share the point $F$, and two lines share exactly one point, so the drawn crossing is an accident of the picture, like the crossing of the diagonals in Lesson 39's four-point geometry.

questions.stem: What is known about a projective plane of order 12?
choices: It is ruled out by the Bruck–Ryser theorem.
Nobody knows: 12 is the smallest order still unsettled.
It was ruled out by a computer search in 1989.
questions.explanation: Prime-power orders exist; 6 is excluded by Bruck–Ryser; 10 was excluded by the 1989 computer search of Lam, Thiel and Swiercz. Twelve leaves remainder 0 when divided by 4, so Bruck–Ryser says nothing about it, and the question is open.

questions.stem: Which statements are true in a projective plane of order 3? Select all that apply.
choices: Each point is on exactly 3 lines.
Any two lines meet in exactly one point.
questions.explanation: Order 3 means $n + 1 = 4$ points per line, and also 4 lines through each point (not 3). There are $9 + 3 + 1 = 13$ points and 13 lines, and P2 holds in every projective plane.

questions.stem: For a projective plane of order $n$, match each quantity to its formula.
left: Points left after deleting one line
questions.explanation: Points per line is $n + 1$ by definition of the order, and the same number of lines passes through each point. Counting along the lines through one point gives $1 + (n + 1)n = n^2 + n + 1$ points. Deleting a line removes its $n + 1$ points, leaving $n^2$: the affine plane.

questions.stem: Delete the line $DEF$ from the Fano plane. In the affine plane that remains, which line is parallel to $AB$?
questions.explanation: The old lines $ADB$ and $CGD$ met at $D$, which was deleted, so $AB$ and $CG$ no longer meet: they are parallel. $BC$ and $AB$ still share $B$, and $AG$ and $BG$ share points with $AB$ too.

questions.stem: Put the steps for turning an affine plane into a projective plane in order.
choices: Sort the lines into parallel classes.
Create one new point for each parallel class, and put it on every line of that class.
Add one new line containing all the new points.
Check that any two lines now meet in exactly one point.
questions.explanation: The parallel classes must be known before you can give each one a point at infinity; each point at infinity goes on the lines of its class, so parallel lines now meet; the last new line can only be drawn once the points at infinity exist, and it makes P1 and P2 hold for the new points as well. Only then is the result a projective plane, so the check comes last.

questions.stem: What is the dual of axiom P3, "there are four points, no three of which are on one line"?
choices: There are four lines, no three of which are parallel.
There are four lines, no three of which pass through one point.
There are three lines through every point.
Any four points lie on two lines.
questions.explanation: Swap point and line, and "on one line" with "through one point". The dual is a theorem (proved in the lesson from the four points of P3 and the lines $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$), which is why the principle of duality works.

questions.stem: How do we know the projective plane axioms are consistent?
choices: No one has found a contradiction in them.
Duality turns each axiom into another axiom.
They are weaker than Euclid's postulates.
The Fano plane is a model in which all three hold.
questions.explanation: As in Lesson 39, a model proves consistency: if the axioms led to a contradiction, the contradiction would have to be true in the Fano plane, which is impossible.

questions.stem: An affine plane has 5 points on each line (order 5). How many lines does it have? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: An affine plane of order $n$ has $n^2 + n$ lines: $25 + 5 = 30$. They fall into $n + 1 = 6$ parallel classes of $n = 5$ lines each. (It has $n^2 = 25$ points.)

questions.stem: The Bruck–Ryser theorem says: if $n$ leaves remainder 1 or 2 when divided by 4 and a plane of order $n$ exists, then $n$ is a sum of two squares. Which order does it rule out?
questions.explanation: $6$ leaves remainder 2 and is not a sum of two squares ($0+1$, $1+1$, $0+4$, $1+4$, $4+4$ give 1, 2, 4, 5, 8), so no plane of order 6 exists. $10 = 9 + 1$ passes the test (it was ruled out later by computer), $9$ leaves remainder 1 and $9 = 9 + 0$, and $13 = 9 + 4$; both 9 and 13 are prime powers, and their planes exist.

questions.stem: What is neutral geometry?
choices: Euclidean geometry with all of its axioms except the parallel postulate
Euclidean geometry restricted to small regions
questions.explanation: Neutral (absolute) geometry keeps every axiom except the parallel postulate. Euclidean and hyperbolic geometry are both models of it; the sphere is not, because it breaks other axioms too.

questions.stem: Which statement can be proved in neutral geometry?
choices: The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$.
An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than each remote interior angle.
Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel.
questions.explanation: Euclid proved the Exterior Angle Inequality (I.16) with congruent triangles alone. The other three statements are each equivalent to the parallel postulate, so they can't be proved without it.

questions.stem: What does the Saccheri–Legendre theorem say?
choices: Every triangle's angles add to exactly $180^\circ$.
Every triangle's angles add to less than $180^\circ$.
In neutral geometry, every triangle's angles add to at most $180^\circ$.
questions.explanation: The theorem gives an upper bound, $180^\circ$, and nothing more: Euclidean triangles reach it and hyperbolic ones fall short. Neither "exactly" nor "less than" can be proved without choosing a parallel axiom.

questions.stem: In Legendre's construction, $M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ and $E$ is on ray $AM$ beyond $M$ with $ME = AM$. What is the angle of $\triangle AEC$ at $C$?
questions.explanation: $\triangle AMB \cong \triangle EMC$ by SAS, so $\angle BCE = \angle ABC$. The angle at $C$ is $\angle ACB + \angle BCE = \angle C + \angle B$. That is how the new triangle keeps the old angle sum.

questions.stem: A hyperbolic triangle has angles $48^\circ$, $61^\circ$ and $57^\circ$. Its defect is ___ degrees. Give only the number.
A spherical triangle can have angles adding to $270^\circ$. Why doesn't that contradict the Saccheri–Legendre theorem?
choices: The sphere is not a model of neutral geometry: its lines close up and two points can lie on several lines.
The theorem applies only to small triangles.
Spherical angles are measured in radians.
The theorem was later shown to be false.
questions.explanation: The theorem is proved from the axioms of neutral geometry, so it holds only where they hold. On a sphere, opposite points lie on infinitely many great circles and lines can't be extended without coming back, so the Exterior Angle Inequality and the theorem built on it fail.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the proof of the Saccheri–Legendre theorem in order.
choices: Suppose some triangle has angle sum $180^\circ + p$ with $p > 0$.
Apply Legendre's construction repeatedly to get a triangle with the same sum and an angle smaller than $p$.
Conclude that the other two angles of that triangle add to more than $180^\circ$.
Note that this contradicts the fact that any two angles of a triangle add to less than $180^\circ$.
Conclude that every triangle has angle sum at most $180^\circ$.
questions.explanation: It is a proof by contradiction. Halving keeps the sum fixed while one angle shrinks below $p$; then the other two must exceed $180^\circ$, which the Exterior Angle Inequality forbids.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this Saccheri quadrilateral $ABCD$.

image.alt: Quadrilateral ABCD with right angles at A and B, congruent vertical sides AD and BC, a top side DC drawn curving down toward AB, and a dashed segment from M on AB to N on DC.

choices: Segment joining the midpoints of base and summit
questions.explanation: The base $\overline{AB}$ has right angles at both ends; the congruent legs $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BC}$ stand on it; the summit $\overline{DC}$ is opposite the base, and the angles at $D$ and $C$ are the summit angles. $\overline{MN}$ joins the midpoints and is perpendicular to both base and summit.

questions.stem: In proving that the summit angles of Saccheri quadrilateral $ABCD$ are congruent, what does SAS applied to $\triangle DAB$ and $\triangle CBA$ give?
choices: The summit angles are right angles.
questions.explanation: $AD = BC$, the right angles at $A$ and $B$ match, and $\overline{AB}$ is shared, so the triangles are congruent and $DB = CA$. Then SSS on $\triangle ADC$ and $\triangle BCD$ gives the congruent summit angles. Nothing here says the angles are right.

questions.stem: In hyperbolic geometry, the summit angles of a Saccheri quadrilateral are:
questions.explanation: The summit angles are always congruent. Right angles happen exactly in Euclidean geometry, obtuse ones are impossible in neutral geometry, and in hyperbolic geometry they are acute.

questions.stem: Which statements are true of every Saccheri quadrilateral in hyperbolic geometry? Select all that apply.
choices: Its summit is shorter than its base.
Its angles add to less than $360^\circ$.
questions.explanation: Congruent summit angles hold in all of neutral geometry; in hyperbolic geometry they are acute, so the angle sum $180^\circ + 2s$ is below $360^\circ$. The summit is longer than the base, not shorter.

questions.stem: A Saccheri quadrilateral in hyperbolic geometry has summit angles of $80^\circ$. What is its defect, $360^\circ$ minus its angle sum?
questions.explanation: Angle sum $= 90 + 90 + 80 + 80 = 340^\circ$, so the defect is $360 - 340 = 20^\circ$. Each half cut off by $\overline{MN}$ is a Lambert quadrilateral with defect $10^\circ$.

questions.stem: Match each mathematician to the contribution described in the lesson.
choices: Studied quadrilaterals with congruent legs perpendicular to a base (1733)
Studied quadrilaterals with three right angles
Gave a halving construction showing angle sums are at most 180°
Published hyperbolic geometry as a genuine alternative geometry
Proved the parallel postulate from the other four
questions.explanation: Saccheri hoped to prove the parallel postulate by contradiction and instead found many hyperbolic theorems; Lambert studied the three-right-angle quadrilateral (half a Saccheri quadrilateral); Legendre's construction proves the Saccheri–Legendre theorem; Bolyai and Lobachevsky accepted the new geometry. Nobody proved the parallel postulate from the other four: it is independent.

questions.stem: A segment from vertex $A$ to side $\overline{BC}$ splits a hyperbolic triangle into two triangles with defects $4^\circ$ and $9^\circ$. What is the defect of the whole triangle?
questions.explanation: Defect is additive: the two angles at the split point add to $180^\circ$, so the defects of the pieces add to the defect of the whole: $4 + 9 = 13^\circ$.

questions.stem: In Buffon's needle problem with lines $d$ apart, $x$ is the distance from the needle's center to the nearest line. What values can $x$ take?
questions.explanation: The center is somewhere between two lines $d$ apart, and the nearest one is at most halfway across: $0 \le x \le \tfrac d2$. The range $0$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ belongs to the angle $\theta$.

questions.stem: A needle of length $\ell \le d$ makes acute angle $\theta$ with the lines, and its center is $x$ from the nearest line. When does it cross that line?
questions.explanation: Half the needle, of length $\tfrac{\ell}{2}$, rises a vertical distance $\tfrac{\ell}{2}\sin\theta$ (opposite side over hypotenuse). It reaches the line when that is at least $x$. Using the whole length $\ell$ forgets that the center is in the middle.

questions.stem: With $\theta$ in radians, what is the area of the sample-space rectangle $0 \le \theta \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $0 \le x \le \tfrac{d}{2}$?
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot \tfrac{d}{2} = \tfrac{\pi d}{4}$. The favorable area under $x = \tfrac{\ell}{2}\sin\theta$ is $\tfrac{\ell}{2}$, and their ratio is $\tfrac{2\ell}{\pi d}$.

questions.stem: A needle as long as the line spacing ($\ell = d$) is dropped 200 times and crosses a line 125 times. Using $\pi \approx \tfrac{2\ell N}{dC}$, the estimate of $\pi$ is ___. Give a decimal.
questions.explanation: With $\ell = d$, $\pi \approx \dfrac{2N}{C} = \dfrac{400}{125} = 3.2$. With only 200 drops the typical error is about 0.1 or more, so 3.2 is a normal result.

questions.stem: A needle 6 cm long is dropped on lines 10 cm apart. What is the probability that it crosses a line?
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{2\ell}{\pi d} = \dfrac{12}{10\pi} = \dfrac{6}{5\pi} \approx 0.382$. $\tfrac35$ is just $\tfrac{\ell}{d}$; the other two drop or double the factor 2.

questions.stem: In Barbier's argument, why is a circle of diameter $d$ so useful?
choices: Its area is easy to compute.
It always crosses the lines exactly twice, which fixes the constant in $E = c \cdot (\text{length})$.
It crosses a line with probability $\tfrac{2}{\pi}$.
questions.explanation: Wherever it lands (apart from tangent positions, which have probability 0), the circle straddles exactly one line, so $E = 2$ for length $\pi d$. That gives $c = \tfrac{2}{\pi d}$.

questions.stem: Put the steps of Barbier's argument for Buffon's needle in order.
choices: Expected crossings add when a needle is cut into pieces, so $E = c \cdot (\text{length})$.
The same rule holds for bent wires and, in the limit, for curves.
A circle of diameter $d$ always crosses exactly twice, so $c \cdot \pi d = 2$.
A needle with $\ell \le d$ crosses at most once, so $P = E = \tfrac{2\ell}{\pi d}$.
questions.explanation: First the rule that expected crossings are proportional to length, then its extension to curves (needed to use a circle), then the circle fixes the constant, and finally a short needle's expected crossings equal its probability of crossing.

questions.stem: For a needle three times as long as the line spacing ($\ell = 3d$), $\tfrac{2\ell}{\pi d} = \tfrac{6}{\pi} \approx 1.91$. What does this number mean?
choices: The probability of crossing a line
The probability of crossing two lines
The expected number of lines the needle crosses
questions.explanation: A probability can't exceed 1. Barbier's argument still applies to long needles, so $\tfrac{2\ell}{\pi d}$ is the expected number of crossings; only for $\ell \le d$ is it also the probability of crossing.

questions.stem: Which statements about estimating $\pi$ with Buffon's needle are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The typical error shrinks roughly in proportion to $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$.
Quadrupling the number of drops roughly halves the typical error.
A hundred drops usually give $\pi$ correct to five decimal places.
Lazzarini's 1901 result, $\tfrac{355}{113}$, is widely regarded as too good to be true.
questions.explanation: The error goes like $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt N}$, so $4N$ drops give about half the error. A hundred drops typically miss by a tenth or more, nowhere near five decimals. Lazzarini's 3408 tosses should have had an error of about 0.05, so his six correct decimals are widely suspected of being arranged.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the Buffon's needle setup.

image.alt: Three horizontal parallel lines. A tilted needle lies between the top two lines with its center marked, a dashed vertical segment from the center down to the nearest line, an arc between the needle and a horizontal dashed reference line, and a double arrow between two lines at the left.

choices: Distance from the needle's center to the nearest line
Angle between the needle and the lines
questions.explanation: The double arrow is the spacing $d$; the dashed vertical segment from the center to the line below is $x$; the arc measures the acute angle $\theta$ between the needle and the lines; the thick segment is the needle, of length $\ell$.

questions.stem: Match each of Bertrand's ways of choosing a random chord to the probability that the chord is longer than a side of the inscribed equilateral triangle.
left: Two random endpoints on the circle
Random point on a random radius
questions.explanation: A chord is longer than the side $r\sqrt3$ when its distance from the center is under $\tfrac r2$. Random endpoints: the second endpoint must land on the far $120^\circ$ arc, $\tfrac13$. Random radius: the distance is uniform on $[0, r]$, $\tfrac12$. Random midpoint: the midpoint must land in a disk of half the radius, $\tfrac14$ of the area.

questions.stem: What is the main lesson of Bertrand's paradox?
choices: Geometric probability gives wrong answers for circles.
A probability isn't determined until you say exactly how the random choice is made.
The correct answer is always the average of the methods.
Chords can't be chosen at random.
questions.explanation: Each method is a different probability model, and each computes its own answer correctly. "At random" has to be made precise; which model fits depends on the physical situation.

questions.stem: A chord's midpoint is chosen uniformly at random in a disk of radius $r$ (Bertrand's method 3). What is the probability that the chord is longer than the radius?
questions.explanation: A chord at distance $t$ from the center has length $2\sqrt{r^2 - t^2}$, which exceeds $r$ when $t < \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}r$. The midpoint must land in a disk of that radius: $P = \left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac34$. $\tfrac23$ is method 1's answer and $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is method 2's.

questions.stem: Estimating a number by repeated random sampling, as in estimating $\pi$ with needles, is called the ___ method.
questions.explanation: The Monte Carlo method is named after the casino in Monaco. Today it runs on computers, which can simulate millions of random trials.

questions.stem: A case in which the hypothesis of a conjecture is true but its conclusion is false is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A counterexample satisfies the hypothesis and breaks the conclusion. One counterexample is enough to show a conjecture is false, but no number of examples proves one.

questions.stem: Start from the conditional "If a quadrilateral is a square, then it has four right angles." Match each related statement to its name.
left: If a quadrilateral has four right angles, then it is a square.
If a quadrilateral is not a square, then it does not have four right angles.
If a quadrilateral does not have four right angles, then it is not a square.
questions.explanation: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion. The inverse negates both. The contrapositive swaps and negates. Only the contrapositive is guaranteed to be true here; the converse and inverse are false (a 2-by-5 rectangle has four right angles but is not a square). A biconditional would be an "if and only if" statement.

questions.stem: The statement "If two angles are vertical angles, then they are congruent" is true. Which of these must also be true? Select all that apply.
choices: If two angles are not congruent, then they are not vertical angles.
If two angles are congruent, then they are vertical angles.
If two angles are not vertical angles, then they are not congruent.
Any two vertical angles are congruent.
Two angles are vertical angles if and only if they are congruent.
questions.explanation: The first choice is the contrapositive, which always has the same truth value as the conditional. "Any two vertical angles are congruent" is the same statement in different words. The second is the converse and the third is the inverse; both are false, because two $40^\circ$ angles in different corners of a page are congruent but not vertical. The biconditional needs the converse, so it is false too.

questions.stem: The diagram pictures the true statement "If a quadrilateral is a square, then it is a rectangle." The outer box holds all quadrilaterals. Name the numbered regions.

image.alt: Inside a box, a large oval contains a smaller circle. A small square is drawn inside the circle, a long thin rectangle inside the oval but outside the circle, and a trapezoid outside the oval. Marker 1 is in the circle, marker 2 in the oval outside the circle, and marker 3 outside the oval.

questions.explanation: A true conditional puts the hypothesis set (squares, 1) inside the conclusion set (rectangles). Region 2 holds rectangles that are not squares, such as a 2-by-5 rectangle; each one is a counterexample to the converse. Region 3 holds quadrilaterals that are not rectangles, such as a trapezoid. There is no region for "squares that are not rectangles", because the conditional is true.

questions.stem: Twenty points are marked on a circle and every pair is joined by a segment. How many segments are there? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Each of the 20 points joins the 19 others, giving $20 \cdot 19 = 380$ ends of segments, but every segment has two ends, so there are $\tfrac{20 \cdot 19}{2} = 190$ segments.

questions.stem: Match each argument to the rule it uses or the error it makes.
left: If an angle is obtuse, it measures more than $90^\circ$. $\angle K$ is obtuse. So $m\angle K > 90^\circ$.
If a figure is a square, it has four sides. Figure $F$ has four sides. So $F$ is a square.
questions.explanation: The first argument meets the hypothesis and detaches the conclusion: detachment. The second chains two conditionals whose middle parts match: syllogism. The third starts from the conclusion of the conditional and runs it backward, which is affirming the consequent; $F$ could be a rectangle or a trapezoid.

questions.stem: Match each step to the property that justifies it.
left: If $m\angle 1 = m\angle 2$ and $m\angle 2 = m\angle 3$, then $m\angle 1 = m\angle 3$.
questions.explanation: Symmetric flips one equation. Transitive links two equations through the shared middle quantity $m\angle 2$. Reflexive says anything is congruent (or equal) to itself. Substitution replaces $x$ by the equal value 7 inside a larger expression.

questions.stem: Put the statements of this algebraic proof in order, from the given equation to the conclusion.
questions.explanation: Given; distributive property; subtraction property (subtract $2x$); subtraction property (subtract 8); division property (divide by 2). Each statement is the only one that follows from the one before it. Check: $4(-7 + 2) = -20$ and $2(-7) - 6 = -20$.

questions.stem: The diagram pictures the chain "If a quadrilateral is a square, then it is a rhombus" and "If a quadrilateral is a rhombus, then its diagonals are perpendicular." The outer box holds all quadrilaterals. Name the numbered regions.

image.alt: Inside a box, three nested regions: a large oval, a smaller oval inside it, and a circle inside that. A square with its diagonals is in the circle (marker 1), a rhombus with unequal perpendicular diagonals is in the middle oval (marker 2), a kite with perpendicular diagonals is in the large oval only (marker 3), and a rectangle whose diagonals are not perpendicular is outside all three (marker 4).

choices: Perpendicular diagonals but not a rhombus
questions.explanation: Each true conditional puts its hypothesis set inside its conclusion set, so squares (1) sit inside rhombuses (2), which sit inside the quadrilaterals with perpendicular diagonals (3). Following the nesting from 1 to 3 is the Law of Syllogism: every square has perpendicular diagonals. The kite in region 3 shows the converse fails, and the rectangle (4) has diagonals that are not perpendicular. No square lies outside the rhombus region.

questions.stem: You know the true statement "If two angles form a linear pair, then they are supplementary." Which conclusions are valid? Select all that apply.
choices: $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ form a linear pair, so they are supplementary.
$\angle 3$ and $\angle 4$ are supplementary, so they form a linear pair.
$\angle 5$ and $\angle 6$ are not supplementary, so they do not form a linear pair.
$\angle 7$ and $\angle 8$ do not form a linear pair, so they are not supplementary.
questions.explanation: The first is the Law of Detachment. The third uses the contrapositive ("if not supplementary, then not a linear pair"), which is true whenever the conditional is. The second affirms the consequent and the fourth uses the inverse: supplementary angles can sit in different places, such as $100^\circ$ and $80^\circ$ angles in two corners of a page.

questions.stem: From "If $p$, then $q$" and "If $q$, then $r$", the Law of ___ lets you conclude "If $p$, then $r$."
questions.explanation: The Law of Syllogism chains two conditionals when the conclusion of the first matches the hypothesis of the second.

questions.stem: Put the statements of the proof of the Vertical Angles Theorem in order.
choices: $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ form a linear pair; $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$ form a linear pair.
$\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ are supplementary; $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$ are supplementary.
questions.explanation: Given; definition of linear pair (opposite rays in the diagram); Linear Pair Postulate; Congruent Supplements Theorem. Each step needs the one before it: you can't call the angles supplementary until you know they form linear pairs.

questions.stem: $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ are complementary, and $\angle C$ and $\angle B$ are complementary. If $m\angle A = 28^\circ$, then $m\angle C$ is ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: By the Congruent Complements Theorem, complements of the same angle are congruent, so $m\angle C = m\angle A = 28^\circ$. (Directly: $m\angle B = 90^\circ - 28^\circ = 62^\circ$, so $m\angle C = 90^\circ - 62^\circ = 28^\circ$.)

questions.stem: Given: $M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. Prove: $AM = \tfrac{1}{2}AB$. Match each statement of the proof to its reason.
questions.explanation: The definition of midpoint turns the geometry word into the equation $AM = MB$. Segment addition gives $AM + MB = AB$. Substituting $AM$ for $MB$ gives $AM + AM = AB$, that is $2 \cdot AM = AB$, and dividing both sides by 2 gives $AM = \tfrac12 AB$.

questions.stem: Which of these may be used as a reason in a geometric proof? Select all that apply.
choices: The angles look congruent in the diagram
The statement you are trying to prove
questions.explanation: Allowed reasons are given information, definitions, postulates, properties and previously proved theorems. Appearance in a diagram is never a reason for a measure or congruence, and using the statement you are proving assumes the conclusion.

questions.stem: In the flowchart version of the proof of the Vertical Angles Theorem, two arrows lead into the box "$\angle 1 \cong \angle 3$". Why two?
choices: The theorem is proved twice, once from each side.
Each arrow is a separate case, and either one alone would be enough.
The Congruent Supplements Theorem needs both supplementary pairs.
The arrows show the order in which the statements were discovered.
questions.explanation: Arrows show what each statement depends on. The Congruent Supplements Theorem needs two angles that are each supplementary to the same angle, so the conclusion depends on both "$\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ are supplementary" and "$\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$ are supplementary".

questions.stem: How many rows does a truth table need for a compound statement built from $p$, $q$ and $r$?
questions.explanation: Each simple statement can be T or F, and each one doubles the number of cases: $2^3 = 8$. 6 comes from $2 \cdot 3$, 9 from $3^2$.

questions.stem: A compound statement that is true in every row of its truth table, such as $p \vee \sim p$, is called a ___.
questions.explanation: A tautology is true in every case. A statement that is false in every case, such as $p \wedge \sim p$, is a contradiction.

questions.stem: When is the disjunction $p \vee q$ false?
choices: When exactly one part is false
questions.explanation: "Or" in logic is inclusive: $p \vee q$ is true when at least one part is true, including when both are. It is false only when both parts are false.

questions.stem: Which is the negation of "If $\angle A$ is a right angle, then $m\angle A = 90^\circ$"?
choices: $\angle A$ is a right angle and $m\angle A \ne 90^\circ$.
If $\angle A$ is not a right angle, then $m\angle A \ne 90^\circ$.
If $\angle A$ is a right angle, then $m\angle A \ne 90^\circ$.
If $m\angle A \ne 90^\circ$, then $\angle A$ is not a right angle.
questions.explanation: A conditional is false only when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion is false, so $\sim(p \to q) \equiv p \wedge \sim q$. The second choice is the inverse, the fourth is the contrapositive (equivalent to the original, not its negation), and the third is another conditional that is true whenever $\angle A$ is not a right angle.

questions.stem: Which is the negation of "All rectangles are squares"?
choices: Some rectangle is not a square.
Some square is not a rectangle.
questions.explanation: To negate "All A are B", switch to "some" and negate what follows: some A is not B. "No rectangle is a square" is the opposite extreme: it is false (a square is a rectangle), just like the original, so it can't be the negation, which always has the opposite truth value. "All squares are rectangles" is the converse.

questions.stem: Match each negation to an equivalent statement.
choices: if not p, then not q
questions.explanation: De Morgan's laws: "not both" is "at least one fails", and "not either" is "both fail". A conditional fails only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. Negating twice returns the original. "If not $p$, then not $q$" is the inverse, which is not the negation of anything here.

questions.stem: Which argument forms are valid? Select all that apply.
choices: From $p \to q$ and $\sim q$, conclude $\sim p$.
From $p \to q$ and $\sim p$, conclude $\sim q$.
From $p \to q$ and $q \to r$, conclude $p \to r$.
questions.explanation: Valid: modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism and the Law of Syllogism. The second is affirming the consequent and the fourth is denying the antecedent; in each, the row with $p$ false and $q$ true makes the premises true and the conclusion false.

questions.stem: If $p$ is true, $q$ is false and $r$ is true, then $(p \vee q) \to (q \wedge r)$ is ___. (Type true or false.)
questions.explanation: $p \vee q$ is true (because $p$ is). $q \wedge r$ is false (because $q$ is). A conditional with a true hypothesis and a false conclusion is false.

questions.stem: Put the steps of testing an argument with a truth table in order.
choices: List the simple statements in the argument.
Write every combination of T and F as a row.
Fill in a column for each premise and for the conclusion.
Mark the rows where every premise is true.
Check whether the conclusion is true in every marked row.
questions.explanation: You can't write the rows until you know the statements, can't mark rows until the premise columns are filled in, and can only judge the conclusion in the marked rows. If it is true in all of them, the argument is valid; a marked row with a false conclusion is a counterexample.

questions.stem: "If two angles are vertical angles, then they are congruent. $\angle P$ and $\angle Q$ are not congruent. Therefore $\angle P$ and $\angle Q$ are not vertical angles." Which describes this argument?
choices: Valid: it is the Law of Syllogism.
questions.explanation: The form is $p \to q$; $\sim q$; therefore $\sim p$. That is modus tollens, which is valid: it is detachment applied to the contrapositive "if not congruent, then not vertical".

questions.stem: Which statement is logically equivalent to $p \to q$?
questions.explanation: $\sim p \vee q$ is false only when $\sim p$ and $q$ are both false, that is, when $p$ is true and $q$ is false: exactly the row where $p \to q$ is false. $p \vee \sim q$ is equivalent to the converse $q \to p$, and $\sim p \wedge q$ is true in only one row.

questions.stem: Which statements mean the same as "Not every angle in the figure is acute"? Select all that apply.
choices: Some angle in the figure is not acute.
There is at least one angle in the figure that is not acute.
No angle in the figure is acute.
Every angle in the figure is obtuse.
questions.explanation: "Not every A is B" is "some A is not B", which can also be said as "there is at least one A that is not B". "No angle is acute" and "every angle is obtuse" are much stronger: a figure with one right angle and two acute angles makes the original true but both of those false.

questions.stem: "If a polygon has three sides, then it is a quadrilateral. Polygon $ABC$ has three sides. Therefore $ABC$ is a quadrilateral." Which describes this argument?
choices: Invalid, because the conclusion is false
Sound, because it uses modus ponens
Invalid, because it affirms the consequent
Valid but not sound, because a premise is false
questions.explanation: The form is modus ponens ($p \to q$; $p$; so $q$), so the argument is valid. But the first premise is false (a three-sided polygon is a triangle), so the argument is not sound, and its false conclusion is no surprise. A false conclusion does not by itself make an argument invalid.

questions.stem: To prove "If $p$, then $q$" by contrapositive, which statement do you prove directly?
questions.explanation: The contrapositive $\sim q \to \sim p$ is logically equivalent to $p \to q$, so proving it proves the original. Proving the converse ($q \to p$) or the inverse proves nothing about the original, and "$p$ and not $q$" is the negation, which is what a proof by contradiction would assume.

questions.stem: An indirect proof of "A triangle has at most one obtuse angle" begins by assuming what?
choices: A triangle has at least two obtuse angles.
A triangle has no obtuse angles.
A triangle has exactly one obtuse angle.
Every angle of a triangle is acute.
questions.explanation: An indirect proof assumes the negation of the statement. The negation of "at most one" is "at least two". (The contradiction comes in Module 4: two obtuse angles already add to more than $180^\circ$.)

questions.stem: A proof by contradiction is also called an ___ proof.
questions.explanation: It proves a statement indirectly, by showing that its negation leads to something impossible.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the proof that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational in order.
choices: Assume $\sqrt{2} = \tfrac{a}{b}$ with the fraction in lowest terms.
Then $a^2 = 2b^2$, so $a^2$ is even and $a$ is even.
Both $a$ and $b$ are even, which contradicts lowest terms.
So $\sqrt{2}$ cannot be written as a fraction of whole numbers.
questions.explanation: The assumption comes first, then the chain of consequences ($a$ even must be known before writing $a = 2c$, which is needed to show $b$ even), then the contradiction, then the conclusion that the assumption was false.

questions.stem: Match each proof outline to its method.
left: Assume the statement is false and reason until something impossible appears.
To show "if $p$, then $q$", show "if not $q$, then not $p$".
Show the result separately for even $n$ and for odd $n$.
Start from the givens and chain forward to the conclusion.
questions.explanation: Contradiction assumes the negation; contrapositive proves the equivalent statement $\sim q \to \sim p$; cases split the possibilities and handle each; a direct proof goes straight from hypothesis to conclusion. Induction (base case plus inductive step) matches none of these outlines.

questions.stem: You want to prove a fact about every angle $\angle A$ with $0^\circ < m\angle A \le 180^\circ$ by cases. Which lists of cases cover every possibility? Select all that apply.
choices: $\angle A$ is acute; right; obtuse; straight
questions.explanation: Cases must leave no gap; they may overlap. The first and third lists cover every measure from just above $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$. The fourth overlaps at exactly $90^\circ$, which is allowed. The second misses the right angle, $m\angle A = 90^\circ$.

questions.stem: What is the negation of "Neither $\angle 1$ nor $\angle 2$ is a right angle"?
choices: At least one of $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ is a right angle.
$\angle 1$ is a right angle and $\angle 2$ is not.
questions.explanation: "Neither is right" means "$\angle 1$ is not right and $\angle 2$ is not right". By De Morgan's law its negation is "$\angle 1$ is right or $\angle 2$ is right", that is, at least one is right. "Both are right" is only one of the ways that can happen.

questions.stem: Which statement can be proved by giving a single example?
choices: No two vertical angles are supplementary.
Some angle is congruent to its own complement.
questions.explanation: "Some angle is …" is an existential statement, so one example proves it: a $45^\circ$ angle has a $45^\circ$ complement. The two universal statements need general arguments. "No two vertical angles are supplementary" is a universal claim too, and it is false: two $90^\circ$ vertical angles are supplementary.

questions.stem: In the proof that an odd number has an odd square, $n = 2k + 1$ gives $n^2 = 2m + 1$, where $m =$ ___ (write $m$ in terms of $k$).
questions.explanation: $n^2 = (2k + 1)^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$, so $m = 2k^2 + 2k$. Since $m$ is a whole number, $n^2$ is one more than an even number, so it is odd.

questions.stem: A student wants to prove "If two angles are congruent, then they are vertical angles." She correctly proves that vertical angles are congruent. What has she shown?
choices: Only the converse, which says nothing about the original
That the original statement is false
questions.explanation: She proved "if vertical, then congruent", the converse of her statement. A conditional and its converse are independent. Her original statement is in fact false (two congruent angles can be far apart), but proving the converse doesn't show that either.

questions.stem: In the indirect proof that two distinct lines meet in at most one point, what does the assumption contradict?
choices: The given fact that the lines are distinct, because exactly one line passes through two points
The Linear Pair Postulate, because the lines would form a straight angle
The Ruler Postulate, because the points would have no distance between them
The definition of parallel lines, because the lines would not intersect
questions.explanation: Assuming the lines share two points $P$ and $Q$, both lines pass through $P$ and $Q$. Exactly one line does, so the two lines are the same, contradicting the given fact that they are distinct.

questions.stem: A proof by cases shows $n^2 + n$ is even for every whole number $n$. Which fact finishes the case where $n$ is odd?
choices: $n^2 + n$ is odd plus odd, which is odd.
questions.explanation: $n^2 + n = n(n + 1)$. If $n$ is odd, then $n + 1$ is even, and a product with an even factor is even. (Odd plus odd is actually even, so the last choice has its arithmetic wrong.)

questions.stem: Why does Example 1 of the lesson prove "if $\angle 1 \not\cong \angle 2$, then neither angle is right" by contrapositive instead of directly?
choices: The statement is false, so it can't be proved directly.
A contrapositive proof is shorter than every direct proof.
Direct proofs can't use the Linear Pair Postulate.
"Not congruent" gives no equation to work with, but "one angle is right" gives $m = 90^\circ$.
questions.explanation: The contrapositive turns two negative statements into positive ones: "at least one angle is right" supplies a measure of $90^\circ$, and "congruent" is the goal. Contrapositive proofs aren't always shorter; they help when the negated conclusion gives you something concrete to use.

questions.stem: Which two parts make up a proof by mathematical induction?
choices: Checking several cases and finding a pattern
Assuming the statement is false and reaching a contradiction
Proving the converse and the contrapositive
A base case and an inductive step
questions.explanation: The base case proves the first case; the inductive step proves that each case implies the next. Checking cases is inductive reasoning, which proves nothing; the second choice describes proof by contradiction.

questions.stem: In the inductive step you assume that $P(k)$ is true. This assumption is called the inductive ___.
questions.explanation: The inductive hypothesis is the "if" part of the conditional $P(k) \to P(k + 1)$ that the inductive step proves.

questions.stem: Ten lines are drawn in a plane so that no two are parallel and no three pass through one point. Into how many regions do they divide the plane? Give only the number.
Find $1 + 3 + 5 + \dots + 39$. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The last term $39 = 2n - 1$ gives $n = 20$ odd numbers, and the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is $n^2 = 400$.

questions.stem: Put the inductive step for "$n$ points have $\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ connecting segments" in order.
choices: Add one more point; it joins each of the $k$ old points, adding $k$ segments.
With the base case $n = 2$, the formula holds for every $n \ge 2$.
questions.explanation: The step starts from the inductive hypothesis, counts what the new point adds, and simplifies to the formula for $k + 1$. Only then, together with the base case, does induction give the result for every $n$.

questions.stem: Five lines in general position divide the plane into 16 regions. A sixth line is added, still in general position. How many new regions does it create?
questions.explanation: The new line crosses the 5 old lines at 5 different points, which cut it into 6 pieces. Each piece splits a region in two, so it adds 6 regions: $16 + 6 = 22 = \tfrac{6 \cdot 7}{2} + 1$. Answering 5 counts crossing points instead of pieces.

questions.stem: The formula $\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2} + 1$ for the regions made by $n$ lines needs which conditions? Select all that apply.
choices: No two of the lines are parallel.
No three of the lines pass through one point.
All of the lines pass through one common point.
Every pair of lines is perpendicular.
questions.explanation: The inductive step needs the new line to cross every old line (no parallels) at points that are all different (no three concurrent). If all lines passed through one point, $n$ lines would make only $2n$ regions, and three or more lines can't all be pairwise perpendicular in a plane.

questions.stem: A student "proves" that $n^2 + n + 1$ is even for every $n \ge 1$. Her inductive step correctly shows that if $k^2 + k + 1$ is even, so is $(k+1)^2 + (k+1) + 1$. What is wrong?
choices: The base case fails: $1^2 + 1 + 1 = 3$ is odd.
The inductive step is wrong, because $2k + 2$ is odd.
Induction can't be used for statements about even numbers.
questions.explanation: The step is fine: $(k+1)^2 + (k+1) + 1 = (k^2 + k + 1) + (2k + 2)$, and $2k + 2$ is even. But the base case is false, so the dominoes never start. In fact $n^2 + n = n(n+1)$ is always even, so $n^2 + n + 1$ is always odd.

questions.stem: Match each count to its formula.
left: Segments joining every pair of $n$ points
Regions made by $n$ lines in general position
Sum of the first $n$ odd numbers
questions.explanation: These are the three results proved by induction in the lesson. Powers of 2 come from the doubling pattern, which looked right for small cases but fails for both the lines and the circle regions.

questions.stem: Suppose the base case $P(1)$ and the inductive step are proved, but $P(n)$ fails for some $n$. Let $m$ be the smallest such $n$. Why is that impossible?
choices: Because $m$ would have to be negative
Because $P(m - 1)$ is true, and the inductive step then makes $P(m)$ true
Because the inductive hypothesis assumes $P(m)$ is true
Because there is no smallest whole number
questions.explanation: $m \ne 1$ because the base case holds, so $m - 1 \ge 1$. Since $m$ is the smallest failure, $P(m - 1)$ is true, and the inductive step gives $P(m)$, a contradiction. The argument relies on the well-ordering principle: every nonempty set of whole numbers does have a smallest member.

questions.stem: Seven points on a circle are joined in every possible way, with no three chords meeting at one point. Using $1 + \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2} + \tfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}{24}$, how many regions are inside the circle?
questions.explanation: $1 + \tfrac{7 \cdot 6}{2} + \tfrac{7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4}{24} = 1 + 21 + 35 = 57$. The doubling pattern would predict $2^6 = 64$, which is wrong.

questions.stem: A 5-by-5 square of unit squares is turned into a 6-by-6 square by adding an L-shaped layer. How many unit squares are in the layer? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The layer around a $k$-by-$k$ square has $2k + 1$ squares: here $2 \cdot 5 + 1 = 11$. Check: $36 - 25 = 11$.

questions.stem: The joke "proof" that all horses are the same color says: in a group of $k + 1$ horses, the first $k$ match and the last $k$ match, and the two groups overlap, so all match. For which step does this break?
choices: It never breaks; the base case is the problem.
questions.explanation: With $k + 1 = 2$ horses, "the first 1" and "the last 1" are different horses with no overlap, so nothing links their colors. For larger groups the overlap exists, but one broken link is enough to stop the chain. The base case (one horse matches itself) is fine.

questions.stem: Lines $\ell$ and $m$ are cut by transversal $t$, and one angle is shaded. Name how each numbered angle is related to the shaded angle.

image.alt: Two horizontal lines, l on top and m below, cut by a transversal t that slants up to the right. At the top intersection, the angle below l and to the left of t is shaded. Numbered markers sit in four other angles.

questions.explanation: The shaded angle is below $\ell$ and left of $t$, so it is an interior angle. Marker 1 (above $\ell$, right of $t$, same intersection) shares its vertex and is opposite it: a vertical angle. At the lower intersection, marker 2 (above $m$, left of $t$) is interior on the same side: consecutive interior. Marker 3 (above $m$, right of $t$) is interior on the opposite side: alternate interior. Marker 4 (below $m$, left of $t$) is in the same position as the shaded angle: corresponding. No marker is outside both lines, so none is alternate exterior, and the shaded angle's linear-pair partners are at the top intersection, next to it.

questions.stem: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Match each kind of angle pair to how its two angles are related.
questions.explanation: With parallel lines, corresponding angles are congruent (the postulate), and so are alternate interior and alternate exterior angles (theorems proved from it). Consecutive interior angles add to $180^\circ$. Complementary angles (sum $90^\circ$) play no role here.

questions.stem: $\ell \parallel m$, and consecutive interior angles measure $(4x + 12)^\circ$ and $(2x + 30)^\circ$. Put the steps for finding the angles in order.
questions.explanation: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary, so their sum is $180$. Then $6x = 138$, $x = 23$, and the angles are $4(23) + 12 = 104^\circ$ and $2(23) + 30 = 76^\circ$, which add to $180^\circ$.

questions.stem: $\ell \parallel m$, with the angles numbered as in the lesson's figure: at $\ell$, angles 1 and 2 are above the line and 3 and 4 below it (left to right), and angles 5–8 sit the same way at $m$. If $m\angle 2 = 65^\circ$, which angles also measure $65^\circ$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\angle 3$ is vertical to $\angle 2$, $\angle 6$ corresponds to $\angle 2$, and $\angle 7$ is its alternate exterior angle, so all three measure $65^\circ$. $\angle 4$ forms a linear pair with $\angle 2$, so it measures $180 - 65 = 115^\circ$.

questions.stem: Two lines are cut by a transversal, and a pair of corresponding angles measure $(5x - 20)^\circ$ and $(3x + 16)^\circ$. The lines are parallel exactly when each of these angles measures ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: By the Corresponding Angles Converse, the lines are parallel when the angles are congruent: $5x - 20 = 3x + 16$, so $2x = 36$, $x = 18$, and each angle is $5(18) - 20 = 70^\circ$. (18 is $x$, not the angle.)

questions.stem: Consecutive interior angles are also called ___ interior angles, because they lie on the same side of the transversal.
questions.explanation: "Consecutive interior" and "same-side interior" name the same pair: both angles are between the two lines and on the same side of the transversal. With parallel lines they are supplementary.

questions.stem: The picture shows a line with a shaded slope triangle, and a point $P$ with two segments drawn from it to the line. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A line on a grid rising to the right. Under its left end, a shaded right triangle has a dashed horizontal leg and a dashed vertical leg. From a point P below the line, a solid segment meets the line at a right angle, and a dotted segment runs from P to a point farther up the line.

choices: Distance from P to the line
questions.explanation: In the slope triangle the horizontal leg is the run and the vertical leg is the rise (here 4 and 3, so the slope is $\tfrac34$). The segment from $P$ that meets the line at a right angle is the shortest one, so its length is the distance from $P$ to the line; it meets the line at the foot of the perpendicular. Any other segment from $P$ to the line, like the dotted one, is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the perpendicular as a leg, so it is longer.

questions.stem: Match each pair of lines to how they are related.
questions.explanation: Equal slopes with different intercepts are parallel ($2$ and $2$). Slopes $2$ and $-\tfrac12$ multiply to $-1$: perpendicular. Slopes $2$ and $-2$ multiply to $-4$: neither. A vertical and a horizontal line are perpendicular. $2x - y = 2$ rearranges to $y = 2x - 2$, the same line. Skew lines are not in one plane, so two lines in the coordinate plane are never skew.

questions.stem: A line passes through $(-1, 4)$ and $(3, -2)$. As a fraction, the slope of a line perpendicular to it is ___.
questions.explanation: The slope of the given line is $\dfrac{-2 - 4}{3 - (-1)} = \dfrac{-6}{4} = -\dfrac32$. The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, $\dfrac23$. Check: $-\tfrac32 \cdot \tfrac23 = -1$.

questions.stem: Which lines are perpendicular to $y = -\tfrac34 x + 2$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular slope is $\tfrac43$. $y = \tfrac43 x - 1$ has it, and $4x - 3y = 6$ becomes $y = \tfrac43 x - 2$, slope $\tfrac43$ too. $3x + 4y = 8$ has slope $-\tfrac34$, so it is parallel; $y = -\tfrac43 x$ has the reciprocal without the sign change (product $1$, not $-1$).

questions.stem: Put the steps for writing the equation of the line through a given point perpendicular to a given line in order.
choices: Find the slope of the given line
Take the negative reciprocal to get the new slope
Put the point and the new slope into point-slope form
Solve for $y$ to get slope-intercept form
questions.explanation: You need the given slope before you can take its negative reciprocal, and you need the new slope and the point before you can write point-slope form, which is then rearranged into $y = mx + b$.

questions.stem: The distance from $(-1, 3)$ to the line $5x - 12y + 2 = 0$ is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $d = \dfrac{|5(-1) - 12(3) + 2|}{\sqrt{5^2 + 12^2}} = \dfrac{|-39|}{13} = 3$. Without the absolute value you would get $-3$, but a distance is never negative.

questions.stem: In the proof of the Corresponding Angles Converse, a line $\ell'$ through $P$ parallel to $m$ is constructed and shown to make the same angle with $t$ as $\ell$. Which fact then shows that $\ell'$ and $\ell$ are the same line?
choices: The Protractor Postulate: only one ray on a given side makes a given angle
The Ruler Postulate: points on a line can be matched with real numbers
