questions.explanation: $\ell$ and $\ell'$ both pass through $P$ and make angles of the same measure with the same ray of $t$, on the same side. The Protractor Postulate allows only one such ray, so the lines share a ray and coincide. The other facts say nothing about uniqueness of a ray.

questions.stem: In Book I of Euclid's Elements, which proposition is the first to use the parallel postulate?
choices: Proposition 16: an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than each remote interior angle
Proposition 27: congruent alternate angles imply parallel lines
Proposition 29: parallel lines make congruent alternate angles
questions.explanation: Propositions 16 and 27 are proved without the fifth postulate. Proposition 29, the forward direction ("parallel lines make congruent alternate angles"), is the first place Euclid uses it. Proposition 47 depends on it too, but comes much later.

questions.stem: Euclid proves "congruent alternate interior angles imply parallel lines" indirectly: if the lines met at $R$, they would form a triangle. Which fact about that triangle gives the contradiction?
choices: The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$
An exterior angle is greater than each remote interior angle
The base angles of an isosceles triangle are congruent
Any two sides add to more than the third side
questions.explanation: One of the congruent alternate interior angles is an exterior angle of the triangle and the other is a remote interior angle, so the Exterior Angle Inequality says one is strictly larger: a contradiction. The angle sum would also work in Euclidean geometry, but it depends on the parallel postulate, which Euclid was avoiding here.

questions.stem: Which statement can be proved in neutral geometry, that is, without the parallel postulate?
choices: The angles of every triangle add to exactly $180^\circ$.
Parallel lines cut by a transversal make congruent alternate interior angles.
Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel to the line.
Through a point not on a line there is at least one parallel to the line.
questions.explanation: Copy an angle to make congruent alternate interior angles; Euclid's Proposition 27 (proved without the fifth postulate) then says the new line is parallel. So a parallel always exists. Uniqueness ("exactly one") is the parallel postulate itself, and the forward theorem and the $180^\circ$ angle sum both depend on it.

questions.stem: $\ell \parallel m$. A path goes from $A$ on $\ell$ to a point $P$ between the lines and on to $B$ on $m$. The angles at $A$ and $B$ between the path and the lines, on the side toward which the path bends, are $34^\circ$ and $51^\circ$. Find $m\angle APB$.
questions.explanation: Draw the auxiliary line through $P$ parallel to $\ell$ and $m$. It splits $\angle APB$ into a $34^\circ$ part and a $51^\circ$ part (alternate interior angles), so $m\angle APB = 34 + 51 = 85^\circ$. $95^\circ$ is its supplement, $17^\circ$ is the difference, and $42.5^\circ$ is half the sum.

questions.stem: $\ell \parallel m$ and a path bends once at $P$ between them. At $A$ the angle between the path and $\ell$ on the side away from the bend is $140^\circ$; at $B$ the angle between the path and $m$ on the side toward the bend is $30^\circ$. Find $m\angle APB$.
questions.explanation: The bend theorem needs the angles that open toward the bend. At $A$ that angle is the supplement of $140^\circ$, namely $40^\circ$. So $m\angle APB = 40 + 30 = 70^\circ$. $170^\circ$ comes from adding $140 + 30$ (the wrong angle at $A$), $110^\circ$ from $140 - 30$, and $40^\circ$ is only the corrected angle at $A$.

questions.stem: $\ell \parallel m$ and a single bend at $P$ has $m\angle APB = (4x + 6)^\circ$. The angles at $A$ and $B$ that open toward the bend measure $(x + 20)^\circ$ and $(2x + 1)^\circ$. Find $m\angle APB$.
questions.explanation: Bend theorem: $4x + 6 = (x + 20) + (2x + 1) = 3x + 21$, so $x = 15$ and $m\angle APB = 4(15) + 6 = 66^\circ$. Check: $35 + 31 = 66$. The other choices are $x$ and the two smaller angles.

questions.stem: A student's proof begins: "Draw the line through $P$ that is parallel to $\ell$ and passes through the midpoint $M$ of $\overline{AB}$." What is wrong with this step?
choices: Nothing: any line may be added to a figure.
The line must meet two conditions, and the parallel through $P$ usually misses $M$, so such a line need not exist.
Lines through a midpoint cannot be parallel to anything.
Auxiliary lines must be perpendicular, not parallel.
questions.explanation: Exactly one line through $P$ is parallel to $\ell$, and exactly one line passes through both $P$ and $M$. Unless these happen to be the same line, no line meets both conditions, so the proof rests on an object that may not exist. An auxiliary line should be fixed by one condition.

questions.stem: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the bisectors of the two consecutive interior angles on one side meet at $P$. The angle between the bisectors at $P$ measures ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The consecutive interior angles add to $180^\circ$, so their halves add to $90^\circ$. The bisectors form a bend between the parallel lines, and by the bend theorem the angle at $P$ is the sum of the halves: $90^\circ$. This is true whatever the transversal's angle.

questions.stem: $\ell \parallel m$. A path from $\ell$ to $m$ switches between heading right and heading left at each of its two bends. The angles that open to the right are $30^\circ$ (where it leaves $\ell$) and $85^\circ$ (at the second bend); the angle at the first bend, opening left, is $50^\circ$. The acute angle where the path meets $m$, which opens left, measures ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Zigzag rule: right-opening angles total the same as left-opening ones, so $30 + 85 = 50 + x$ and $x = 65$. Check the long way: the segments make $30^\circ$, $50 - 30 = 20^\circ$ and $85 - 20 = 65^\circ$ with the parallels, and the last one meets $m$ at $65^\circ$.

questions.stem: Put the steps of Euclid's indirect proof that congruent alternate interior angles make the lines parallel in order.
choices: Assume the two lines are not parallel.
Then they meet at a point $R$, forming a triangle with the transversal.
One of the congruent angles is an exterior angle of that triangle, and the other is a remote interior angle.
By the Exterior Angle Inequality, the exterior angle is larger.
This contradicts the angles being congruent, so the lines are parallel.
questions.explanation: An indirect proof starts by assuming the opposite of the conclusion, follows the consequences (a triangle, then an exterior angle and a remote interior angle), applies a known theorem to reach a contradiction, and concludes the original statement.

questions.stem: Match each statement to whether it depends on the parallel postulate.
left: Congruent alternate interior angles imply parallel lines
Parallel lines make congruent alternate interior angles
An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than each remote interior angle
The angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees
Through a point off a line there is at least one parallel
questions.explanation: Euclid proved the Exterior Angle Inequality (I.16) and the converse (I.27) without the fifth postulate, and the converse gives the existence of parallels. The forward theorem (I.29) is his first use of the postulate, and the $180^\circ$ angle sum depends on it; in hyperbolic geometry both fail. All five statements are true in Euclidean geometry.

questions.stem: Which of these auxiliary objects can always be drawn in a plane (they exist and are unique)? Select all that apply.
choices: The line through a point $P$ parallel to a line $\ell$ not containing $P$
The segment joining two given points
The line through a point $P$ perpendicular to a line $\ell$
The line through $P$ parallel to $\ell$ that also passes through the midpoint of a given segment
questions.explanation: One parallel through an outside point (parallel postulate), one segment between two points, and one perpendicular through a point in a plane all exist and are unique, so each may be drawn in a proof. A line asked to satisfy a parallel condition and also pass through another chosen point is overdetermined and generally does not exist.

questions.stem: To prove the perpendicular slope rule, take $O = (0, 0)$, $A = (1, m_1)$ and $B = (1, m_2)$. What does the Pythagorean condition $OA^2 + OB^2 = AB^2$ simplify to?
questions.explanation: $OA^2 + OB^2 = 2 + m_1^2 + m_2^2$ and $AB^2 = m_1^2 - 2m_1 m_2 + m_2^2$. Setting them equal leaves $2 = -2m_1 m_2$, so $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

questions.stem: The lines $y = m x + b_1$ and $y = m x + b_2$ have the same slope and $b_1 \ne b_2$. Why do they never meet?
choices: Because a slope can only belong to one line
Because $mx + b_1 = mx + b_2$ would mean $b_1 = b_2$, which is false
questions.explanation: A common point would satisfy both equations, so $mx + b_1 = mx + b_2$; subtracting $mx$ leaves $b_1 = b_2$, a contradiction. Many lines share a slope, so the first choice is false; the sign of the intercepts is irrelevant; and equal slopes multiply to $m^2$, never $-1$ (slopes multiplying to $-1$ is the test for perpendicular lines).

questions.stem: The dot product $\langle 3, -2 \rangle \cdot \langle 4, 6 \rangle$ equals ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $3(4) + (-2)(6) = 12 - 12 = 0$. A zero dot product means the vectors are perpendicular: slopes $-\tfrac23$ and $\tfrac32$ multiply to $-1$.

questions.stem: Which vector is a normal vector (perpendicular) to the line $2x - 5y = 7$?
questions.explanation: For $Ax + By = C$ the normal vector is $\langle A, B \rangle = \langle 2, -5 \rangle$. $\langle 5, 2 \rangle$ is a direction vector: it runs along the line (slope $\tfrac25$). $\langle 2, 5 \rangle$ and $\langle -2, -5 \rangle$ are not multiples of $\langle 2, -5 \rangle$, so they are not normal vectors (their dot products with the direction vector $\langle 5, 2 \rangle$ are $20$ and $-20$, not $0$).

questions.stem: Which is the line through $(1, 4)$ parallel to $3x - 7y = 2$?
questions.explanation: Keep $A$ and $B$ and put in the point: $3x - 7y = 3(1) - 7(4) = -25$. $7x + 3y = 19$ is the perpendicular through $(1, 4)$; $3x - 7y = 25$ has a sign error; $3x - 7y = 2$ is the original line, which misses the point.

questions.stem: To the nearest tenth of a degree, what is the angle between the lines $y = x$ and $y = 3x$?
questions.explanation: Direction vectors $\langle 1, 1 \rangle$ and $\langle 1, 3 \rangle$: dot product $4$, lengths $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt{10}$. $\cos\varphi = \tfrac{4}{\sqrt{20}} \approx 0.894$, so $\varphi \approx 26.6^\circ$. ($45^\circ$ and $71.6^\circ$ are the two lines' angles with the $x$-axis, whose difference is the answer; $63.4^\circ$ is the complement.)

questions.stem: The angle between the lines $y = 3x$ and $y = -2x$ is ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Direction vectors $\langle 1, 3 \rangle$ and $\langle 1, -2 \rangle$: dot product $1 - 6 = -5$, lengths $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt5$. $\cos\varphi = \tfrac{|-5|}{\sqrt{50}} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $\varphi = 45^\circ$. (Without the absolute value you get $135^\circ$, the obtuse angle at the crossing.)

questions.stem: What is the foot of the perpendicular from $(5, 1)$ to the line $x + 2y = 2$?
questions.explanation: Write $x + 2y - 2 = 0$. Then $Ax_0 + By_0 + C = 5 + 2 - 2 = 5$ and $A^2 + B^2 = 5$, so $t = -1$ and the foot is $(5 - 1,\ 1 - 2) = (4, -1)$. Check: $4 + 2(-1) = 2$. $(6, 3)$ uses $t = +1$, $(3, -3)$ is the reflection (using $2t$), and $(2, 0)$ is on the line but not at the foot.

questions.stem: The reflection of the point $(5, 1)$ in the line $x + 2y = 2$ is the point (___, ___).
questions.explanation: Here $t = -\tfrac{5 + 2 - 2}{1 + 4} = -1$. The reflection is $(5 + 2t \cdot 1,\ 1 + 2t \cdot 2) = (3, -3)$. Its midpoint with $(5, 1)$ is $(4, -1)$, the foot of the perpendicular, which lies on the line.

questions.stem: What is the distance between the parallel lines $4x - 3y = 10$ and $8x - 6y = -5$?
questions.explanation: Divide the second equation by 2: $4x - 3y = -2.5$. In the form $Ax + By + C = 0$ the constants are $-10$ and $2.5$, so $d = \dfrac{|-10 - 2.5|}{\sqrt{16 + 9}} = \dfrac{12.5}{5} = 2.5$. Using $-5$ without scaling gives $3$ or $1$; $12.5$ forgets to divide by $5$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the foot of the perpendicular from $P(x_0, y_0)$ to a line in order.
choices: Write the line as $Ax + By + C = 0$
Move from $P$ along the normal vector: $F = (x_0 + tA,\ y_0 + tB)$
Check that $F$ satisfies the equation of the line
questions.explanation: You need $A$, $B$ and $C$ before computing $t$, and $t$ before finding $F$; the check comes last.

questions.stem: For the line $Ax + By = C$ and vectors $\vec u$, $\vec v$, match each expression to what it is.
choices: A normal vector of the line
A direction vector of the line
The cosine of the angle between two lines
questions.explanation: $\langle A, B \rangle$ is perpendicular to the line and $\langle B, -A \rangle$ runs along it. A zero dot product means perpendicular, and $\cos\varphi = \tfrac{|\vec u \cdot \vec v|}{|\vec u||\vec v|}$ gives the non-obtuse angle between lines with direction vectors $\vec u$ and $\vec v$. The slope of the line is $-\tfrac{A}{B}$, a number rather than a vector.

questions.stem: Which pairs of lines are perpendicular? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A vertical and a horizontal line are perpendicular. $\langle 2, 5 \rangle \cdot \langle 5, -2 \rangle = 10 - 10 = 0$. The normals $\langle 2, 3 \rangle$ and $\langle 3, -2 \rangle$ have dot product $6 - 6 = 0$. Slopes $2$ and $-2$ multiply to $-4$, so $y = 2x$ and $y = -2x$ are not perpendicular; and $2x + 3y = 1$, $2x + 3y = 7$ are parallel.

questions.stem: The slope formula $\tan\varphi = \left|\dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{1 + m_1 m_2}\right|$ for the angle between two lines cannot be used when…
choices: the lines cross at the origin
the slopes multiply to $-1$, or one line is vertical
questions.explanation: If $m_1 m_2 = -1$ the denominator is $0$ (the lines are perpendicular, and $\tan 90^\circ$ is undefined), and a vertical line has no slope. The cosine formula with direction vectors handles both cases.

questions.stem: Side $\overline{AC}$ of $\triangle ABC$ has been extended past $C$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Triangle ABC with side AC extended to the right past C. Four parts are marked: the angle at A, the interior angle at C, the angle outside the triangle at C between the extension and side CB, and the extension itself.

questions.explanation: 1 is the angle at $A$, one of the two interior angles not next to the exterior angle: a remote interior angle (the angle at $B$ is the other). 2 is the interior angle at $C$, which forms a linear pair with the exterior angle. 3 is the exterior angle, between the extension and side $\overline{CB}$. 4 is the extension of side $\overline{AC}$. By the Exterior Angle Theorem, angle 3 equals the sum of the angles at $A$ and $B$.

questions.stem: At each vertex of a triangle, one exterior angle is drawn. The three exterior angles add to ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Each exterior angle and its interior angle form a linear pair, so the three pairs total $3 \cdot 180^\circ = 540^\circ$. The interior angles use $180^\circ$ of that, leaving $540 - 180 = 360^\circ$ for the exterior angles.

questions.stem: Each line gives the three angles of a triangle. Match each triangle to its most specific classification by angles (an equiangular triangle is also acute, so choose the more specific name).
questions.explanation: Look at the largest angle. $130^\circ$ is obtuse, so that triangle is obtuse; $90^\circ$ makes a right triangle; with all angles less than $90^\circ$ a triangle is acute; and three equal angles make it equiangular (every equiangular triangle is also acute, but "equiangular" is the more specific name). "Scalene" classifies by sides, not angles.

questions.stem: Which of these triangles can exist? Select all that apply.
choices: A triangle with two right angles
questions.explanation: An obtuse isosceles triangle exists (for example $120^\circ, 30^\circ, 30^\circ$), and so does a right scalene one (for example $30^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$, whose sides all differ). An equilateral triangle has three $60^\circ$ angles, so it is never obtuse. Two right angles would already use up $180^\circ$, leaving $0^\circ$ for the third angle.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = (x + 10)^\circ$, $m\angle B = (2x)^\circ$ and $m\angle C = (3x - 10)^\circ$. Put the steps for classifying the triangle in order.
choices: All three angles are less than $90^\circ$, so the triangle is acute
questions.explanation: Each step uses the one before it: the angle sum gives the equation, which simplifies to $6x = 180$ and $x = 30$. Then $m\angle A = 40^\circ$, $m\angle B = 60^\circ$, $m\angle C = 80^\circ$ (check: $40 + 60 + 80 = 180$), and since the largest is less than $90^\circ$, the triangle is acute.

questions.stem: $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle PQR$. The side of $\triangle PQR$ that corresponds to $\overline{BC}$ is ___. Type its two letters.
questions.explanation: $B$ and $C$ are the second and third letters of $ABC$, so they match the second and third letters of $PQR$: $Q$ and $R$. The corresponding side is $\overline{QR}$.

questions.stem: $\triangle KLM \cong \triangle XYZ$. Match each part of $\triangle KLM$ to the corresponding part of $\triangle XYZ$.
questions.explanation: The letters pair up by position: $K \leftrightarrow X$, $L \leftrightarrow Y$, $M \leftrightarrow Z$. So $\angle L$ matches $\angle Y$, $\angle M$ matches $\angle Z$, $\overline{KM}$ (first and third letters) matches $\overline{XZ}$, and $\overline{LM}$ matches $\overline{YZ}$. Side XY would match $\overline{KL}$ and angle X would match $\angle K$, which aren't listed.

questions.stem: Which sets of facts prove $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$? Select all that apply.
choices: $\angle A \cong \angle D$, $\angle B \cong \angle E$, $\angle C \cong \angle F$
questions.explanation: Three pairs of sides is SSS. $\overline{AB}$, $\angle B$, $\overline{BC}$ is SAS, since $\angle B$ lies between those sides. $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{BC}$ and $\angle A$ is SSA: $\angle A$ is not between $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$, so it doesn't prove congruence. Three pairs of angles (AAA) gives the same shape but not necessarily the same size.

questions.stem: In this picture, $\angle A$ and side $\overline{AC}$ are fixed, and side $\overline{CB}$ has a fixed length but can swing. What does the picture show?

image.alt: Angle A with point C on its upper side. A dashed circle around C crosses the lower ray at two points, B1 and B2, and C is joined to both.

choices: SAS fails when the angle is acute
Every SSA triangle is a right triangle
questions.explanation: Triangles $AB_1C$ and $AB_2C$ share $\angle A$, side $\overline{AC}$ and a side of length $CB_1 = CB_2$ opposite $\angle A$, yet they are clearly different triangles. So two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do not force congruence. SAS is not involved, because the fixed angle is not between the two fixed sides.

questions.stem: For SAS to apply, the congruent angle must be the ___ angle: the angle formed by the two congruent sides.
questions.explanation: SAS needs the included angle, the angle between the two given sides. An angle that is not between them gives SSA, which is not a congruence test.

questions.stem: In each triangle, tick marks show sides and arcs show angles that match another triangle. Name the congruence test each one shows.

image.alt: Five numbered triangles. Triangle 1 has all three sides marked. Triangle 2 has two sides and the angle between them marked. Triangle 3 has two angles and the side between them marked. Triangle 4 has two angles and a side that is not between them marked. Triangle 5 is a right triangle with its hypotenuse and one leg marked.

questions.explanation: 1: three sides, SSS. 2: two sides with the marked angle between them, SAS. 3: two angles with the marked side between their vertices, ASA. 4: two angles and a side that is not between them, AAS. 5: a right angle with the hypotenuse and a leg, HL. SSA and AAA are not congruence tests, so none of the pictures shows them.

questions.stem: Given: $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$ at $D$, and $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$. Prove: $\overline{AD}$ bisects $\angle BAC$. Put the steps of the proof in order.
choices: $\angle ADB$ and $\angle ADC$ are right angles (definition of perpendicular)
questions.explanation: HL needs right triangles, so the right angles come first. Then the hypotenuses $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{AC}$ and the shared leg $\overline{AD}$ give the congruence. Only after that can CPCTC give $\angle BAD \cong \angle CAD$, and two congruent halves mean $\overline{AD}$ is the bisector.

questions.stem: Two right triangles have congruent legs, and their hypotenuses measure $2x + 7$ and $4x - 5$. If the triangles are congruent by HL, each hypotenuse is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Congruent hypotenuses: $2x + 7 = 4x - 5$, so $2x = 12$ and $x = 6$. Each hypotenuse is $2(6) + 7 = 19$ (check: $4(6) - 5 = 19$).

questions.stem: $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ have $\angle A \cong \angle D$ and $\angle B \cong \angle E$. Which one additional fact would prove the triangles congruent? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\overline{AB}$ lies between the two angles, so it gives ASA. $\overline{BC}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are not between them, so each gives AAS. $\angle C \cong \angle F$ follows anyway from the Third Angles Theorem, and three pairs of angles (AAA) only make the triangles the same shape.

questions.stem: Match each set of known matching parts to the congruence test it uses.
left: Two angles and the side between them
Two angles and a side not between them
The hypotenuse and a leg of two right triangles
Two sides and the angle between them
questions.explanation: The letters list the parts in order around the triangle: in ASA the side sits between the two angles, in AAS it doesn't, and in SAS the angle sits between the two sides. HL is the special test for right triangles. SSA (two sides and an angle not between them) is not a valid test.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this isosceles triangle. The tick marks show the two congruent sides.

image.alt: Isosceles triangle ABC with apex B; sides AB and CB carry tick marks. Marked are side AB, side AC, the angle at B and the angle at A.

questions.explanation: The congruent sides $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CB}$ are the legs, and the third side $\overline{AC}$ is the base. The angle between the legs (at $B$) is the vertex angle, and the angles at the ends of the base ($A$ and $C$) are the base angles. "Hypotenuse" belongs to right triangles.

questions.stem: The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle measures $52^\circ$. Each base angle measures ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The base angles are equal and share what's left: $\dfrac{180 - 52}{2} = \dfrac{128}{2} = 64$. Check: $52 + 64 + 64 = 180$.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CB}$, and $\overline{BD}$ bisects $\angle ABC$, meeting $\overline{AC}$ at $D$. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle CBD$ by SAS, and CPCTC gives $\angle A \cong \angle C$, $\overline{AD} \cong \overline{CD}$, and $\angle ADB \cong \angle CDB$; those last two form a linear pair, so each is $90^\circ$ and $\overline{BD} \perp \overline{AC}$. Nothing says the base $\overline{AC}$ equals a leg; that would make the triangle equilateral.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the proof of the Base Angles Theorem in order. ($\overline{AB} \cong \overline{CB}$ is given.)
choices: Draw the bisector of $\angle B$, meeting $\overline{AC}$ at $D$
questions.explanation: The bisector has to exist before you can say what it does, the congruent angles at $B$ are needed for SAS, and CPCTC can only come after the triangles are proved congruent.

questions.stem: Match each statement to the theorem it is.
left: A triangle with three congruent sides has three congruent angles
choices: Converse of the Base Angles Theorem
questions.explanation: Congruent sides give congruent opposite angles: the Base Angles Theorem. Going from congruent angles back to congruent sides is its converse. Applying the theorem to every pair of sides gives the corollary that an equilateral triangle is equiangular. The Third Angles Theorem compares two different triangles, and the Exterior Angle Theorem is about an angle outside the triangle.

questions.stem: In $\triangle PQR$, $m\angle P = 35^\circ$, $m\angle Q = 85^\circ$ and $m\angle R = 60^\circ$. Name each numbered side by its length compared with the others.

image.alt: Triangle PQR with angle P of 35 degrees, angle Q of 85 degrees and angle R of 60 degrees. The three sides are numbered: side QR, side PR and side PQ.

questions.explanation: Each side is opposite one angle, and larger angles face longer sides. Side 1, $\overline{QR}$, is opposite the $35^\circ$ angle at $P$, so it is shortest. Side 2, $\overline{PR}$, is opposite the $85^\circ$ angle at $Q$, so it is longest. Side 3, $\overline{PQ}$, is opposite the $60^\circ$ angle at $R$, the middle one. There's no hypotenuse: no angle is $90^\circ$.

questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle are 8 and 13. The third side is a whole number. How many lengths are possible for it? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The third side is strictly between the difference and the sum: $13 - 8 = 5 < x < 21 = 13 + 8$. The whole numbers allowed are 6 through 20, and there are $20 - 6 + 1 = 15$ of them.

questions.stem: Which sets of lengths can be the sides of a triangle? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Add the two shorter lengths and compare with the longest. $5 + 6 = 11 > 10$: yes. $3 + 4 = 7$, not more than 7: the figure collapses into a segment, so no. $2 + 9 = 11 > 10$: yes. $1 + 2 = 3 < 4$: no.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $m\angle A = 70^\circ$ and $m\angle B = 45^\circ$. Put the sides in order from shortest to longest.
questions.explanation: $m\angle C = 180 - 70 - 45 = 65^\circ$. Order the angles: $\angle B$ ($45^\circ$) < $\angle C$ ($65^\circ$) < $\angle A$ ($70^\circ$). The sides opposite them come in the same order: $\overline{AC}$ (opposite $B$), $\overline{AB}$ (opposite $C$), $\overline{BC}$ (opposite $A$).

questions.stem: Match each task to the theorem that handles it.
left: Order the sides of one triangle using its angles
Two pairs of congruent sides, different included angles: which third side is longer?
Two pairs of congruent sides, different third sides: which included angle is larger?
Decide whether three lengths can form a triangle
questions.explanation: Within one triangle, sides and opposite angles are ordered together (Side-Angle Inequality). Across two triangles with two pairs of congruent sides, the Hinge Theorem goes from angles to third sides and its converse goes from third sides to angles. Whether three lengths make a triangle is the Triangle Inequality Theorem.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$, $\angle A \cong \angle D$ (each $40^\circ$), $AC = DF = 6$, and $BC = EF = 8$, where $\overline{BC}$ and $\overline{EF}$ are opposite the $40^\circ$ angles. What can you conclude?
choices: The triangles are congruent by the Long Side SSA Theorem
The triangles are congruent by SAS
The triangles are congruent by HL
questions.explanation: The angle is not between the two given sides, so this is SSA, not SAS. But the side opposite the angle (8) is at least as long as the other given side (6), so the Long Side SSA Theorem applies and the triangles are congruent. HL needs right angles.

questions.stem: $\angle A$ is acute, $AC = 10$, and $C$ is 6 units from the other side of $\angle A$. How many different triangles $ABC$ have $BC = 8$?
questions.explanation: Here $d = 6$ and $b = 10$. Since $6 < 8 < 10$, the circle of radius 8 around $C$ crosses the other side of the angle twice, giving two triangles. (With $a < 6$ there would be none, with $a = 6$ one right triangle, and with $a \ge 10$ one triangle.)

questions.stem: Two triangles have two pairs of congruent sides and a pair of congruent angles that are not between those sides. In which situations must the triangles be congruent? Select all that apply.
choices: The angles are acute, and the side opposite each angle is longer than the other given side
The angles are acute, and the side opposite each angle is shorter than the other given side
questions.explanation: A right or obtuse angle is the largest angle of its triangle, so the side opposite it is automatically the longest, and the Long Side SSA Theorem applies (for a right angle this is HL). With an acute angle, the theorem applies when the opposite side is at least as long as the other side. If the opposite side is shorter, two different triangles may fit, so congruence is not guaranteed.

questions.stem: $\angle A$ is acute, $AC = 10$, and $C$ is 6 units from the other side of $\angle A$. There is exactly one triangle $ABC$ with $BC$ less than 10 when $BC =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: For $BC$ less than $AC = 10$, the circle of radius $BC$ around $C$ meets the other side of the angle twice if $BC > 6$, never if $BC < 6$, and exactly once (touching at the foot of the perpendicular) when $BC = 6$. That single triangle has a right angle at $B$.

questions.stem: The proof of the Long Side SSA Theorem starts from $\angle A \cong \angle D$, $\overline{AC} \cong \overline{DF}$, $\overline{BC} \cong \overline{EF}$ and $BC \ge AC$. Put its steps in order.
choices: $\triangle AGC \cong \triangle DEF$ by SAS, so $CG = EF = BC$
If $G \ne B$, the triangle formed by $C$, $B$ and $G$ is isosceles, so its base angles are acute
The angle at whichever of $B$, $G$ is nearer $A$ is obtuse in its triangle with $A$ and $C$, so $AC$ is longer than $BC$
This contradicts $BC \ge AC$, so $G = B$ and the triangles are congruent
questions.explanation: The point $G$ must be built before SAS can be used on it. SAS gives $CG = BC$, which is what makes the triangle $CBG$ isosceles. Its acute base angles make the supplementary angle obtuse, the obtuse angle faces the longest side, and that inequality contradicts the hypothesis.

questions.stem: $\angle A$ is acute, $AC = b$, $BC = a$, and $d$ is the distance from $C$ to the other side of $\angle A$. Match each case to the number of triangles.
questions.explanation: The third vertex is where the circle of radius $a$ around $C$ meets the ray. Shorter than $d$, the circle misses; equal to $d$, it touches at the foot of the perpendicular (a right angle at $B$); between $d$ and $b$, it crosses twice on the ray; at least $b$, the second crossing is at $A$ or behind it, leaving one triangle.

questions.stem: This picture shows the construction of a triangle from SSA. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Angle A with point C on its upper side. A dashed circle around C crosses the lower ray at B1 and B2, and a dashed perpendicular drops from C to the lower ray. Marked are the angle at A, segment AC, the circle and the perpendicular.

choices: Side next to the given angle
All points at distance a from C
Distance from C to the other side
questions.explanation: 1 is the given angle $\angle A$. 2 is $\overline{AC}$, the given side next to it. 3 is the circle of radius $a$ around $C$: the possible positions of $B$. 4 is the perpendicular from $C$ to the other side, whose length $d$ decides how many times the circle meets the ray. The sides opposite $\angle A$ are $\overline{CB_1}$ and $\overline{CB_2}$, which are not numbered.

questions.stem: Why is HL a special case of the Long Side SSA Theorem?
choices: The hypotenuse is between the right angle and the leg
The legs of a right triangle are always congruent
The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is longer than either leg
A right triangle has two acute angles
questions.explanation: In HL the known parts are the right angle, a leg (next to it) and the hypotenuse (opposite it). The right angle is the largest angle, so the hypotenuse is the longest side, longer than the leg. That's exactly the condition of the Long Side SSA Theorem. The hypotenuse is not between the right angle and the leg; it's opposite the right angle.

questions.stem: In the SSA construction with an acute $\angle A$, the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ is $F$, with $AF = 15$ and $CF = 8$. If $BC = 10$, what are the two possible lengths of $\overline{AB}$?
questions.explanation: The two positions of $B$ are the same distance from $F$, one on each side. By the Pythagorean theorem that distance is $\sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = 6$, so $AB = 15 - 6 = 9$ or $15 + 6 = 21$. Both are on the ray because $6 < 15$ (equivalently, $BC = 10$ is less than $AC = 17$). $5$ and $25$ use $10$ instead of $6$; $7$ and $23$ use $8$.

questions.stem: In the two-triangle SSA case, the third vertex can be $B_1$ or $B_2$. If $m\angle AB_1C = 112^\circ$, what is $m\angle AB_2C$?
questions.explanation: $CB_1 = CB_2$, so the triangle $CB_1B_2$ is isosceles and its base angles are equal. $\angle AB_1C$ forms a linear pair with the base angle at $B_1$, so the base angles are $180 - 112 = 68^\circ$, and $\angle AB_2C$ is the base angle at $B_2$: $68^\circ$. The two angles are supplementary, not congruent.

questions.stem: A student writes: "$\angle A \cong \angle D = 30^\circ$, $AC = DF = 9$, $BC = EF = 5$, with $\overline{BC}$ opposite $\angle A$, so $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$ by SSA." What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; SSA always works for acute angles
The side opposite the acute angle is the shorter one, so two different triangles may fit
The angle must be obtuse for any SSA argument
The student should have used SAS
questions.explanation: The angle is acute and the opposite side (5) is shorter than the adjacent side (9), the one situation where SSA can fail. Here $C$ is $9 \cdot \tfrac12 = 4.5$ from the other side of the $30^\circ$ angle (in a 30-60-90 triangle the short leg is half the hypotenuse, Module 6), and $4.5 < 5 < 9$, so two different triangles really do fit. SAS doesn't apply because the angle isn't between the given sides.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A$ is acute and $AC = 12$. Another triangle has a congruent angle and congruent sides matching $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BC}$. The smallest length of $\overline{BC}$ for which the Long Side SSA Theorem guarantees congruence is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The theorem needs the side opposite $\angle A$ to be at least as long as the other given side: $BC \ge AC = 12$. So the smallest such length is 12 (the case $BC = AC$, an isosceles triangle, is included).

questions.stem: Which statement about the history of the congruence tests is accurate?
choices: Euclid's Elements contains HL as a numbered proposition
Euclid proved SAS by superposition, and many modern axiom systems take SAS as an axiom instead
SSA was proved by Euclid for acute angles
Hilbert showed that SAS can be proved from SSS
questions.explanation: Euclid proved SAS (Book I, Proposition 4) by imagining one triangle laid on the other. Because that step is hard to justify from his postulates, axiom systems such as Hilbert's (1899) take a form of SAS as an axiom. HL and the Long Side SSA Theorem are not among Euclid's numbered propositions.

questions.stem: Three sides of a quadrilateral are 5, 6 and 15. Which range gives the possible lengths of the fourth side $s$?
questions.explanation: If $s$ is the longest side, $s < 5 + 6 + 15 = 26$. If 15 is the longest, $15 < 5 + 6 + s$, so $s > 4$. Together $4 < s < 26$. $9 < s < 21$ treats it like a triangle with sides 6 and 15; $0 < s$ forgets that 5 and 6 alone can't span 15.

questions.stem: Three sides of a quadrilateral are 2, 3 and 10. The smallest whole-number length the fourth side can have is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The longest given side, 10, must be shorter than the other three together: $10 < 2 + 3 + s$, so $s > 5$. The smallest whole number above 5 is 6. (The upper limit is $s < 15$.)

questions.stem: Put the steps of Euclid's proof that $AB + BC > AC$ in order.
choices: Triangle $BCD$ is isosceles, so $\angle BDC \cong \angle BCD$
$\angle ACD$ is larger than $\angle BCD$, so it is larger than $\angle ADC$
In $\triangle ACD$ the larger angle faces the longer side, so $AD > AC$
Since $AD = AB + BC$, conclude $AB + BC > AC$
questions.explanation: The point $D$ must exist before the isosceles triangle does; its base angles let you compare $\angle ACD$ with $\angle ADC$; the side–angle inequality turns that into $AD > AC$; and $AD = AB + BD = AB + BC$ finishes the proof.

questions.stem: A river runs along the $x$-axis. A path starts at $A(0, 2)$, touches the river at $P$, and ends at $B(9, 4)$. Which point $P$ makes the path shortest?
questions.explanation: Reflect $A$ to $A'(0, -2)$. The segment from $A'$ to $B(9, 4)$ has slope $\tfrac{6}{9} = \tfrac23$, so it is $y = \tfrac23 x - 2$, which crosses $y = 0$ at $x = 3$. $(4.5, 0)$ is just halfway along; $(6, 0)$ comes from swapping the roles of the two heights; $(0, 0)$ goes straight down from $A$.

questions.stem: This picture solves Heron's problem for a path from one point to the horizontal line and then to another point. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A horizontal line with two points above it. Below the line is a third point, joined by a dotted perpendicular segment to the upper left point. A dashed segment from the lower point to the upper right point crosses the line at a marked point, and the solid path runs from the upper left point to that crossing and on to the upper right point.

choices: Point that makes the path shortest
questions.explanation: 1 is $A$, the starting point, which is reflected across the line. 2 is its image $A'$: the dotted segment $\overline{AA'}$ is perpendicular to the line and bisected by it. 3 is $P$, where the straight segment from $A'$ to $B$ crosses the line; that point makes $AP + PB$ smallest. 4 is the mirror line $\ell$ that the path must touch.

questions.stem: In Heron's problem, $A'$ is the reflection of $A$ across $\ell$ and $P$ is the best point on $\ell$. Which statements are always true? Select all that apply.
choices: $P$ is halfway between the feet of the perpendiculars from $A$ and $B$ to $\ell$
questions.explanation: The best $P$ is where segment $\overline{A'B}$ crosses $\ell$, so $A'$, $P$, $B$ are collinear, and the equal angles follow (CPCTC plus vertical angles). $PA = PB$ and "halfway" are true only when $A$ and $B$ are the same distance from $\ell$; in general $P$ is nearer the point that is closer to the line.

questions.stem: $P$ is a point inside $\triangle ABC$, with $AB = 7$ and $AC = 9$. Which value could $PB + PC$ have?
questions.explanation: Euclid's theorem says $PB + PC < AB + AC = 16$. Only 15 is less than 16. Equality (16) would need $P$ at the vertex $A$, which is not inside the triangle.

questions.stem: $ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral. Where is the point $P$ that makes $PA + PB + PC + PD$ as small as possible?
choices: At the midpoint of the longest side
At the vertex with the largest angle
At the midpoint of the shorter diagonal
questions.explanation: $PA + PC \ge AC$ with equality only on $\overline{AC}$, and $PB + PD \ge BD$ with equality only on $\overline{BD}$. Both equalities hold at the intersection of the diagonals, where the total is $AC + BD$, its smallest possible value.

questions.stem: Match each result to the key idea in its proof.
choices: Extend a side to build an isosceles triangle
Reflect one point across the line
Apply the triangle inequality one step at a time
Extend BP to meet the opposite side
Draw a line parallel to one side
questions.explanation: Euclid extends $\overline{AB}$ by $BD = BC$ and uses the isosceles triangle $BCD$. Heron reflects $A$ to $A'$ so the broken path becomes comparable to a straight segment. A polygonal path is shortened one corner at a time. For an inside point, extending $\overline{BP}$ to $E$ on $\overline{AC}$ splits the comparison into two triangle inequalities. A parallel line is the idea behind the Triangle Angle Sum Theorem.

questions.stem: Convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ has $AB = 3$, $BC = 10$, $CD = 5$ and $DA = 6$. Using $AB + CD < AC + BD$ and $AD + BC < AC + BD$, what is the best lower bound for $AC + BD$?
questions.explanation: The first inequality gives $AC + BD > 3 + 5 = 8$, and the second gives $AC + BD > 6 + 10 = 16$. Both are true, so the stronger one, 16, is the best bound. 12 is half the perimeter (also true but weaker), and 24 is the whole perimeter, which is an upper bound.

questions.stem: A path goes from $A(0, 5)$ to a point on the $x$-axis and then to $B(24, 5)$. The shortest possible length of the path is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Reflect $A$ to $A'(0, -5)$. The shortest path has length $A'B = \sqrt{24^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{676} = 26$, touching the axis at $(12, 0)$ (halfway here, because $A$ and $B$ are the same height).

questions.stem: In Heron's problem, $\ell$ is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AA'}$, meeting it at $M$. Why is $PA = PA'$ for every point $P$ of $\ell$ other than $M$?
choices: Triangles $PMA$ and $PMA'$ are congruent by SAS
Triangles $PMA$ and $PMA'$ are congruent by SSS
The Triangle Inequality makes them equal
questions.explanation: The triangles share $\overline{PM}$, have right angles at $M$, and $AM = A'M$: two sides and the included angle, so SAS. Then CPCTC gives $PA = PA'$. SSS would need $PA = PA'$ already, which is what we want to prove.

questions.stem: For three points $A$, $B$, $C$, when is $AB + BC = AC$?
choices: When $\angle B$ is a right angle
questions.explanation: For a real triangle the inequality is strict. Equality means the "triangle" is degenerate: $B$ sits on $\overline{AC}$, so the path through $B$ is the straight segment itself. A right angle at $B$ gives $AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$, not $AB + BC = AC$.

questions.stem: The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle's sides meet at the ___, and the angle bisectors meet at the ___.
questions.explanation: Perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at the circumcenter, which is equidistant from the three vertices. Angle bisectors meet at the incenter, which is equidistant from the three sides.

questions.stem: Match each point to what it is equidistant from.
left: A point on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$
A point on the bisector of $\angle A$
choices: The two sides of angle A
The midpoints of the three sides
questions.explanation: The Perpendicular Bisector Theorem gives equal distances to the endpoints, and the Angle Bisector Theorem gives equal distances to the sides of the angle. The circumcenter is on all three perpendicular bisectors, so it is equidistant from all three vertices; the incenter is on all three angle bisectors, so it is equidistant from all three sides.

questions.stem: Which statements are true for every triangle? Select all that apply.
choices: The incenter lies inside the triangle.
The circumcenter lies inside the triangle.
The circumcenter is equidistant from the three vertices.
The incenter is equidistant from the three vertices.
questions.explanation: The incenter is always inside, and the circumcenter is always equidistant from the vertices. The circumcenter is outside an obtuse triangle (and on the hypotenuse of a right triangle), and the incenter is equidistant from the sides, not the vertices.

questions.stem: Put the steps for constructing the inscribed circle of a triangle in order.
choices: Construct the bisectors of two of the angles.
Mark the point $I$ where the two bisectors cross.
Construct the perpendicular from $I$ to one side.
Draw the circle centered at $I$ through the foot of that perpendicular.
questions.explanation: You need the incenter $I$ before you can drop a perpendicular from it, and you need the perpendicular to know the radius. The perpendicular segment's length is the distance from $I$ to the sides, which is the inradius.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. How far is its circumcenter from each vertex? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse is $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = 15$. A right triangle's circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so the circumradius is half of 15: $7.5$.

questions.stem: Name the numbered lines. Tick marks show equal lengths, and small squares show right angles.

image.alt: Triangle ABC with three segments from vertex C to side AB, and a dashed line through the midpoint of AB. Segment 1 meets AB at a right angle. Segment 2 splits angle C into two equal angles. Segment 3 ends at the midpoint of AB. Line 4 is dashed, passes through the midpoint of AB at a right angle, and misses C.

questions.explanation: 1 meets the opposite side at a right angle: an altitude. 2 splits angle $C$ into two equal parts (the matching arcs): an angle bisector. 3 goes from $C$ to the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ (the tick marks): a median. 4 passes through the midpoint at a right angle but needn't go through a vertex: the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$. A midsegment joins the midpoints of two sides, and none is drawn.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $G$ is the centroid and median $\overline{AD}$ has length 27. Then $AG =$ ___ and $GD =$ ___.
questions.explanation: The centroid is two-thirds of the way from the vertex: $AG = \tfrac23 \cdot 27 = 18$ and $GD = \tfrac13 \cdot 27 = 9$. Check: $18 = 2 \cdot 9$.

questions.stem: Match each triangle center to the lines that meet there.
questions.explanation: Circumcenter: perpendicular bisectors. Incenter: angle bisectors. Centroid: medians. Orthocenter: altitudes (or the lines containing them). The three midsegments form a triangle; they don't meet at one point.

questions.stem: Which statements are true for every obtuse triangle? Select all that apply.
choices: Its orthocenter lies outside the triangle.
Its centroid lies outside the triangle.
Two of its altitudes lie outside the triangle.
Its circumcenter lies inside the triangle.
questions.explanation: The altitudes from the two acute angles fall outside, onto extensions of the opposite sides, and the lines containing the altitudes meet outside, so the orthocenter is outside. The centroid is always inside (two-thirds of the way along each median, which lies inside the triangle). The circumcenter of an obtuse triangle is outside.

questions.stem: $\overline{DE}$ is a midsegment of $\triangle ABC$, parallel to $\overline{BC}$, and $BC = 19$. Find $DE$. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: A midsegment is half as long as the side it is parallel to: $DE = \tfrac12 \cdot 19 = 9.5$.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this pentagon.

image.alt: A convex pentagon. Marker 1 is on the left side. Marker 2 is on the upper left corner point. Marker 3 is on a dashed segment joining two corners that are not next to each other. Marker 4 is on a shaded angle inside the top corner. Marker 5 is on a shaded angle at the lower right corner, between one side and the dashed extension of the bottom side.

questions.explanation: 1 is one of the segments forming the polygon: a side. 2 is where two sides meet: a vertex. 3 joins two non-adjacent vertices: a diagonal. 4 is the angle inside the polygon at a vertex: an interior angle. 5 is formed by one side and the extension of the next: an exterior angle, which forms a linear pair with the interior angle there.

questions.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is $24^\circ$. How many sides does it have? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The exterior angles add to $360^\circ$ and are all equal, so $n = 360 / 24 = 15$.

questions.stem: Put these regular polygons in order from smallest to largest interior angle.
questions.explanation: Each interior angle of a regular $n$-gon is $180^\circ - \tfrac{360^\circ}{n}$, which grows with $n$: $60^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $108^\circ$, $135^\circ$, $162^\circ$.

questions.stem: Which of these could be the measure of each interior angle of a regular polygon? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Check the exterior angle: $360$ divided by it must be a whole number. $150^\circ$: exterior $30^\circ$, $n = 12$. $140^\circ$: exterior $40^\circ$, $n = 9$. $130^\circ$: exterior $50^\circ$, $360/50 = 7.2$. $100^\circ$: exterior $80^\circ$, $360/80 = 4.5$. So only $150^\circ$ and $140^\circ$ work.

questions.stem: Match each number of sides to the polygon's name.
questions.explanation: 5 pentagon, 7 heptagon, 9 nonagon, 12 dodecagon. A decagon has 10 sides and an octagon 8.

questions.stem: Which facts about quadrilateral $ABCD$ are enough, on their own, to prove it is a parallelogram? Select all that apply.
choices: Both pairs of opposite angles are congruent.
One pair of opposite sides is parallel and the other pair is congruent.
questions.explanation: Congruent opposite angles (both pairs) and diagonals that bisect each other are both parallelogram tests. "One pair parallel, the other pair congruent" describes an isosceles trapezoid too, and so do congruent diagonals, so neither is enough.

questions.stem: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DC}$ and $AB = DC$. Put the steps of the proof that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram in order.
choices: $\angle BAC \cong \angle DCA$, because they are alternate interior angles for $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{DC}$.
$\overline{BC} \parallel \overline{AD}$, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
questions.explanation: The diagonal must exist before you can name angles on it; the angle pair gives the A in SAS (with $AB = DC$ and the shared side $\overline{AC}$); CPCTC then gives the second pair of angles, which are alternate interior angles for $\overline{BC}$ and $\overline{AD}$, so those sides are parallel.

questions.stem: In $\square ABCD$, $m\angle A = 68^\circ$. Then $m\angle B =$ ___ degrees and $m\angle C =$ ___ degrees.
questions.explanation: Consecutive angles are supplementary: $m\angle B = 180 - 68 = 112^\circ$. Opposite angles are congruent: $m\angle C = 68^\circ$.

questions.stem: For a parallelogram, is each statement always true or not always true?
questions.explanation: The four parallelogram properties are congruent opposite sides, congruent opposite angles, supplementary consecutive angles and diagonals that bisect each other. Congruent diagonals belong to rectangles and perpendicular diagonals to rhombuses; a general parallelogram has neither.

questions.stem: Three vertices of $\square ABCD$ are $A(1, 1)$, $B(6, 2)$ and $C(8, 6)$. Where is $D$?
questions.explanation: The diagonals $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$ share a midpoint. The midpoint of $\overline{AC}$ is $(4.5, 3.5)$, so $D = (2 \cdot 4.5 - 6, 2 \cdot 3.5 - 2) = (3, 5)$. Equivalently $D = A + C - B$. $(13, 7)$ is $B + C - A$ and $(-1, -3)$ is $A + B - C$: those complete parallelograms with the vertices in a different order. $(4.5, 3.5)$ is the shared midpoint of the diagonals, not a vertex.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this trapezoid. Arrowheads mark parallel sides; tick marks show equal lengths.

image.alt: A trapezoid with a long bottom side and a short top side, both marked parallel. Marker 1 is on the bottom side. Marker 2 is on the right slanted side. Marker 3 is on a dashed segment joining the midpoints of the two slanted sides. Marker 4 is on the shaded angle at the bottom left corner.

questions.explanation: The parallel sides are the bases (1); the other two sides are the legs (2). The segment joining the midpoints of the legs is the midsegment (3), whose length is the average of the bases. The two angles along one base are base angles (4). No diagonal or altitude is drawn.

questions.stem: Which quadrilaterals always have perpendicular diagonals? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Rhombus diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular. A rectangle's diagonals are congruent but perpendicular only when it's a square; an isosceles trapezoid's diagonals are congruent but generally not perpendicular.

questions.stem: Match each quadrilateral to its definition in this course.
choices: A parallelogram with four right angles
A parallelogram with four congruent sides
A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides
Two pairs of congruent consecutive sides and no congruent opposite sides
A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides congruent
questions.explanation: Those are the definitions from the lesson. "Both pairs of opposite sides congruent" is a test for a parallelogram, not the definition of any of these four.

questions.stem: A trapezoid has bases 11 and 25. How long is its midsegment? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The midsegment is the average of the bases: $\tfrac{11 + 25}{2} = 18$.

questions.stem: Put these in order from the most general to the most specific, so that each is a special case of the one before it.
questions.explanation: Every square is a rhombus (four congruent sides), every rhombus is a parallelogram, and every parallelogram is a quadrilateral. None of the reverse statements is true.

questions.stem: In the proof that the centroid splits each median $2 : 1$, why is $MNDE$ a parallelogram?
choices: $\overline{MN}$ and $\overline{ED}$ are both parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and both half as long as $\overline{AB}$.
Its opposite angles at $G$ are vertical angles.
$M$, $N$, $D$ and $E$ are all midpoints of segments.
questions.explanation: $\overline{ED}$ is a midsegment of $\triangle ABC$ and $\overline{MN}$ is a midsegment of $\triangle ABG$, so both are parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and half its length. One pair of opposite sides both parallel and congruent makes a parallelogram. The diagonals' congruence isn't known, and $G$ is where the diagonals cross, not a vertex of $MNDE$. Being midpoints alone proves nothing.

questions.stem: Medians $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BE}$ meet at $G$; $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $\overline{AG}$ and $\overline{BG}$. Put the steps of the proof in order.
choices: $\overline{ED}$ and $\overline{MN}$ are midsegments, each parallel to $\overline{AB}$ and half as long.
Its diagonals bisect each other, so $MG = GD$.
The third median also meets $\overline{AD}$ two-thirds of the way from $A$, so it passes through $G$.
questions.explanation: The midsegments give the parallelogram; the parallelogram gives bisected diagonals; with $AM = MG$ that cuts the median into thirds; and since only one point of $\overline{AD}$ is two-thirds of the way from $A$, the third median must pass through it.

questions.stem: Medians $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BE}$ of $\triangle ABC$ meet at $G$, and $GD = 4$. How long is median $\overline{AD}$? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The proof shows $AM = MG = GD$, so the median is three times $GD$: $AD = 3 \cdot 4 = 12$ (and $AG = 8$).

questions.stem: In the picture, lines through $A$, $B$ and $C$ parallel to the opposite sides form $\triangle A'B'C'$. Why is $A$ the midpoint of $\overline{B'C'}$?

image.alt: A small triangle ABC inside a larger triangle A′B′C′, with A, B and C the midpoints of the big triangle's sides. The altitudes of ABC are dashed and meet at H.

choices: Because the altitude from $A$ is perpendicular to $\overline{B'C'}$.
Because $\triangle ABC$ is the medial triangle of every triangle.
Because $AB'CB$ and $AC'BC$ are parallelograms, so $AB' = BC = AC'$.
questions.explanation: Both quadrilaterals have both pairs of opposite sides parallel by construction, so they are parallelograms, and opposite sides give $AB' = BC$ and $AC' = BC$. A perpendicular through $A$ says nothing about lengths, and $A$ is generally not equidistant from $B$ and $C$.

questions.stem: Triangle $A'B'C'$ is formed by the lines through $A$, $B$ and $C$ parallel to the opposite sides of $\triangle ABC$. Which statements are true for every triangle $ABC$? Select all that apply.
choices: The altitudes of $\triangle ABC$ lie on the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of $\triangle A'B'C'$.
The orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$ is the circumcenter of $\triangle A'B'C'$.
The centroid of $\triangle ABC$ is the orthocenter of $\triangle A'B'C'$.
questions.explanation: The first three are the steps and conclusion of the orthocenter proof. The fourth is false in general: the orthocenter of $\triangle A'B'C'$ is a different point (the two triangles actually share the same centroid).

questions.stem: Find the orthocenter of the triangle with vertices $A(0, 0)$, $B(8, 0)$ and $C(10, 4)$.
questions.explanation: The altitude from $C$ is vertical: $x = 10$. $\overline{BC}$ has slope $\tfrac{4}{2} = 2$, so the altitude from $A$ has slope $-\tfrac12$: $y = -\tfrac12 x$, which gives $y = -5$ at $x = 10$. The orthocenter $(10, -5)$ is outside, below the triangle, since the angle at $B$ is obtuse. $(10, 5)$ is a sign slip, $(6, \tfrac43)$ is the centroid.

questions.stem: A triangle has circumcenter $O(2, 1)$ and centroid $G(4, 3)$. Its orthocenter is $H($___, ___$)$.
questions.explanation: $3G = H + 2O$, so $H = 3G - 2O = (12 - 4, 9 - 2) = (8, 7)$. Check: $G - O = (2, 2)$ and $H - G = (4, 4)$, twice as far in the same direction.

questions.stem: For the circumcenter $O$, centroid $G$ and orthocenter $H$ of a triangle that isn't equilateral, which is always true?
questions.explanation: From $G - O = \tfrac13(H - O)$, the centroid is one-third of the way from $O$ to $H$, so $OG : GH = 1 : 2$. The centroid sits closer to the circumcenter.

questions.stem: Match each result to the idea its proof in this lesson used.
left: The medians meet two-thirds of the way along each
A right triangle's circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse
choices: They are perpendicular bisectors of a larger triangle
Coordinates with the altitude from C on the y-axis
Completing the triangle to a rectangle
Points on angle bisectors are equidistant from the sides
questions.explanation: Those are the four proofs in the lesson. Equidistance from the sides is the idea behind the incenter (Lesson 15), not one of this lesson's proofs.

questions.stem: Which points always lie on the Euler line of a triangle that isn't equilateral? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The Euler line is defined by the circumcenter and orthocenter, and the centroid always lies between them. The incenter is on it only when the triangle is isosceles.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. How far is the vertex of the right angle from the circumcenter?
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse is 10 and the circumcenter is its midpoint $M$. Completing the triangle to a rectangle makes $\overline{CM}$ half of a diagonal, and the diagonals are congruent, so $CM = \tfrac12 \cdot 10 = 5$. 4.8 is the altitude to the hypotenuse ($\tfrac{6 \cdot 8}{10}$), not the distance to $M$.

questions.stem: $\triangle ABC$ has its right angle at $C$. Its orthocenter is the vertex ___. (Give the letter.)
questions.explanation: The legs $\overline{CA}$ and $\overline{CB}$ are altitudes (each is perpendicular to the other leg), and they meet at $C$. So all three altitude lines pass through $C$.

questions.stem: The last step of the proof that the altitudes are concurrent quotes which theorem?
questions.explanation: The altitude lines of $\triangle ABC$ are the perpendicular bisectors of $\triangle A'B'C'$, and the Circumcenter Theorem says those are concurrent. Midsegments appear earlier in the course but not in that step.

questions.stem: Join the midpoints of the sides of a rhombus that isn't a square. What shape do you get?
questions.explanation: The Varignon parallelogram's sides are parallel to the diagonals. A rhombus's diagonals are perpendicular, so the Varignon parallelogram has right angles: a rectangle. Its sides are half the diagonals, which differ unless the rhombus is a square, so it isn't a square.

questions.stem: A quadrilateral has diagonals of lengths 14 and 20. What is the perimeter of its Varignon parallelogram? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Two sides are $\tfrac12 \cdot 14 = 7$ and two are $\tfrac12 \cdot 20 = 10$, so the perimeter is $2(7 + 10) = 34$, the sum of the diagonals.

questions.stem: A convex quadrilateral has area 90. What is the area of its Varignon parallelogram? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The four corner triangles cut off by the Varignon parallelogram take half the area, so the parallelogram has the other half: 45.

questions.stem: Each picture shows only the diagonals of a convex quadrilateral. Matching tick marks show equal lengths and a small square shows a right angle; lengths without matching marks are not equal, and angles without a square are not right. Name each quadrilateral.

image.alt: Five pairs of crossing segments. 1: perpendicular; the horizontal one is cut in half, the vertical one is not. 2: perpendicular; each is cut in half, and they have different lengths. 3: not perpendicular; each is cut in half, and they have different lengths. 4: not perpendicular; they cut each other into a short piece and a long piece, with the two short pieces equal and the two long pieces equal. 5: not perpendicular; all four half-diagonals are equal.

questions.explanation: 1: one diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other, which isn't bisected: kite. 2: bisect each other and perpendicular, different lengths: rhombus. 3: bisect each other only: parallelogram. 4: same two lengths without bisecting: isosceles trapezoid. 5: bisect each other and congruent, not perpendicular: rectangle. A square would need all four halves equal and a right angle.

questions.stem: Match each fact about the diagonals of a convex quadrilateral to the shape it guarantees.
left: They bisect each other and are congruent.
They bisect each other and are perpendicular.
They bisect each other, are congruent and are perpendicular.
questions.explanation: Bisecting diagonals make a parallelogram; adding congruent diagonals makes it a rectangle, adding perpendicular ones makes it a rhombus, and both make a square. A kite's diagonals don't bisect each other.

questions.stem: Using only its diagonals, classify the quadrilateral $W(0, 0)$, $X(5, 1)$, $Y(6, 6)$, $Z(1, 5)$ as precisely as possible.
questions.explanation: Both diagonals have midpoint $(3, 3)$, so they bisect each other. $\overrightarrow{WY} = (6, 6)$ and $\overrightarrow{XZ} = (-4, 4)$ have dot product $-24 + 24 = 0$, so they're perpendicular. Their lengths are $\sqrt{72}$ and $\sqrt{32}$, not equal. Bisecting and perpendicular but not congruent: a rhombus, not a square.

questions.stem: Which facts about the diagonals of a convex quadrilateral guarantee that it is a parallelogram? Select all that apply.
choices: They are congruent and bisect each other.
questions.explanation: Bisecting each other is the parallelogram test (with congruence added, it's a rectangle, still a parallelogram). Perpendicular diagonals occur in kites, and congruent perpendicular diagonals occur in irregular quadrilaterals like Example 4, neither of which is a parallelogram.

questions.stem: Which quadrilateral is a counterexample to "A quadrilateral with congruent diagonals is a rectangle"?
choices: A rhombus that isn't a square
A parallelogram that isn't a rectangle
questions.explanation: An isosceles trapezoid has congruent diagonals but is not a rectangle (not even a parallelogram). A square is a rectangle, so it isn't a counterexample; the other two don't have congruent diagonals, so they don't satisfy the hypothesis.

questions.stem: Under the inclusive definition (a trapezoid has at least one pair of parallel sides), which statement is true?
questions.explanation: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides, so it has at least one: under the inclusive definition it's a trapezoid. Rectangles are parallelograms, so they're trapezoids too. A trapezoid with only one pair of parallel sides isn't a parallelogram, and a kite (other than a rhombus) has no parallel sides.

questions.stem: $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$ are the midpoints of sides $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{BC}$, $\overline{CD}$, $\overline{DA}$ of quadrilateral $ABCD$. Put the steps of the proof that $EFGH$ is a parallelogram in order.
choices: $\overline{EF}$ and $\overline{HG}$ are midsegments of $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$, each parallel to $\overline{AC}$ and half as long.
$EFGH$ is a parallelogram, because one pair of opposite sides is parallel and congruent.
questions.explanation: The diagonal creates the two triangles; the Triangle Midsegment Theorem relates both segments to $\overline{AC}$; that makes them parallel and congruent to each other; and test 5 from Lesson 18 finishes the proof.

questions.stem: A quadrilateral's diagonals are perpendicular, with lengths 6 and 8. Its Varignon parallelogram is a rectangle. How long is a diagonal of that rectangle? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The rectangle's sides are half the quadrilateral's diagonals: 3 and 4. Its diagonal is $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$.

questions.stem: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, diagonal $\overline{AC}$ is the perpendicular bisector of diagonal $\overline{BD}$. Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: $A$ and $C$ are on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{BD}$, so each is equidistant from $B$ and $D$: $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. That makes $ABCD$ a kite (or a rhombus). Nothing forces the diagonals to be congruent, and in a kite the congruent angles are $\angle B$ and $\angle D$.

questions.stem: What is the Varignon parallelogram of an isosceles trapezoid?
questions.explanation: An isosceles trapezoid has congruent diagonals, so the Varignon parallelogram's sides (half the diagonals) are all equal: a rhombus. Its diagonals are generally not perpendicular, so it's usually not a rectangle or square.

questions.stem: A concave hexagon has five interior angles of $100^\circ$ each. What is its sixth angle?
questions.explanation: Every hexagon whose sides don't cross has an angle sum of $(6 - 2) \cdot 180 = 720^\circ$, so the sixth angle is $720 - 500 = 220^\circ$, a reflex angle (as a concave polygon needs). $140^\circ$ is $360 - 220$, and $40^\circ$ is what's left from $540^\circ$, a pentagon's sum.

questions.stem: Walking once around a polygon whose sides don't cross, counting left turns as positive and right turns as negative, the turns add to ___ degrees. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: You end facing the way you started after one net revolution, so the signed turns add to $360^\circ$, whether the polygon is convex or concave.

questions.stem: What is the tip angle of the star polygon $\{9/4\}$, in degrees? Give only the number.
Which symbols name a single star polygon? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\{n/k\}$ is a single star when $k$ and $n$ have no common factor and $1 < k < \tfrac n2$. 7 and 2 share no factor, nor do 8 and 3. $\{6/2\}$ and $\{8/2\}$ share the factor 2: joining every second point closes up after 3 or 4 points, giving a triangle or a square, not a star.

questions.stem: What is the sum of the five tip angles of a pentagram $\{5/2\}$?
questions.explanation: Each tip is $180 - \tfrac{360 \cdot 2}{5} = 36^\circ$, and $5 \cdot 36 = 180^\circ$; the formula $180(n - 2k) = 180(5 - 4)$ agrees. $540^\circ$ is the sum for a convex pentagon, and $36^\circ$ is one tip.

questions.stem: A square and a regular octagon meet at a vertex, and one more regular polygon fills the rest of the $360^\circ$. How many sides does it have? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $90 + 135 = 225$, leaving $135^\circ$, the angle of a regular octagon. The vertex is $4.8.8$.

questions.stem: Give the vertex configuration of each tiling.

image.alt: Four square patches of tilings by regular polygons, numbered 1 to 4. 1: dodecagons with small triangles in the gaps. 2: octagons with small squares in the gaps. 3: dodecagons separated by squares, with hexagons filling the remaining gaps. 4: hexagons meeting corner to corner with triangles between them.

questions.explanation: Look at one vertex and list the polygons around it. 1: a triangle and two dodecagons, $3.12.12$. 2: a square and two octagons, $4.8.8$. 3: a square, a hexagon and a dodecagon, $4.6.12$. 4: triangle, hexagon, triangle, hexagon, $3.6.3.6$.

questions.stem: Put these star polygons in order from the smallest tip angle to the largest.
Match each vertex type to what is true of it.
choices: Fits around a point but appears in no tiling
Appears only mixed with other vertex types
Does not fit around a point
questions.explanation: $60 + \tfrac{900}{7} + \tfrac{1200}{7} = 360$, so $3.7.42$ fits, but the odd-triangle argument rules it out. $4.8.8$ is one of the 8 semiregular tilings and $6.6.6$ is a regular one. $3.3.6.6$ fits ($60 + 60 + 120 + 120$) but can't be the only vertex type; it appears in tilings with more than one kind of vertex.

questions.stem: Why can't a tiling have every vertex of type $5.5.10$?
choices: Around one of the pentagons, the neighbors across its sides would have to alternate between pentagons and 10-gons, which is impossible with 5 sides.
The angles at the vertex add to more than $360^\circ$.
Regular pentagons can't tile the plane by themselves, so they can't appear in any tiling.
questions.explanation: The angles do fit: $108 + 108 + 144 = 360$. But at each corner of a pentagon, its two sides touch the other two polygons, a pentagon and a 10-gon, so the neighbors must alternate; an odd number of sides can't alternate. A polygon that can't tile alone can still appear in mixed tilings (regular octagons can't, yet they appear in $4.8.8$), and 10 not dividing 360 is irrelevant.

questions.stem: How many tilings of the plane by regular polygons have every vertex alike (regular and semiregular together)?
questions.explanation: 3 regular tilings plus 8 semiregular ones make 11. 17 counts the combinations of polygons that fit around a point and 21 counts the vertex types; most of those can't be the only vertex type.

questions.stem: Which star polygon has tip angles of $100^\circ$?
questions.explanation: $180 - \tfrac{360k}{n} = 100$ gives $\tfrac{k}{n} = \tfrac{80}{360} = \tfrac29$, so $\{9/2\}$. Check: $180 - \tfrac{720}{9} = 100$. The others have tips of $20^\circ$, $36^\circ$ and about $77.14^\circ$.

questions.stem: Three regular polygons with $a$, $b$ and $c$ sides fit exactly around a point. Which equation must hold?
questions.explanation: Adding the angles $180 - \tfrac{360}{a}$ and so on gives $540 - 360\left(\tfrac1a + \tfrac1b + \tfrac1c\right) = 360$, so the sum of reciprocals is $\tfrac12$. The sum is 1 for four polygons and $\tfrac32$ for five.

questions.stem: Two similar triangles have areas 18 and 50. The scale factor from the smaller to the larger is ___. (A fraction or a decimal is fine.)
questions.explanation: The area ratio is $\tfrac{50}{18} = \tfrac{25}{9}$, and the area ratio is $k^2$. So $k = \sqrt{\tfrac{25}{9}} = \tfrac53 \approx 1.67$. (Answering $\tfrac{25}{9}$ forgets to take the square root.)

questions.stem: Two similar prisms have scale factor 4 (large to small). Match each measure of the large prism to how it compares with the small one.
questions.explanation: Every length (perimeters and diagonals included) scales by $k = 4$, areas by $k^2 = 16$ and volumes by $k^3 = 64$. Multiplying by 8 would be $2k$, which matches nothing.

questions.stem: Which pairs of figures must be similar? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Squares all have right angles and four equal sides, so the side ratios are all equal. Equilateral triangles all have $60^\circ$ angles and equal sides. Isosceles right triangles all have angles $45^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$, so they are similar by AA. Rectangles can have different side ratios ($2 \times 3$ vs $2 \times 5$), and rhombuses can have different angles, so neither pair must be similar.

questions.stem: Two similar hexagons have perimeters 24 and 36, and the smaller has area 40. Put the steps for finding the larger area in order.
choices: Divide the perimeters to get the scale factor: $k = \tfrac{36}{24} = 1.5$
Square it to get the area ratio: $k^2 = 2.25$
questions.explanation: Perimeters are lengths, so their ratio is $k$. Areas scale by $k^2$, so square $k$ before multiplying. The larger hexagon's area is 90.

questions.stem: A cube is enlarged so that each edge is twice as long. Its volume is multiplied by ___.
questions.explanation: Volume scales by $k^3 = 2^3 = 8$. (Multiplying by 2 treats volume like a length; by 4 treats it like an area.)

questions.stem: A person and a tree stand in the sun at the same time. Name the numbered parts of the picture used to find the tree's height.

image.alt: A person and a taller tree stand on level ground with the sun at the upper left. Each casts a shadow to the right, and a dashed line runs from the top of each to the tip of its shadow. A dashed vertical measuring line is drawn beside the tree.

questions.explanation: 1 is the height being found, 2 the tree's long shadow, 3 the person's short shadow and 4 a sun ray from the treetop to the tip of its shadow. Because the sun's rays are parallel, both triangles have the same angle at the shadow tip and a right angle at the ground, so they are similar by AA, and $\tfrac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}}$ is the same for both.

questions.stem: Match what is known about $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ to the conclusion it supports.
questions.explanation: Two angle pairs give AA. Three proportional side pairs give SSS similarity. $\angle A$ is between $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$, so the third line is SAS similarity. In the last line $\angle A$ is not between $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$ (the included angle is $\angle B$), which is the SSA pattern and proves nothing. HL is a congruence test for right triangles.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$ with $D$ on $\overline{AB}$ and $E$ on $\overline{AC}$. If $AD = 9$, $DB = 6$ and $AE = 12$, then $EC =$ ___.
questions.explanation: Side Splitter Theorem: $\tfrac{AD}{DB} = \tfrac{AE}{EC}$, so $\tfrac{9}{6} = \tfrac{12}{EC}$ and $9 \cdot EC = 72$, giving $EC = 8$.

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $\overline{DE} \parallel \overline{BC}$ with $D$ on $\overline{AB}$ and $E$ on $\overline{AC}$. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The parallel lines make $\angle ADE \cong \angle ABC$ (corresponding angles), and $\angle A$ is shared, so the triangles are similar by AA. The Side Splitter Theorem gives $\tfrac{AD}{DB} = \tfrac{AE}{EC}$. But $\tfrac{DE}{BC}$ compares a side of the small triangle with a side of the large one, so it equals $\tfrac{AD}{AB}$ (piece to whole), not $\tfrac{AD}{DB}$ (piece to piece).

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 15$, $AC = 21$ and $BC = 24$, and the bisector of $\angle A$ meets $\overline{BC}$ at $D$. Put the steps for finding $BD$ in order.
questions.explanation: The bisector splits $BC$ in the ratio of the adjacent sides, $15 : 21 = 5 : 7$. Out of $12$ equal parts, $BD$ gets 5, so $BD = 10$ and $DC = 14$.

questions.stem: This is the picture behind the rearrangement proof: four copies of a right triangle with legs $a < b$ inside a large square. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A large square with a tilted square inside it whose corners touch the four sides. The four corner regions are right triangles. Each side of the large square is split into a shorter piece and a longer piece.

questions.explanation: The hypotenuses enclose the tilted square of side $c$ (1). Each corner piece is a right triangle with area $\tfrac12 ab$ (2). Each side of the big square is a shorter leg $a$ (3) plus a longer leg $b$ (4). Counting the big square's area two ways gives $(a + b)^2 = 4 \cdot \tfrac12 ab + c^2$, so $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs 20 and 21. Its hypotenuse is ___.
questions.explanation: $c = \sqrt{20^2 + 21^2} = \sqrt{400 + 441} = \sqrt{841} = 29$. (20-21-29 is a Pythagorean triple.)

questions.stem: A triangle has sides 7, 11 and 13. Put the steps for classifying it in order.
choices: Compare: $169 < 170$, so the triangle is acute
questions.explanation: The test always uses the longest side as $c$. Since $c^2$ is (just) less than the sum of the other two squares, the angle opposite 13 is a little less than $90^\circ$ and the triangle is acute.

questions.stem: Which sets of side lengths form a right triangle? Select all that apply.
Match each set of side lengths to the kind of triangle it makes.
questions.explanation: $13^2 = 169 = 25 + 144$: right. $6^2 = 36 < 16 + 25 = 41$: acute. $7^2 = 49 > 41$: obtuse. $2 + 3 = 5 < 6$ fails the triangle inequality, so there is no triangle. None of the sets has three equal sides.

questions.stem: On the left, a square with side $s$ is cut by a diagonal. On the right, an equilateral triangle with side $2s$ is cut by an altitude, and the left half is shaded. Name the numbered segments.

image.alt: Left: a square with one diagonal drawn and the lower triangle shaded. Right: an equilateral triangle with an altitude from the top vertex to the base, the left half shaded.

questions.explanation: The altitude bisects the base of side $2s$, so the short leg (1) is $s$. The hypotenuse (3) is a full side of the equilateral triangle, $2s$. The altitude (2) is the long leg, $\sqrt{(2s)^2 - s^2} = s\sqrt3$. The diagonal of the square (4) is $\sqrt{s^2 + s^2} = s\sqrt2$.

questions.stem: A 30°-60°-90° triangle has a long leg of $7\sqrt3$. Its hypotenuse is ___.
questions.explanation: Find the short leg first: $\tfrac{7\sqrt3}{\sqrt3} = 7$. The hypotenuse is twice the short leg: $14$.

questions.stem: Put the sides of a 30°-60°-90° triangle in order from shortest to longest.
questions.explanation: The ratio is $1 : \sqrt3 : 2$ with $1 < \sqrt3 \approx 1.73 < 2$. The shortest side is opposite the smallest angle, and the hypotenuse (opposite $90^\circ$) is the longest.

questions.stem: A 30°-60°-90° triangle has a short leg of 4. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Hypotenuse $= 2 \cdot 4 = 8$ and long leg $= 4\sqrt3$. The area is $\tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 4\sqrt3 = 8\sqrt3$. $4\sqrt2$ would be the hypotenuse of a 45°-45°-90° triangle with legs 4.

questions.stem: The altitude to the hypotenuse of a right triangle splits the hypotenuse into pieces 2 and 8. Match each length to its value.
left: The leg next to the piece of 2
The leg next to the piece of 8
questions.explanation: $h = \sqrt{2 \cdot 8} = 4$. The hypotenuse is $2 + 8 = 10$. Each leg is $\sqrt{c \cdot \text{adjacent piece}}$: $\sqrt{10 \cdot 2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt{10 \cdot 8} = \sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt5$. Check: $20 + 80 = 100 = 10^2$. (16 is $2 \cdot 8$ without the square root.)

questions.stem: A person on the ground looks up at a person on top of a cliff. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A person on level ground and another person standing on top of a cliff, joined by a straight line. Dashed horizontal lines run from each person's eye level, and a shaded angle is marked at each end of the straight line.

questions.explanation: The line of sight (4) joins the two observers. The angle from the horizontal up to it is the angle of elevation (1); the angle from the upper horizontal (3) down to it is the angle of depression (2). The two horizontals are parallel, so these are alternate interior angles and are equal.
