questions.stem: In the 1830s Jakob Steiner gave arguments that any closed curve other than a circle can be improved to enclose more area with the same length. Why weren't they a complete proof that the circle is best?
choices: They used the AM–GM inequality incorrectly
They assumed that a best shape exists
They assumed the curve was already a circle
questions.explanation: Showing that every non-circle can be improved proves the circle is best only if some best shape exists. Without that, the improvements could go on forever without reaching a winner. Later mathematicians filled this gap, so the isoperimetric inequality is now fully proved.

questions.stem: A closed box must hold 64 cm³. What is the least possible surface area?
questions.explanation: Among boxes with a fixed volume the cube has the least surface area. A $4 \times 4 \times 4$ cube has $6 \cdot 16 = 96$ cm². An $8 \times 4 \times 2$ box needs $2(32 + 16 + 8) = 112$ and a $16 \times 4 \times 1$ box needs $2(64 + 16 + 4) = 168$. 64 is the volume, not an area.

questions.stem: With 100 m of fence around all four sides, the largest rectangular area you can enclose is ___ m². Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The best rectangle is a square with side $\tfrac{100}{4} = 25$ m, so the area is $625$ m².

questions.stem: Two positive numbers add up to 20. The largest their product can be is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: By AM–GM, $\sqrt{ab} \le \tfrac{a + b}{2} = 10$, so $ab \le 100$, with equality when $a = b = 10$.

questions.stem: Match each shape to its isoperimetric quotient $Q = \dfrac{4\pi A}{P^2}$.
questions.explanation: $Q$ does not depend on size, only on shape. For a regular $n$-gon, $Q = \tfrac{\pi}{n\tan(180^\circ/n)}$: about 0.605 for $n = 3$, 0.785 for $n = 4$, 0.907 for $n = 6$, approaching 1 (the circle) as $n$ grows. No shape has $Q > 1$; that is the isoperimetric inequality.

questions.stem: Each shape has perimeter 24. Put them in order of area, smallest first.
questions.explanation: Rectangle: 20. Triangle (side 8): $16\sqrt3 \approx 27.71$. Square (side 6): 36. Hexagon (side 4): $24\sqrt3 \approx 41.57$. Circle: $\tfrac{24^2}{4\pi} \approx 45.84$. A long thin rectangle wastes perimeter, and the area grows as the shape gets rounder.

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Among rectangles with perimeter $P$, the square has the most area
Two shapes with the same perimeter always have the same area
Among closed curves of length $P$, the circle encloses the most area
Among closed cylinders with a given volume, the tallest one uses the least metal
questions.explanation: The square and the circle are the winners for rectangles and for all closed curves. Equal perimeters do not mean equal areas (a 1-by-19 rectangle and a 10-by-10 square both have perimeter 40). A very tall, thin can needs a lot of side metal; the least metal goes with $h = 2r$.

questions.stem: A closed can is shaped to use the least metal for its volume, and its radius is 5 cm. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: The least-metal can has $h = 2r = 10$ cm, so $V = \pi(25)(10) = 250\pi \approx 785.4$ cm³. $125\pi$ uses $h = r$; $500\pi$ uses $h = 4r$; $50\pi$ is $2\pi r^2$, an area.

questions.stem: Point $P$ is three-fourths of the way from $A(2, -3)$ to $B(10, 9)$. Its $x$-coordinate is ___ and its $y$-coordinate is ___.
questions.explanation: $k = \tfrac34$. The changes are $\Delta x = 8$ and $\Delta y = 12$, so $P = \left(2 + \tfrac34 \cdot 8,\; -3 + \tfrac34 \cdot 12\right) = (8, 6)$.

questions.stem: Match each property you want to show with the coordinate tool that shows it.
questions.explanation: Lengths come from the distance formula, parallel lines have equal slopes, perpendicular lines (neither vertical) have slopes multiplying to $-1$, and two segments bisect each other exactly when they have the same midpoint. Slopes adding to zero (like $2$ and $-2$) say nothing special.

questions.stem: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ has vertices $A(0, 0)$, $B(4, 2)$, $C(3, 4)$, $D(-1, 2)$. Which names apply to it? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Side vectors: $\overrightarrow{AB} = (4, 2)$, $\overrightarrow{BC} = (-1, 2)$, $\overrightarrow{CD} = (-4, -2)$, $\overrightarrow{DA} = (1, -2)$. Opposite sides are parallel and equal, so it is a parallelogram. Slopes $\tfrac12$ and $-2$ multiply to $-1$, so the angles are right: a rectangle. But $AB = \sqrt{20}$ and $BC = \sqrt5$ differ, so it is not a rhombus, and therefore not a square.

questions.stem: This setup proves that the midpoint of a right triangle's hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices. The right angle is at the origin, and the legs have lengths $2a$ and $2b$. Give the coordinates of each numbered point.

image.alt: A right triangle with its right angle at the origin, one leg along the positive x-axis and one along the positive y-axis. Point 1 is the right-angle vertex, point 2 the end of the horizontal leg, point 3 the top of the vertical leg, and point 4 the midpoint of the hypotenuse, joined to point 1 by a dashed segment.

questions.explanation: The right angle sits at $(0, 0)$, the horizontal leg ends at $(2a, 0)$ and the vertical leg at $(0, 2b)$. The midpoint of the hypotenuse averages $(2a, 0)$ and $(0, 2b)$: $(a, b)$. Using $2a$ and $2b$ keeps that midpoint free of fractions.

questions.stem: In the coordinate proof about a right triangle's hypotenuse, why are the legs placed at $(2a, 0)$ and $(0, 2b)$ rather than $(a, 0)$ and $(0, b)$?
choices: Because the legs of a right triangle must have even lengths
Because it makes the triangle isosceles, which the proof needs
So the midpoint of the hypotenuse is $(a, b)$, with no fractions
Because the distance formula only works with even coordinates
questions.explanation: With $(a, 0)$ and $(0, b)$ the midpoint would be $\left(\tfrac a2, \tfrac b2\right)$; doubling avoids the fractions. Since $a$ and $b$ can be any positive numbers, $2a$ and $2b$ can still be any lengths, so nothing is lost. The triangle is not assumed isosceles, and the distance formula works for any coordinates.

questions.stem: Rotating $(3, -7)$ by $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin gives a point with $x$-coordinate ___ and $y$-coordinate ___.
questions.explanation: The $90^\circ$ counterclockwise rule is $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$, so $(3, -7) \to (7, 3)$. Check with a sketch: a point in Quadrant IV turns into Quadrant I.

questions.stem: Put the steps for rotating a point $P$ about a center $C(a, b)$ that is not the origin in order.
choices: Subtract the center: $(x - a,\; y - b)$
Apply the rotation rule for the origin to that point
Add the center back: add $a$ to $x$ and $b$ to $y$
Check that the image is the same distance from $C$ as $P$
questions.explanation: The origin rules only work about the origin, so first slide $C$ to the origin, then rotate, then slide back. The check comes last because it tests the finished image.

questions.stem: Which of these does every rigid motion preserve? Select all that apply.
choices: Orientation (the clockwise order of labeled points)
questions.explanation: Rigid motions keep distance, and with it angle measure, collinearity and parallelism. Orientation is not always kept: a reflection turns clockwise labels counterclockwise.

questions.stem: In this picture, the point marked 1 is reflected in the slanted line. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A slanted line with a point on each side, joined by a dashed segment that crosses the line at a right angle. Tick marks show the two halves of the dashed segment are equal. A green triangle and its mirror-image tan triangle lie on opposite sides of the line.

choices: Midpoint of the segment from a point to its image
questions.explanation: A reflection sends $P$ to $P'$ so that the line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{PP'}$: the dashed segment meets the line at a right angle, at its midpoint. Point 1 is the preimage $P$ and point 2 its image $P'$. There is no center of rotation or translation vector in a single reflection.

questions.stem: Match each coordinate rule with the transformation it describes.
choices: Reflection in the line y = x
Rotation of 90° counterclockwise about the origin
Rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin
questions.explanation: Swapping coordinates reflects in $y = x$. $(-y, x)$ is the $90^\circ$ counterclockwise turn (test: $(1, 0) \to (0, 1)$). Negating both is a $180^\circ$ turn. Negating only $y$ reflects in the $x$-axis. The $y$-axis reflection would be $(-x, y)$ and the clockwise turn $(y, -x)$.

questions.stem: A dilation centered at the origin maps $(6, -4)$ to $(15, -10)$. The scale factor is ___.
questions.explanation: $k = \tfrac{15}{6} = \tfrac{-10}{-4} = 2.5$. Both coordinates must give the same ratio for a dilation centered at the origin.

questions.stem: Match each figure with its number of lines of symmetry.
left: Rectangle that is not a square
Parallelogram that is not a rectangle or rhombus
Isosceles triangle that is not equilateral
questions.explanation: A non-square rectangle folds along its two midlines; a square adds the two diagonals; a regular $n$-gon has $n$; a general parallelogram has none (folding on a diagonal does not match it up); a non-equilateral isosceles triangle has only the line through its vertex angle. Three would be an equilateral triangle.

questions.stem: Which figures are mapped onto themselves by a $180^\circ$ rotation about their center? Select all that apply.
choices: A rhombus that is not a square
A parallelogram that is not a rectangle or rhombus
questions.explanation: Every parallelogram, including every rhombus, has $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry about the point where its diagonals cross. An equilateral triangle's rotation angles are multiples of $120^\circ$ and a regular pentagon's are multiples of $72^\circ$; neither list includes $180^\circ$.

questions.stem: The picture shows a dilation with scale factor 2.5. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A point at the lower left with three dashed rays leaving it. Each ray passes through a vertex of a small blue triangle and continues to the matching vertex of a large tan triangle. Point 1 is where the rays start, marker 2 is on the small triangle, marker 3 on the large triangle and marker 4 on one of the dashed rays.

choices: Ray from the center through a vertex
questions.explanation: Every image point lies on the ray from the center through its preimage, $k = 2.5$ times as far out. With $k > 1$ the image is the larger triangle (an enlargement), so the small triangle is the preimage.

questions.stem: A rigid motion reverses orientation and leaves no point where it was. What kind of rigid motion is it?
questions.explanation: Reversing orientation means a reflection or a glide reflection. A reflection fixes every point on its mirror line, so a motion with no fixed points must be a glide reflection. Rotations and translations keep orientation.

questions.stem: The parabola $y = \tfrac{1}{12}x^2$ can be written $x^2 = 4py$. Its focus is $(0, p)$, where $p$ is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 12: $x^2 = 12y$, so $4p = 12$ and $p = 3$. Equivalently $a = \tfrac{1}{12}$ and $p = \tfrac{1}{4a} = 3$. The value $\tfrac{1}{48}$ comes from using $\tfrac{a}{4}$ by mistake.

questions.stem: Put the steps deriving the equation of the parabola with focus $(0, p)$ and directrix $y = -p$ in order.
choices: Set the distances equal: $\sqrt{x^2 + (y - p)^2} = |y + p|$
questions.explanation: The definition gives the distance equation; squaring removes the root and the absolute value; expanding shows $y^2$ and $p^2$ on both sides, and cancelling them leaves $x^2 = 4py$.

questions.stem: Which statements about the parabola $x^2 = -8y$ are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $4p = -8$, so $p = -2$: the focus is 2 units below the vertex at $(0, -2)$, the parabola opens down toward it, and the directrix is 2 units above the vertex, $y = 2$. $(0, -8)$ uses $4p$ in place of $p$.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this parabola.

image.alt: A parabola opening upward with a dotted vertical line through its lowest point and a dashed horizontal line below it. Marker 1 is a point inside the curve on the dotted line, marker 2 is on the dashed line, marker 3 is the lowest point of the curve and marker 4 is on the dotted line high above. A point on the curve is joined to marker 1 and, by a perpendicular, to the dashed line, with tick marks showing the two segments are equal.

questions.explanation: Every point of the parabola is as far from the focus (inside the curve) as from the directrix (the line below). The vertex is the point of the curve halfway between them, and the axis of symmetry passes through the focus perpendicular to the directrix. Parabolas have no center or asymptotes.

questions.stem: Match each parabola with the direction it opens.
questions.explanation: When $x$ is squared the parabola opens up ($4p > 0$) or down ($4p < 0$); when $y$ is squared it opens right ($4p > 0$) or left ($4p < 0$). The sign of the number multiplying the unsquared side is the sign of $4p$.

questions.stem: A translation followed by a dilation about the new center maps the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ onto $(x - 3)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 36$. What is the scale factor of the dilation?
questions.explanation: The radii are $\sqrt4 = 2$ and $\sqrt{36} = 6$, so $k = \tfrac{6}{2} = 3$. Nine compares $r^2$ values ($36 \div 4$), $\tfrac13$ maps the large circle to the small one, and 6 is the new radius, not the ratio.

questions.stem: A figure is reflected in the line through the origin at $20^\circ$ to the positive $x$-axis, and then in the line through the origin at $65^\circ$. What single transformation is this?
choices: A rotation of $45^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin
A rotation of $90^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin
A rotation of $90^\circ$ clockwise about the origin
A rotation of $170^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin
questions.explanation: Two reflections in lines through $O$ give a rotation about $O$ by twice the angle from the first line to the second: $2(65^\circ - 20^\circ) = 90^\circ$ counterclockwise. $45^\circ$ forgets the doubling, clockwise has the order backward, and $170^\circ$ doubles the sum of the angles.

questions.stem: Reflect in the line $x = -1$, then in the line $x = 3$. What single transformation is this?
questions.explanation: $x \to 2(-1) - x = -2 - x \to 2(3) - (-2 - x) = x + 8$. Parallel mirrors 4 apart give a translation by twice the gap, 8, in the direction from the first mirror toward the second: right. Two reflections keep orientation, so the result cannot be a single reflection.

questions.stem: A rotation of $70^\circ$ about $O$ can be written as two reflections in lines through $O$ that meet at an angle of ___ degrees.
questions.explanation: Two reflections in lines meeting at angle $\theta$ make a rotation by $2\theta$, so $2\theta = 70^\circ$ and $\theta = 35^\circ$. Any pair of lines through $O$ at that angle works, with the first line turned $35^\circ$ clockwise from the second.

questions.stem: An isometry sends $A(0, 0)$ to $(0, 0)$, $B(1, 0)$ to $(1, 0)$ and $C(0, 1)$ to $(0, -1)$. Which isometry is it?
choices: A rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin
questions.explanation: Reflection in the $x$-axis, $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$, sends the three points to exactly those images, and an isometry is determined by what it does to three noncollinear points, so it is the only answer. The $180^\circ$ rotation and the $y$-axis reflection both send $B$ to $(-1, 0)$, and a glide reflection has no fixed points, but $A$ is fixed.

questions.stem: An isometry sends noncollinear points $A$, $B$, $C$ to $A'$, $B'$, $C'$. Put the steps of the proof that it is a composition of at most three reflections in order.
choices: Reflect in the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AA'}$, moving $A$ onto $A'$
Reflect in the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{B_1B'}$, which passes through $A'$, moving $B_1$ onto $B'$
If needed, reflect in line $A'B'$, moving $C_2$ onto $C'$
Conclude that the reflections equal the isometry, since three noncollinear points determine an isometry
questions.explanation: Each reflection puts one more point in place without disturbing the ones already placed: the second mirror passes through $A'$, and the third is line $A'B'$ itself. Once all three points match, the uniqueness claim says the composition is the original isometry.

questions.stem: Match each isometry with its fixed points.
choices: A whole line of fixed points
questions.explanation: A translation moves every point. A rotation fixes only its center. A reflection fixes its mirror line. The identity fixes everything. An isometry fixing exactly two points is impossible: fixing two points fixes the whole line through them.

questions.stem: Which of these are opposite isometries (they reverse orientation)? Select all that apply.
choices: A rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin
A reflection in the $x$-axis followed by a reflection in the $y$-axis
questions.explanation: One reflection reverses orientation, and a glide reflection is a reflection plus a translation, so it reverses it too. A rotation keeps orientation, and two reflections (here in perpendicular lines, giving the $180^\circ$ rotation) keep it as well.

questions.stem: Describe the isometry $U(x, y) = (x - 2,\; 4 - y)$.
choices: A glide reflection: reflect in $y = 2$, then slide 2 units left
A glide reflection: reflect in $y = 4$, then slide 2 units left
questions.explanation: $y$ and $4 - y$ always average 2, so the mirror is $y = 2$, and $x$ decreases by 2. Orientation is reversed and $x - 2 = x$ has no solution, so there are no fixed points: a glide reflection, not a plain reflection. Reflecting in $y = 4$ would give $8 - y$, and the $180^\circ$ rotation about $(-1, 2)$ is $(-2 - x,\; 4 - y)$.

questions.stem: Reflect in the $x$-axis and then translate by $\langle 0, 10 \rangle$. What single transformation is this?
questions.explanation: $(x, y) \to (x, -y) \to (x, 10 - y) = (x, 2 \cdot 5 - y)$, the rule for reflection in $y = 5$. A translation perpendicular to the mirror just moves the mirror by half the translation. There is no sideways slide, so it is not a glide reflection, and orientation is reversed, so it is not a translation.

questions.stem: How many symmetries, including the identity, does a regular octagon have?
questions.explanation: A regular octagon has symmetry group $D_8$: 8 rotations (multiples of $45^\circ$, including $0^\circ$) and 8 reflections, 16 in all. 8 counts only one kind, and 9 and 17 count the identity twice.

questions.stem: Match each figure with its symmetry group.
left: Three-bladed pinwheel with all blades leaning the same way
questions.explanation: The pentagon has 5 rotations and 5 lines of symmetry. Z has a $180^\circ$ turn but no mirror (a mirror reverses the slant of its diagonal). H has a $180^\circ$ turn and horizontal and vertical mirror lines. The pinwheel has 3 rotations and no mirror lines, since a mirror would reverse the lean of the blades.

questions.stem: Why can a bounded figure (one that fits inside some circle) never have a glide reflection as a symmetry?
choices: Glide reflections do not preserve distances
Doing it twice is a translation, and repeating that would carry the figure arbitrarily far away
Glide reflections keep orientation, and bounded figures cannot
Every glide reflection has a fixed point, which a bounded figure cannot have
questions.explanation: A glide reflection done twice is a translation by twice the slide. If the figure were mapped onto itself, so would be its images under that translation repeated over and over, which move farther and farther away: impossible for a bounded figure. Glide reflections do preserve distance, reverse orientation, and have no fixed points.

questions.stem: A non-square rectangle is centered at the origin with sides parallel to the axes. Reflect it in the $x$-axis, then in the $y$-axis. Which single symmetry of the rectangle is this?
questions.explanation: $(x, y) \to (x, -y) \to (-x, -y)$: the $180^\circ$ rotation, as the two-mirror rule predicts for mirrors at $90^\circ$. The $90^\circ$ rotation and the reflection in $y = x$ are not symmetries of a non-square rectangle at all.

questions.stem: Which of these figures have a cyclic symmetry group (rotations only, no line of symmetry)? Select all that apply.
choices: An isosceles triangle that is not equilateral
questions.explanation: S and N are each mapped onto themselves by a $180^\circ$ turn and have no mirror line: group $C_2$. A square has 4 lines of symmetry ($D_4$), and a non-equilateral isosceles triangle has one line of symmetry (its group, $D_1$, is the identity and that reflection).

questions.stem: A point is reflected in line $m$ and then in line $n$; the lines cross at the point marked 4. Name the numbered points.

image.alt: Two lines crossing at the lower left, one at a shallow angle and one steeper. Point 1 lies below the shallow line; a dashed segment perpendicular to that line joins it to point 2, which lies between the lines. A dashed segment perpendicular to the steeper line joins point 2 to point 3 beyond it. An arc with an arrow turns from the direction of point 1 toward point 3 around the crossing point, marker 4.

choices: Midpoint of the original point and its final image
questions.explanation: Each dashed segment is perpendicular to a mirror and bisected by it: point 1 reflects in the shallow line to point 2, which reflects in the steep line to point 3. The two reflections together turn point 1 to point 3 about the crossing point by twice the angle between the lines.

questions.stem: Rotate $(2, 0)$ by $120^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin.
questions.explanation: The image is $(2\cos 120^\circ,\; 2\sin 120^\circ) = \left(2 \cdot (-\tfrac12),\; 2 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = (-1, \sqrt3)$, in Quadrant II as a $120^\circ$ turn should be. $(1, \sqrt3)$ is the $60^\circ$ rotation, and $(-1, -\sqrt3)$ the $240^\circ$ one.

questions.stem: The determinant of $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ is ___.
questions.explanation: $ad - bc = 3 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 1 = 10$. The transformation multiplies every area by 10 and keeps orientation.

questions.stem: Which matrix reflects points in the $y$-axis?
questions.explanation: Reflection in the $y$-axis sends $(1, 0)$ to $(-1, 0)$ and keeps $(0, 1)$; those images are the columns. The others reflect in the $x$-axis, reflect in $y = x$, and rotate $180^\circ$.

questions.stem: Find the image of $(2, 3)$ under $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
questions.explanation: Row times column: $1 \cdot 2 + (-2) \cdot 3 = -4$ and $3 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 3 = 6$, giving $(-4, 6)$. $(11, -4)$ uses the columns as rows.

questions.stem: Reflect in the line $y = x$, then rotate $180^\circ$ about the origin. Which single transformation is this?
questions.explanation: The reflection is done first, so it goes on the right: $\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, which sends $(x, y)$ to $(-y, -x)$: reflection in $y = -x$. Its determinant is $-1$, so it cannot be a rotation.

questions.stem: Reflect $(10, 0)$ in the line $y = 3x$.
questions.explanation: With $m = 3$: $\cos 2\alpha = \tfrac{1 - 9}{10} = -0.8$ and $\sin 2\alpha = \tfrac{6}{10} = 0.6$, so $(10, 0) \to (10 \cdot (-0.8),\; 10 \cdot 0.6) = (-8, 6)$. Check: the midpoint $(1, 3)$ is on $y = 3x$, and the segment's direction $(-18, 6)$ is perpendicular to the line's direction $(1, 3)$ because $-18 + 18 = 0$.

questions.stem: A region of area 5 is transformed by $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$. What is the area of the image?
questions.explanation: $\det = 3 \cdot 4 - 1 \cdot (-2) = 14$, and areas are multiplied by $|\det|$: $5 \cdot 14 = 70$. 50 comes from $ad + bc = 10$; 14 is the factor, not the area; $\sqrt{14}$ would be a length factor, which a non-similarity does not have.

questions.stem: Which matrices represent rigid motions? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A matrix is a rigid motion when its columns are perpendicular and both have length 1. The first is the $90^\circ$ rotation. The second has columns $(0.6, 0.8)$ and $(-0.8, 0.6)$, each of length 1 and perpendicular: a rotation by about $53^\circ$. The third doubles every length (a dilation), and the fourth has a column $(1, 1)$ of length $\sqrt2$ (it slants squares into parallelograms).

questions.stem: Match each matrix with the transformation it performs.
choices: Reflection in the line y = x
Rotation of 90° counterclockwise about the origin
questions.explanation: Read the columns as the images of $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$. The $x$-axis reflection keeps $(1, 0)$ and flips $(0, 1)$; $y = x$ swaps them; $180^\circ$ negates both; the $90^\circ$ turn sends $(1, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$ to $(-1, 0)$. A dilation by 2 would be $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the proof of the angle-addition formulas in order.
choices: Note that rotating by $\beta$ and then by $\alpha$ is a rotation by $\alpha + \beta$
Write this as the matrix equation $R_\alpha R_\beta = R_{\alpha + \beta}$
Multiply out the left side of that equation, $R_\alpha R_\beta$
Compare the first columns of the two sides
questions.explanation: The geometric fact comes first, then its matrix form, then the computation, and comparing entries gives $\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta$ and $\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta$.

questions.stem: What transformation does $\begin{bmatrix} 0.6 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & -0.6 \end{bmatrix}$ perform?
questions.explanation: The columns are perpendicular unit vectors and the determinant is $-0.36 - 0.64 = -1$, so it is a reflection in a line through the origin. A point on the mirror stays put: $(2, 1) \to (1.2 + 0.8,\; 1.6 - 0.6) = (2, 1)$, so the mirror is $y = \tfrac12 x$. (Check with the formulas: $m = \tfrac12$ gives $\cos 2\alpha = \tfrac{3/4}{5/4} = 0.6$ and $\sin 2\alpha = \tfrac{1}{5/4} = 0.8$.) A rotation would have determinant $+1$.

questions.stem: A matrix has determinant $-3$. It maps a triangle of area 4 to a triangle of area ___.
questions.explanation: Areas are multiplied by $|\det| = 3$: $4 \cdot 3 = 12$. The negative sign means the image has the opposite orientation; an area is never negative.

questions.stem: Why is the translation by $\langle 2, 0 \rangle$ not given by any $2 \times 2$ matrix?
choices: Translations change distances, and matrices never do
Every matrix sends $(0, 0)$ to $(0, 0)$, but this translation moves the origin
questions.explanation: A matrix times the zero column is the zero column, so every linear transformation fixes the origin. The translation sends $(0, 0)$ to $(2, 0)$. Translations keep distances and orientation; many matrices change distances.

questions.stem: Rotate $(2, 2)$ by $45^\circ$ counterclockwise about the origin.
questions.explanation: $(2, 2)$ is $2\sqrt2$ from the origin at angle $45^\circ$; turning $45^\circ$ more puts it on the positive $y$-axis: $(0, 2\sqrt2)$. By the formula: $x' = 2\cos 45^\circ - 2\sin 45^\circ = 0$ and $y' = 2\sin 45^\circ + 2\cos 45^\circ = 2\sqrt2$. $(2\sqrt2, 0)$ is the clockwise turn.

questions.stem: Find the ellipse with foci $(\pm 6, 0)$ whose points have distances to the foci adding up to 20.
questions.explanation: $2a = 20$ gives $a = 10$; $c = 6$; $b^2 = a^2 - c^2 = 100 - 36 = 64$. The foci are on the $x$-axis, so $a^2 = 100$ goes under $x^2$. Using $c^2$ as $b^2$ gives 36; swapping the denominators turns the major axis vertical; 10 and 8 forget to square.

questions.stem: The ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{169} + \dfrac{y^2}{25} = 1$ has foci $(\pm c, 0)$, where $c$ is ___. Give only the number.
Find the foci of $\dfrac{(x + 3)^2}{9} + \dfrac{(y - 1)^2}{25} = 1$.
questions.explanation: The center is $(-3, 1)$. The larger denominator, 25, is under the $y$-term, so the major axis is vertical: $c^2 = 25 - 9 = 16$, $c = 4$, and the foci are 4 above and below the center. Moving sideways treats the axis as horizontal, $(3, \ldots)$ has the sign of $h$ wrong, and $\sqrt{34}$ adds instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this ellipse.

image.alt: A wide ellipse with a dashed horizontal axis and a dotted vertical axis. Two points on the horizontal axis inside the ellipse are joined to a point on the ellipse. Marker 1 is the right-hand inner point, marker 2 is the left end of the horizontal axis, marker 3 the top end of the vertical axis, and marker 4 the point where the axes cross.

questions.explanation: The foci lie inside the ellipse on the major (long) axis, and lines to them from any point of the ellipse add to $2a$. The vertices are the ends of the major axis, the co-vertices the ends of the minor axis, and the center is where the axes cross, halfway between the foci.

questions.stem: Which statements are true of every ellipse that is not a circle? Select all that apply.
choices: The distances from any of its points to the two foci add up to the same number
$c^2 = a^2 - b^2$, where $a$ is half the major axis and $b$ half the minor axis
Its foci lie on the minor axis
questions.explanation: The constant sum is the definition, and the right triangle formed by the center, a focus and a co-vertex gives $a^2 = b^2 + c^2$. An ellipse has $0 < e < 1$ (greater than 1 is a hyperbola), and its foci lie on the major axis.

questions.stem: Find the hyperbola with foci $(\pm 10, 0)$ whose points have distances to the foci differing by 12.
questions.explanation: $2a = 12$ gives $a = 6$; $c = 10$; for a hyperbola $b^2 = c^2 - a^2 = 100 - 36 = 64$. The plus sign makes an ellipse, swapping $a^2$ and $b^2$ moves the vertices to $(\pm 8, 0)$, and 136 adds $a^2$ and $c^2$.

questions.stem: What are the asymptotes of $\dfrac{y^2}{16} - \dfrac{x^2}{9} = 1$?
questions.explanation: This hyperbola opens up and down with $a = 4$ (under $y^2$) and $b = 3$. Its box is 6 wide and 8 tall, so the asymptotes are $y = \pm\tfrac{a}{b}x = \pm\tfrac43 x$. Far from the center, $\tfrac{y^2}{16} \approx \tfrac{x^2}{9}$, so $y \approx \pm\tfrac43 x$. $\tfrac{16}{9}$ and $\tfrac{9}{16}$ forget the square roots.

questions.stem: The eccentricity of the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{25} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$ is ___. Give it as a decimal or fraction.
Match each eccentricity with the kind of conic section.
questions.explanation: $e = \tfrac{c}{a}$ is 0 when the foci merge (a circle), between 0 and 1 for an ellipse, exactly 1 for a parabola, and greater than 1 for a hyperbola, where $c > a$.

questions.stem: Put the steps deriving the equation of the ellipse with foci $(\pm c, 0)$ and distance sum $2a$ in order.
choices: Write the definition: $\sqrt{(x + c)^2 + y^2} + \sqrt{(x - c)^2 + y^2} = 2a$
Move one square root to the other side and square both sides
Simplify to $a\sqrt{(x - c)^2 + y^2} = a^2 - cx$
Square again and collect terms: $(a^2 - c^2)x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2(a^2 - c^2)$
Replace $a^2 - c^2$ with $b^2$ and divide by $a^2b^2$
questions.explanation: Two square roots need two squarings, isolating one root before each. The last step uses $b^2 = a^2 - c^2$ and gives $\tfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \tfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.

questions.stem: Radio stations $A(-40, 0)$ and $B(40, 0)$ (in km) send pulses at the same instant. A ship finds it is 24 km closer to $B$ than to $A$. On which curve is the ship?
questions.explanation: The fixed difference $PA - PB = 24$ puts the ship on a hyperbola with foci $A$ and $B$: $2a = 24$, $a = 12$, $c = 40$, $b^2 = 1600 - 144 = 1456$. Being closer to $B(40, 0)$ puts it on the right branch, $x > 0$. Using $a = 24$ forgets to halve the difference, and the plus sign gives an ellipse.

questions.stem: For $\dfrac{x^2}{20} + \dfrac{y^2}{36} = 1$, which way does the major axis run, and what is $c$?
questions.explanation: The larger denominator, 36, is under $y^2$, so the major axis is vertical, with $a^2 = 36$ and $b^2 = 20$. Then $c^2 = 36 - 20 = 16$ and $c = 4$. $\sqrt{56}$ adds the denominators, and 16 is $c^2$.

questions.stem: A light sits at one focus of an elliptical mirror. Where do the rays go after they reflect off the mirror?
choices: Out parallel to the major axis
Through the center of the ellipse
questions.explanation: The reflection property of the ellipse sends every ray from one focus through the other focus. Leaving parallel to the axis is the parabola's property (Lesson 38).

questions.stem: Which statements about $\dfrac{x^2}{9} - \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$ are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $a = 3$ gives the vertices. $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$, so the foci are $(\pm 5, 0)$; $\sqrt7$ uses the ellipse relation. At $x = 0$ the equation says $-\tfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$, which has no solution, so the curve never meets the $y$-axis.

cards.back: A length you can build from a unit segment with compass and straightedge. Exactly the numbers reached from 1 by $+$, $-$, $\times$, $\div$ and square roots.
Mark $OU = 1$, $OB = b$ on one side of an angle and $OA = a$ on the other. The parallel to $\overline{UA}$ through $B$ meets the second side at $P$, and $OP = ab$ (similar triangles).
Put $AB = a$ and $BC = 1$ on a line, draw the semicircle on $\overline{AC}$, and raise the perpendicular at $B$ to meet it at $D$. Then $BD = \sqrt a$ (geometric mean).

cards.front: Divide a segment into $n$ equal parts
cards.back: Step off $n$ equal pieces on a ray from $A$, join the last mark to $B$, and draw parallels through the other marks (Side Splitter Theorem).

cards.front: Why each construction step adds at most a square root
cards.back: New points come from intersecting lines and circles, which means solving linear or quadratic equations.
A root of a cubic with rational coefficients and no rational root is not constructible.
Doubling the cube (needs $\sqrt[3]{2}$), trisecting every angle ($60^\circ$ needs $\cos 20^\circ$), squaring the circle (needs $\sqrt\pi$).

cards.front: Who proved them impossible, and when?
cards.back: Wantzel (1837): doubling the cube and trisection. Lindemann (1882): $\pi$ is transcendental, so the circle can't be squared.
$8c^3 - 6c - 1 = 0$, from $\cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$ with $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$. It has no rational root.
A regular $n$-gon is constructible exactly when $n$ is a power of 2 times distinct Fermat primes (known: 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537).

cards.front: Constructible regular polygons up to 20 sides

cards.back: A segment from a vertex of a triangle to a point on the opposite side.
Cevians $\overline{AD}$, $\overline{BE}$, $\overline{CF}$ (feet on the sides) are concurrent exactly when $\tfrac{AF}{FB} \cdot \tfrac{BD}{DC} \cdot \tfrac{CE}{EA} = 1$.

cards.front: How to write the Ceva product
cards.back: Go around the triangle: $A \to F \to B \to D \to C \to E \to A$. Each ratio starts where the last one ended.
Triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of their bases, so $\tfrac{BD}{DC} = \tfrac{[ABP]}{[ACP]}$, and so on; the areas cancel in the product.

cards.front: Ceva for medians and angle bisectors
cards.back: Medians: $1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1$. Angle bisectors: $\tfrac ba \cdot \tfrac cb \cdot \tfrac ac = 1$ by the Triangle Angle Bisector Theorem.
Where the cevians to the incircle's touch points meet. Ceva works because tangent lengths from a vertex are equal: $\tfrac xy \cdot \tfrac yz \cdot \tfrac zx = 1$.
If a line meets lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ (not vertices), then $\tfrac{AF}{FB} \cdot \tfrac{BD}{DC} \cdot \tfrac{CE}{EA} = 1$.
Drop perpendiculars $h_A$, $h_B$, $h_C$ to the line. Similar right triangles give $\tfrac{AF}{FB} = \tfrac{h_A}{h_B}$, and so on; the heights cancel.
Three lines through the vertices meeting at a point: Ceva (feet on the sides). Three points on one line: Menelaus (one or three on extended sides).
The triangle of the three side midpoints. A half-turn about $G$ plus a dilation by $\tfrac12$ from $G$ maps a triangle onto it.
The map $T$ (half-turn about $G$, dilate by $\tfrac12$) sends each altitude to a perpendicular bisector, so it sends $H$ to $O$. Hence $O$ is on line $HG$ with $GO = \tfrac12 GH$.
$G = \tfrac{2O + H}{3}$ and $H = 3G - 2O$.

cards.front: Order and spacing on the Euler line
The nine points of the nine-point circle
cards.back: The 3 side midpoints, the 3 feet of the altitudes, and the 3 midpoints of $\overline{AH}$, $\overline{BH}$, $\overline{CH}$ (Euler points).

cards.front: Center and radius of the nine-point circle
cards.back: Center $N$ = midpoint of $\overline{OH}$; radius $\tfrac R2$.

cards.front: Proof idea of the nine-point circle
cards.back: Dilate the circumcircle by $\tfrac12$ from $H$. It passes through the Euler points and the side midpoints ($BHCA^*$ is a parallelogram), and the feet follow from Thales' theorem.

cards.front: Euler line of a right triangle
cards.back: $H$ is the right-angle vertex, $O$ the midpoint of the hypotenuse, $OH$ = half the hypotenuse, and the nine-point radius is a quarter of the hypotenuse.
The nine-point circle is tangent to the incircle (Feuerbach, 1822).
In cyclic $ABCD$: $AC \cdot BD = AB \cdot CD + AD \cdot BC$ (diagonals versus opposite sides).
Pick $K$ on $\overline{AC}$ with $\angle ABK \cong \angle DBC$. Then $\triangle ABK \sim \triangle DBC$ and $\triangle KBC \sim \triangle ABD$; add $AK \cdot BD$ and $KC \cdot BD$.
$d^2 = a^2 + b^2$: the Pythagorean theorem.
$d^2 = (\text{base}_1)(\text{base}_2) + (\text{leg})^2$.

cards.front: Diagonal of a regular pentagon with side 1
cards.back: Ptolemy gives $d^2 = d + 1$, so $d = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618$.

cards.front: Point $P$ on arc $BC$ of equilateral $\triangle ABC$
cards.back: $PA = PB + PC$ (Ptolemy in $ABPC$).
For any quadrilateral, $AC \cdot BD \le AB \cdot CD + AD \cdot BC$, with equality only for cyclic ones.
Cyclic quadrilateral with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$: area $= \sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$, $s$ = semiperimeter. With $d = 0$ it becomes Heron's formula.
Check that the quadrilateral is cyclic: supplementary opposite angles, equal angles on one side, or equal diagonal products.
When $A$, $B$, $C$ are distinct and collinear and $AB + BC = AC$ (on a number line: $B$'s coordinate is between theirs).

cards.front: Three distinct points on a line: how many are between the other two?
cards.back: Exactly one.
Contains the whole segment joining any two of its points. A disk is convex; a circle (curve) is not.
Always convex. So interiors of angles and triangles (intersections of half-planes) are convex.
A line splits the rest of the plane into two convex half-planes; a segment joining opposite sides meets the line.

cards.front: Coordinate test: same side of $y = mx + b$?
cards.back: Compute $d = y - (mx + b)$ for each point. Same sign: same side. Opposite signs: the segment crosses at $t = \tfrac{d_P}{d_P - d_Q}$ of the way from $P$.
Points on $C$'s side of $\overleftrightarrow{BA}$ AND on $A$'s side of $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$.
A line crossing one side of a triangle (not through a vertex) crosses exactly one other side.
If $D$ is inside $\angle BAC$, ray $\overrightarrow{AD}$ meets $\overline{BC}$. Used whenever an angle bisector of a triangle is said to meet the opposite side.
It assumes both perpendicular feet lie on the sides. Really $P$ is outside the triangle and one foot is on an extension, so one sum is a difference.

cards.front: Lines through $n$ points, no three collinear
cards.back: $\binom{n}{2} = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$

cards.front: $n$ points, $k$ of them collinear (no other three collinear): lines?
cards.back: $\binom{n}{2} - \binom{k}{2} + 1$

cards.front: Planes through $n$ points in space, no four coplanar
$n$ lines in general position: crossing points
cards.back: $\binom{n}{2}$
$\tfrac{n^2 + n + 2}{2}$ (1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, …); each new line adds one region per piece.

cards.front: $n$ lines in general position: bounded and unbounded regions
cards.back: Unbounded $2n$; bounded $\binom{n-1}{2} = \tfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}$.

cards.front: A new line crosses earlier lines at $c$ distinct points. Regions added?
cards.back: $c + 1$ (it is cut into $c + 1$ pieces, each splitting a region).

cards.front: $n$ concurrent lines: angles and vertical pairs
cards.back: $2n(n-1)$ angles (straight angles not counted) in $n(n-1)$ vertical pairs; equally spaced, the smallest is $\tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$.

cards.front: Regions from all chords of $n$ points on a circle
cards.back: $1 + \binom{n}{2} + \binom{n}{4}$ (no three chords concurrent): 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, 57, …

cards.front: Why does $2^{n-1}$ fail for circle regions?
cards.back: It matches only for $n \le 5$; six points give 31. A pattern is a conjecture until proved.
P1: two points are on exactly one line. P2: two lines meet in exactly one point. P3: four points exist, no three on a line.
7 points, 7 lines, 3 points per line, 3 lines per point: the smallest projective plane (order 2).
$n + 1$ points per line, $n + 1$ lines per point, $n^2 + n + 1$ points and $n^2 + n + 1$ lines.

cards.front: Which orders of projective planes exist?
cards.back: Every prime power (2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, …). Not 6 (Bruck–Ryser, 1949) and not 10 (computer search, 1989). 12 is unknown.
In a projective plane, swap point and line in any theorem and you get another theorem.
There are four lines, no three through one point (a theorem, proved from P3 with lines $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$).
$n^2$ points, $n^2 + n$ lines, $n$ points per line, $n + 1$ parallel classes of $n$ lines.
Delete one line and its points; lines that met there become parallel.
Add a point at infinity to each parallel class and one new line through all of them.

cards.front: The four-point geometry inside the Fano plane
cards.back: Delete line $DEF$: points $A, B, C, G$ and six two-point lines, the affine plane of order 2.
In neutral geometry every triangle's angle sum is at most $180^\circ$.
$M$ = midpoint of $\overline{BC}$, extend $AM$ to $E$ with $ME = AM$. $\triangle AEC$ has the same angle sum, and one of its angles is at most $\tfrac12\angle A$.

cards.front: Two angles of a triangle (neutral geometry)
cards.back: Always add to less than $180^\circ$, by the Exterior Angle Inequality.

cards.front: Why the sphere isn't neutral geometry
cards.back: Its lines close up and two opposite points lie on many lines, so the Exterior Angle Inequality fails there.
Cut a triangle from a vertex to the opposite side: defect(whole) = defect(piece 1) + defect(piece 2).
If one triangle has angle sum $180^\circ$, all do (Euclidean); otherwise every triangle has sum below $180^\circ$ (hyperbolic).
Base with two congruent legs perpendicular to it; summit opposite the base. Summit angles congruent (SAS, then SSS).
Summit angles right: Euclidean. Acute: hyperbolic. Obtuse: impossible in neutral geometry.
Three right angles; the fourth is right (Euclidean) or acute (hyperbolic). Half of a Saccheri quadrilateral.
$x$ (center to nearest line) uniform on $[0, \tfrac d2]$, $\theta$ uniform on $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$; crosses when $x \le \tfrac{\ell}{2}\sin\theta$.
Favorable area $\tfrac{\ell}{2}$ (under $\tfrac{\ell}{2}\sin\theta$) over rectangle area $\tfrac{\pi d}{4}$ gives $\tfrac{2\ell}{\pi d}$.
Expected crossings $= c \cdot$ length for any shape; a circle of diameter $d$ crosses exactly twice, so $c = \tfrac{2}{\pi d}$.
The expected number of crossings, not a probability (it can exceed 1).
$\pi \approx \dfrac{2\ell N}{d\,C}$ for $C$ crossings in $N$ drops; error shrinks like $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt N}$.
A chord is longer than the inscribed equilateral triangle's side $r\sqrt3$ when its distance from the center is less than $\tfrac r2$.
Random endpoints $\tfrac13$; random point on a radius $\tfrac12$; random midpoint $\tfrac14$.
"At random" has no meaning until the random process is specified; each method is a different probability model.

cards.front: A true conditional as a picture
cards.back: The hypothesis set sits inside the conclusion set. Anything in the outer set but not the inner one is a counterexample to the converse.
Conclude $p$ is false (use the contrapositive). From "$q$ is true" or "$p$ is false", nothing follows.
Each statement in a box with its reason; arrows show which statements each one depends on.
$2^n$ rows for $n$ simple statements: 4 for two, 8 for three.
$p \wedge q$ ("and"): true only when both are true. $p \vee q$ ("or", inclusive): false only when both are false.
Only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false. With a false hypothesis it is (vacuously) true.
$\sim(p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q$; $\sim(p \vee q) \equiv \sim p \wedge \sim q$.
$p \wedge \sim q$: the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. Not the inverse, and not a conditional at all.
$\sim p \vee q$: either the hypothesis fails or the conclusion holds.
Not (all A are B) = some A is not B. Not (some A is B) = no A is B.
Tautology: true in every row ($p \vee \sim p$). Contradiction: false in every row ($p \wedge \sim p$).
From $p \to q$ and $\sim q$, conclude $\sim p$. Valid.
From $p \to q$ and $\sim p$, conclude $\sim q$. Invalid (the inverse error).
Valid: the conclusion is true whenever all premises are true (a matter of form). Sound: valid AND the premises are actually true.
To prove $p \to q$, prove $\sim q \to \sim p$ directly. Useful when the conclusion is a "not" statement.
Assume the statement is false, reason to something impossible, and conclude the statement is true.
"At least two". (Not "exactly two", not "none".)
List cases that cover every possibility (they may overlap), and prove the conclusion in each.
If $\sqrt2 = a/b$ in lowest terms, then $a^2 = 2b^2$ makes $a$ even, then $b$ even: both even contradicts lowest terms.

cards.front: If $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even
cards.back: Proved by contrapositive: if $n = 2k + 1$, then $n^2 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1$ is odd.
Prove an existential statement, or disprove a universal one (a counterexample). It can never prove a universal statement.

cards.front: Two lines meet in at most one point: why
cards.back: If distinct lines shared two points, two different lines would pass through those points, but exactly one line does.
Base case: prove $P(n_0)$. Inductive step: prove $P(k) \to P(k+1)$ for every $k \ge n_0$. Then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \ge n_0$.
The assumption $P(k)$ at the start of the inductive step. Legitimate because the step proves a conditional.
A smallest failure $m$ can't be the base case, and $P(m - 1)$ true would force $P(m)$ by the step (well-ordering principle).

cards.front: Sum of odd numbers that starts later
Sum of the first $n$ odd numbers
cards.back: $1 + 3 + \dots + (2n - 1) = n^2$. Each L-shaped gnomon of $2k + 1$ squares grows a $k$-by-$k$ square to $(k + 1)$-by-$(k + 1)$.
The new point adds $k$ segments: $\tfrac{k(k-1)}{2} + k = \tfrac{(k+1)k}{2}$.
Inductive reasoning guesses a rule from cases (no proof). Mathematical induction is deductive: base case plus inductive step proves the rule for every $n$.
No base case ($n^2 + n + 1$ "is even"); a step that fails for one $k$ (the all-horses-one-color joke breaks from 1 to 2).
Construct the parallel to $m$ through $P$; it makes the same angle with $t$ as $\ell$, so by the Protractor Postulate it is $\ell$.

cards.front: Consecutive Interior Angles Converse: key step
cards.back: The angle forming a linear pair with one of the angles is congruent to the other (congruent supplements), and the two are corresponding angles.
Congruent alternate interior angles imply parallel lines. Proved indirectly with the Exterior Angle Inequality, without the parallel postulate.
Parallel lines make congruent alternate interior angles: the first proposition in the Elements to use the parallel postulate.
Parallels through an outside point exist without it; the postulate makes the parallel unique, which gives the forward angle theorems and the 180° triangle.
Geometry without the parallel postulate: parallels exist, but need not be unique.
If $\ell \parallel m$ and a path bends once at $P$ between them, $m\angle APB$ equals the sum of the two angles at $A$ and $B$ that open toward the bend.
For a zigzag path between parallel lines, the angles that open right total the same as the angles that open left.
They meet at a right angle: $\tfrac{\alpha}{2} + \tfrac{\beta}{2} = \tfrac{180^\circ}{2} = 90^\circ$.
One fixed by a single condition (e.g. through $P$, parallel to $\ell$), so it exists and is unique.
$m x + b_1 = m x + b_2$ forces $b_1 = b_2$, so different lines with equal slopes never meet.
$\langle a_1, b_1 \rangle \cdot \langle a_2, b_2 \rangle = a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 = |\vec u||\vec v|\cos\varphi$; zero means perpendicular.

cards.front: Normal and direction vectors of $Ax + By = C$
cards.back: Normal: $\langle A, B \rangle$. Direction: $\langle B, -A \rangle$.

cards.front: Parallel and perpendicular lines through $(p, q)$ to $Ax + By = C$
cards.back: Parallel: $Ax + By = Ap + Bq$. Perpendicular: $Bx - Ay = Bp - Aq$.
$\cos\varphi = \dfrac{|\vec u \cdot \vec v|}{|\vec u||\vec v|}$ with direction (or normal) vectors; $0^\circ \le \varphi \le 90^\circ$.

cards.front: Foot of the perpendicular from $(x_0, y_0)$ to $Ax + By + C = 0$
cards.back: $(x_0 + tA,\ y_0 + tB)$ with $t = -\dfrac{Ax_0 + By_0 + C}{A^2 + B^2}$.

cards.front: Reflection of a point in a line
cards.back: Go twice as far along the normal: $(x_0 + 2tA,\ y_0 + 2tB)$; the foot is the midpoint.

cards.front: Distance between $Ax + By + C_1 = 0$ and $Ax + By + C_2 = 0$
cards.back: $\dfrac{|C_1 - C_2|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}$ (make $A$ and $B$ identical first).

cards.front: SSA from an acute $\angle A$: how is $B$ located?
cards.back: On the other side of the angle, where the circle of radius $a = BC$ centered at $C$ crosses that ray.

cards.front: SSA with acute $\angle A$, $AC = b$, distance $d$ from $C$ to the other side: $a < d$
cards.back: No triangle: the circle never reaches the ray.
One triangle, with a right angle at $B$ (the foot of the perpendicular).

cards.front: SSA with acute $\angle A$: $d < a < b$
cards.back: Two triangles, with third vertices the same distance from the foot $F$ on either side.
One triangle: the circle's other crossing is at $A$ or behind it.
SSA proves congruence when the side opposite the angle is at least as long as the other given side.

cards.front: Why HL is a case of the Long Side SSA Theorem
cards.back: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, the largest angle, so it is longer than the leg.

cards.front: SSA with a right or obtuse angle
cards.back: Always proves congruence: the side opposite that angle is automatically the longest.
Their angles at the third vertex are supplementary (one acute, one obtuse), not congruent.
SAS is Proposition 4, SSS is 8, ASA and AAS are 26.

cards.front: Euclid's proof of the Triangle Inequality
cards.back: Extend $\overline{AB}$ past $B$ to $D$ with $BD = BC$; isosceles $\triangle BCD$ makes $\angle ACD > \angle ADC$, so $AD = AB + BC > AC$.
Exactly when $B$ lies on $\overline{AC}$ (a degenerate triangle).
A path $A \to B \to \cdots \to Z$ is at least as long as $AZ$, with equality only if the points lie in order on $\overline{AZ}$.
Each side of a polygon is shorter than the sum of the others; check the longest side.

cards.front: Fourth side of a quadrilateral with sides $p \le q \le r$
cards.back: Less than $p + q + r$, and more than $r - p - q$ when that is positive.
$PB + PC < AB + AC$; and $PA + PB + PC$ is between half the perimeter and the perimeter.
Reflect $A$ across $\ell$ to $A'$; the best $P$ is where $\overline{A'B}$ crosses $\ell$, and the shortest length is $A'B$.

cards.front: Law of reflection from Heron's problem
cards.back: At the best point, $\overline{PA}$ and $\overline{PB}$ make equal angles with the mirror line.

cards.front: Minimize $PA + PB + PC + PD$ for convex $ABCD$
cards.back: Put $P$ where the diagonals cross; the minimum is $AC + BD$.
Their sum is more than half the perimeter and less than the perimeter.
Let two of the three lines meet, then show the meeting point has a property that puts it on the third line.

cards.front: Why the centroid is $\tfrac23$ of the way along each median
cards.back: With medians $\overline{AD}$, $\overline{BE}$ meeting at $G$ and $M$, $N$ the midpoints of $\overline{AG}$, $\overline{BG}$: $MNDE$ is a parallelogram (two midsegments), so $AM = MG = GD$.
They lie on the perpendicular bisectors of the anticomplementary triangle (lines through each vertex parallel to the opposite side), which meet at its circumcenter.
The triangle formed by the three midsegments. $\triangle ABC$ is the medial triangle of its anticomplementary triangle.
$3G = H + 2O$, so $G$ is on $\overline{OH}$ with $OG : GH = 1 : 2$ and $H = 3G - 2O$.

cards.front: Coordinates for the Euler line proof
Is the incenter on the Euler line?
cards.back: Only when the triangle is isosceles (all four centers then lie on the axis of symmetry).
Circumcenter: midpoint of the hypotenuse (complete the triangle to a rectangle). Orthocenter: the right-angle vertex.
The midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram with sides parallel to the diagonals and half as long.
Perimeter $= AC + BD$ (sum of the diagonals); area $=$ half the quadrilateral's area.

cards.front: When is the Varignon parallelogram a rectangle? A rhombus?
cards.back: Rectangle: the diagonals are perpendicular. Rhombus: the diagonals are congruent. Square: both.

cards.front: Varignon parallelogram of a rhombus, rectangle, kite, isosceles trapezoid
cards.back: Rhombus → rectangle; rectangle → rhombus; kite → rectangle; isosceles trapezoid → rhombus.

cards.front: Diagonals bisect each other and are congruent
cards.back: Rectangle. (Add perpendicular: square.)

cards.front: Diagonals bisect each other and are perpendicular
cards.back: Rhombus. (Add congruent: square.)

cards.front: One diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other (they don't bisect each other)
cards.back: Kite: the endpoints of the bisecting diagonal are each equidistant from the ends of the other.
Not necessarily. The diagonals must also bisect each other.
Inclusive: at least one pair of parallel sides (parallelograms count). Exclusive (this course): exactly one pair.
Count left turns positive and right turns negative: the turns add to $360^\circ$, so the angle sum is $(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ$ even for concave polygons.
Join every $k$th of $n$ points on a circle; needs $k$ and $n$ with no common factor and $1 < k < \tfrac n2$.
$180^\circ - \dfrac{360^\circ k}{n}$; the tips add to $180(n - 2k)$ degrees. Pentagram: $36^\circ$ each, $180^\circ$ total.

cards.front: Three regular polygons around a point
cards.back: $\tfrac1a + \tfrac1b + \tfrac1c = \tfrac12$. (Four: the reciprocals add to 1.)

cards.front: How many ways regular polygons fit around a point
cards.back: 17 combinations of polygons, 21 vertex types (order counted).
If $a$ is odd and every vertex is $a.b.c$, then $b = c$, because the neighbors around the $a$-gon must alternate. Rules out $3.7.42$, $4.5.20$, $5.5.10$ and others.
An angle between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. At a reflex vertex of a polygon the walk-around turn is negative (a right turn).
Same polygons, different order around the vertex: different vertex types. $3.6.3.6$ is a semiregular tiling; $3.3.6.6$ only appears mixed with other vertex types.
Two copies of the right triangle and an isosceles right triangle with legs $c$ form a trapezoid: $\tfrac12(a + b)^2 = ab + \tfrac12 c^2$, so $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
Similar figures on the three sides of a right triangle: area on the hypotenuse = sum of areas on the legs (areas scale like $a^2$, $b^2$, $c^2$).

cards.front: Semicircle on a side of length s
cards.back: Area $\tfrac{\pi}{8}s^2$; semicircles on the legs add up to the semicircle on the hypotenuse.
A triple with no common factor greater than 1 (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29, 9-40-41).
The hypotenuse is odd and exactly one leg is even (two odd squares sum to 2 more than a multiple of 4, which no square is).
$a = m^2 - n^2$, $b = 2mn$, $c = m^2 + n^2$ for whole numbers $m > n > 0$.

cards.front: When Euclid's formula gives a primitive triple
cards.back: When $m$ and $n$ have no common factor and one is even, the other odd.
A triple $a, b, c$ gives the rational point $\left(\tfrac{a}{c}, \tfrac{b}{c}\right)$ on $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.
An Old Babylonian clay tablet (roughly 1800 BCE) listing numbers from Pythagorean triples, such as 119 and 169; its purpose is debated.

cards.front: Height from two angles of elevation
cards.back: $h = \dfrac{d\sin\alpha\sin\beta}{\sin(\beta - \alpha)} = \dfrac{d\tan\alpha\tan\beta}{\tan\beta - \tan\alpha}$, with $d$ the distance walked toward the object.

cards.front: Angle at the top in the two-sighting method
cards.back: $\beta - \alpha$ (Exterior Angle Theorem: $\beta = \alpha + \angle T$).
Angle measured clockwise from north, three digits: N $000^\circ$, E $090^\circ$, S $180^\circ$, W $270^\circ$.
Add or subtract $180^\circ$: the return direction.

cards.front: Coordinates from a bearing θ and distance r
cards.back: East $= r\sin\theta$, north $= r\cos\theta$ (sine and cosine swap roles because bearings start from north).

cards.front: Angle at a turn between two bearings
cards.back: Find the back bearing of the first leg, then the angle between it and the second leg's bearing.
Measure one baseline, then only angles; solve triangle after triangle with the Law of Sines.
Where sight lines cross at a small angle, a small angle error moves the crossing point a long way.
$\varphi = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618$, the positive root of $x^2 = x + 1$.
$\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1 \approx 2.618$ and $\tfrac{1}{\varphi} = \varphi - 1 \approx 0.618$.
Long side $= \varphi \times$ short side; cutting off a square leaves a smaller similar golden rectangle.
Whole : longer piece = longer piece : shorter piece; the longer piece is the geometric mean, and the ratio is $\varphi$.
Diagonal $= \varphi \times$ side.
Isosceles with angles 36°, 72°, 72°; legs $= \varphi \times$ base. Bisecting a base angle cuts off a smaller golden triangle.
Isosceles with angles 36°, 36°, 108°; base $= \varphi \times$ leg.
$\cos 36^\circ = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{4} = \tfrac{\varphi}{2} \approx 0.809$; $\cos 72^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4} \approx 0.309$.
Ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers (8/5, 13/8, 21/13, …) approach $\varphi$.

cards.front: Golden ratio claims in art and nature
cards.back: Pentagon and Fibonacci facts are proved; claims about the Parthenon, famous paintings or nautilus shells are mostly unsupported.
$\operatorname{pow}(P) = d^2 - r^2$, with $d$ the distance from $P$ to the center: positive outside, 0 on the circle, negative inside.

cards.front: Power of an outside point and tangents
cards.back: outside · whole $= d^2 - r^2$ for every secant; tangent length $= \sqrt{d^2 - r^2}$.

cards.front: Power of an inside point and chords
cards.back: Every chord through $P$ is cut into pieces with product $r^2 - d^2$.
For $x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0$ (square terms with coefficient 1), the power of $(x_0, y_0)$ is $x_0^2 + y_0^2 + Dx_0 + Ey_0 + F$.

cards.front: Shortest chord through an inside point $P$
cards.back: The chord perpendicular to $\overline{OP}$; $P$ is its midpoint, so each half is $\sqrt{r^2 - d^2}$.
Write both circles in general form and subtract; the square terms cancel, leaving a line.

cards.front: Radical axis and the line of centers
cards.back: Always perpendicular. It passes through the midpoint of the centers only when the radii are equal.

cards.front: Radical axis of two crossing circles
cards.back: The line through the two crossing points (it contains the common chord). For tangent circles: the common tangent line.

cards.front: Tangents from a point on the radical axis
cards.back: The tangent segments to the two circles are equal (each is the square root of the same power).
Three circles with non-collinear centers: the three radical axes meet at one point, with equal power for all three circles.

cards.front: Concentric circles and the radical axis
cards.back: Concentric circles with different radii have no radical axis.

cards.front: Opposite-angle test for a cyclic quadrilateral
cards.back: A convex quadrilateral is cyclic if and only if a pair of opposite angles is supplementary.
If $C$ and $D$ are on the same side of $\overline{AB}$ and $\angle ACB \cong \angle ADB$, then $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are concyclic.

cards.front: Converse of the Intersecting Chords Theorem
cards.back: If $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ cross at $E$ and $EA \cdot EB = EC \cdot ED$, then $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are concyclic.
Rectangles (including squares) and isosceles trapezoids. A parallelogram only if it is a rectangle; a kite only if its equal angles are right angles.
Substitute each point into $x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0$ and solve for $D$, $E$, $F$; or intersect two perpendicular bisectors.
It is concyclic with the other three exactly when it satisfies the equation of their circle (power 0).
$\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C} = 2R$
$R = \dfrac{abc}{4K}$
Half the hypotenuse; the center is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

cards.front: Circumradius of an equilateral triangle with side $s$
cards.back: $R = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt3} = \dfrac{s\sqrt3}{3}$

cards.front: Which formula gives a trapezoid's area, and which parts does it use?
cards.back: $A = \tfrac12(b_1 + b_2)h$: the two bases and the perpendicular height. The legs are not used (except to find a missing height).
Center; radius (center to a vertex); apothem (center to the midpoint of a side, perpendicular to it); central angle $\tfrac{360^\circ}{n}$.
They form a right triangle with the slant height as hypotenuse: $\ell = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$. Volume uses $h$; lateral area uses $\ell$.

cards.front: Cone, sphere and cylinder with radius $r$ and height $2r$
cards.back: Volumes $\tfrac23\pi r^3$, $\tfrac43\pi r^3$, $2\pi r^3$: in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$.
Convex; every face the same regular polygon; the same number of faces at every vertex. Exactly five exist (the Platonic solids).
Tetrahedron 4, 6, 4; cube 8, 12, 6; octahedron 6, 12, 8; dodecahedron 20, 30, 12; icosahedron 12, 30, 20.

cards.front: Why are there only five regular polyhedra?
cards.back: At least 3 faces meet at a vertex and their angles must total less than $360^\circ$: 3, 4 or 5 triangles, 3 squares, or 3 pentagons. Hexagons ($3 \times 120^\circ = 360^\circ$) lie flat.

cards.front: Counting edges and vertices from the faces
cards.back: $E = \tfrac12$(total face sides); with $q$ faces at every vertex, $V = \tfrac1q$(total face corners).
Join the centers of neighboring faces. $V$ and $F$ swap, $E$ stays. Cube ↔ octahedron, dodecahedron ↔ icosahedron, tetrahedron ↔ itself.
$360^\circ$ minus the sum of the face angles at a vertex. Cube: $360^\circ - 270^\circ = 90^\circ$.
The angle defects of a convex polyhedron total $720^\circ$. It follows from (and is equivalent to) $V - E + F = 2$.
12 pentagons, 20 hexagons, 60 vertices, 90 edges; each vertex has defect $360^\circ - 348^\circ = 12^\circ$.

cards.front: Pentagons and hexagons with 3 at each vertex
cards.back: Euler's formula forces exactly 12 pentagons, however many hexagons there are.
$V - E + F$: 2 for a polyhedron without holes, 0 for a ring-shaped one (one hole); it drops by 2 per hole.

cards.front: Volume of a frustum of a cone
cards.back: $V = \tfrac{\pi h}{3}(R^2 + Rr + r^2)$ (big cone minus the similar small cone).

cards.front: Lateral area of a frustum of a cone
cards.back: $L = \pi(R + r)s$, with slant height $s = \sqrt{h^2 + (R - r)^2}$.
$V = \tfrac{h}{3}\left(B_1 + B_2 + \sqrt{B_1 B_2}\right)$; known in Egypt by about 1850 BCE (Moscow Papyrus).

cards.front: Base radius of a spherical cap
cards.back: $a^2 = h(2R - h)$, from the right triangle with legs $R - h$ and $a$ and hypotenuse $R$.
$V = \tfrac{\pi h^2}{3}(3R - h)$; $h = R$ gives a hemisphere, $h = 2R$ the whole ball.
A band of a sphere between parallel planes $h$ apart has curved area $2\pi R h$, the same as the matching band of the surrounding cylinder.
Spinning a region of area $A$ around an axis that does not cut it: $V = A \cdot 2\pi d$, where $d$ is the distance from the axis to the centroid.
A curve of length $\ell$ whose centroid is $d$ from the axis sweeps out area $\ell \cdot 2\pi d$.
Circle of radius $r$ spun around an axis $R$ from its center: $V = 2\pi^2 R r^2$, $S = 4\pi^2 R r$.

cards.front: Best rectangle for a fixed perimeter $P$
cards.back: The square, with area $\tfrac{P^2}{16}$, since $LW = \left(\tfrac{P}{4}\right)^2 - t^2$.

cards.front: Best pen against a wall (fence on 3 sides)
cards.back: Length (parallel to the wall) twice the width: with $P$ of fence, $W = \tfrac{P}{4}$, $L = \tfrac{P}{2}$, area $\tfrac{P^2}{8}$.

cards.front: Area of a regular $n$-gon with perimeter $P$
cards.back: $A = \dfrac{P^2}{4n\tan(180^\circ/n)}$; it increases with $n$ toward the circle's $\tfrac{P^2}{4\pi}$.

cards.front: Can that uses the least metal

cards.front: Every isometry of the plane is a composition of…
cards.back: At most three reflections.

cards.front: Reflections in two parallel lines a distance $d$ apart
cards.back: A translation by $2d$, perpendicular to the lines, from the first line toward the second.

cards.back: A rotation about $O$ by $2\theta$, turning from the first line toward the second.

cards.back: Keeps the distance from $O$ and sends angle $\varphi$ to $2\alpha - \varphi$.

cards.front: Fixed points of each rigid motion
cards.back: Translation: none. Rotation: the center. Reflection: its mirror line. Glide reflection: none.

cards.front: Reflect in a line then translate perpendicular to it
cards.back: A reflection in a parallel line moved by half the translation.

cards.front: Symmetry group of a non-square rectangle
cards.back: $D_2$: identity, $180^\circ$ rotation and two reflections.

cards.front: Why a bounded figure has no translation symmetry
cards.back: Repeating a translation (or glide reflection) would carry the figure arbitrarily far away.

cards.back: $360^\circ$ (one per vertex), for any number of sides.

cards.back: $\sin\theta = \sin(180^\circ - \theta)$ (positive); $\cos\theta = -\cos(180^\circ - \theta)$ (negative).

cards.back: AAS, ASA (find the third angle first) and SSA. Not SAS or SSS.

cards.front: SSA with acute $\angle A$: how many triangles?
cards.back: With $h = b\sin A$: $a < h$ none; $a = h$ one (right); $h < a < b$ two; $a \ge b$ one.

cards.front: Law of Cosines for an angle
cards.back: $\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$; a negative value means $\angle A$ is obtuse.

cards.front: When to use the Law of Cosines
cards.back: SAS (find the third side) and SSS (find an angle).

cards.front: Safe order when solving a triangle
cards.back: Settle the largest angle (opposite the longest side) with the Law of Cosines or by subtraction; the other angles are then acute.
SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS: exactly one. SSA: 0, 1 or 2. AAA: infinitely many (similar triangles).

It bisects the chord and its arc.

Same circle: congruent chords ⟺ congruent arcs ⟺ equidistant from the center.

The tangent segments are congruent.

A right angle (Thales).

cards.back: tangent² = outside · whole

cards.back: $a = \dfrac{s/2}{\tan(180^\circ/n)}$

cards.back: A plane slice of a solid is a cross section (every slice of a sphere is a circle). Spinning a rectangle about a side gives a cylinder; a right triangle about a leg, a cone.

glossary.definition: A length that can be built from a unit segment in finitely many compass-and-straightedge steps. Exactly the numbers reached from 1 by $+$, $-$, $\times$, $\div$ and square roots.
Describes a number that is not a root of any polynomial equation with rational coefficients, such as $\pi$ (proved by Lindemann in 1882). A transcendental number is never constructible.
A regular $n$-gon can be constructed with compass and straightedge exactly when $n$ is a power of 2 times a product of distinct Fermat primes.
A prime of the form $2^{2^k} + 1$. The known ones are 3, 5, 17, 257 and 65537; no others have been found.
The classical problem of constructing the edge of a cube with twice the volume of a given cube; it needs $\sqrt[3]{2}$ and is impossible with compass and straightedge (Wantzel, 1837).
Dividing an angle into three congruent angles. Some angles can be trisected with compass and straightedge, but no method works for every angle; $60^\circ$ cannot be trisected (Wantzel, 1837).
The classical problem of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle; it needs $\sqrt\pi$ and is impossible with compass and straightedge because $\pi$ is transcendental.
A segment from a vertex of a triangle to a point on the opposite side (or its extension). Medians and angle bisectors are cevians.
Cevians $\overline{AD}$, $\overline{BE}$, $\overline{CF}$ of $\triangle ABC$, with feet on the sides, are concurrent exactly when $\tfrac{AF}{FB} \cdot \tfrac{BD}{DC} \cdot \tfrac{CE}{EA} = 1$.

If a line meets lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ of $\triangle ABC$ at $D$, $E$, $F$ (not at vertices), then $\tfrac{AF}{FB} \cdot \tfrac{BD}{DC} \cdot \tfrac{CE}{EA} = 1$. One or three of the points lie on extended sides.
The point where the three cevians from the vertices of a triangle to the touch points of its incircle meet. It is generally not the incenter.
The midpoints of the segments joining the vertices of a triangle to its orthocenter. They lie on the nine-point circle.

The circle through the three side midpoints, the three feet of the altitudes and the three Euler points of a triangle. Its center is the midpoint of $\overline{OH}$ and its radius is half the circumradius.
The center $N$ of the nine-point circle: the midpoint of the segment from the circumcenter to the orthocenter, on the Euler line.
The nine-point circle of a triangle is tangent to its incircle (and to its three excircles). Proved by Karl Feuerbach in 1822.
In a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides: $AC \cdot BD = AB \cdot CD + AD \cdot BC$.
For any quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AC \cdot BD \le AB \cdot CD + AD \cdot BC$, with equality exactly when the quadrilateral is cyclic.
The area of a cyclic quadrilateral with sides $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ and semiperimeter $s$ is $\sqrt{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d)}$.
The relation "$B$ is between $A$ and $C$": the three points are distinct and collinear and $AB + BC = AC$. On a number line, $B$'s coordinate lies between the other two.
A set of points that contains the whole segment joining any two of its points, such as a segment, a ray, a half-plane or a disk (but not a circle curve).
A line in a plane divides the other points of the plane into two convex half-planes, and a segment joining points in different half-planes meets the line.
Either of the two regions into which a line divides a plane; the line is its edge and is not part of it.
Either of the two regions into which a plane divides space; the plane itself is not part of it.
For $\angle ABC$, the points on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{BA}$ as $C$ and on the same side of $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ as $A$; an intersection of two half-planes.
The points of the plane that are neither on the angle nor in its interior.
The points inside a triangle: the intersection of the three half-planes that each have one side's line as edge and contain the opposite vertex.
If a line in the plane of a triangle crosses one side between its endpoints and passes through no vertex, it crosses exactly one of the other two sides (Moritz Pasch, 1882).
If $D$ is in the interior of $\angle BAC$, then ray $\overrightarrow{AD}$ meets segment $\overline{BC}$.
A choice of $k$ objects from $n$ where order does not matter; there are $\binom{n}{k}$ of them, for example $\binom{n}{2} = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
Lines in a plane are in general position when no two are parallel and no three pass through one point.
A rule that gives each term of a sequence from earlier terms, such as $R(k) = R(k-1) + k$ for regions made by lines.
Regions that are completely enclosed and have finite area; $n$ lines in general position make $\binom{n-1}{2}$ of them.
Regions that stretch off without end; $n$ lines in general position make $2n$ of them.
Count the regions made inside a circle by all chords joining $n$ points on it (no three chords through one point): $1 + \binom{n}{2} + \binom{n}{4}$, giving 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, …
An axiom system for geometry whose models have only finitely many points, such as the four-point geometry or the Fano plane.
A geometry in which any two points are on exactly one line, any two lines meet in exactly one point, and four points exist with no three on a line. It has no parallel lines.
The smallest projective plane: 7 points and 7 lines, with 3 points on each line and 3 lines through each point.
The number $n$ such that each line of a finite projective plane has $n + 1$ points. The plane then has $n^2 + n + 1$ points and $n^2 + n + 1$ lines.
A geometry in which any two points are on exactly one line, Playfair's axiom holds, and three points exist that are not on one line. One of order $n$ has $n^2$ points and $n^2 + n$ lines.
In an affine plane, the groups of lines that are all parallel to each other. An affine plane of order $n$ has $n + 1$ classes of $n$ lines each.
A point added to a family of parallel lines so that they meet. Adding one for each parallel class, plus a line through all of them, turns an affine plane into a projective plane.
In projective plane geometry, swapping the words point and line in any theorem gives another theorem, because the axioms stay true when swapped.
In neutral geometry (without the parallel postulate), the angles of every triangle add to at most $180^\circ$.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ with base $\overline{AB}$ and two congruent legs $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BC}$ perpendicular to the base. Its summit angles are congruent: right in Euclidean geometry, acute in hyperbolic geometry.
In a Saccheri quadrilateral, the side opposite the base, joining the tops of the two legs.
The two angles of a Saccheri quadrilateral at the ends of its summit. They are always congruent and never obtuse.
A quadrilateral with three right angles. Its fourth angle is right in Euclidean geometry and acute in hyperbolic geometry; half of a Saccheri quadrilateral is one.
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. For Buffon's needle it is the rectangle of all pairs (angle, distance).
Barbier's 1860 extension of Buffon's needle: a wire of any shape and length $L$ dropped on lines $d$ apart crosses them $\tfrac{2L}{\pi d}$ times on average.
Estimating a number by repeated random sampling, such as estimating $\pi$ from needle drops. Its error shrinks roughly like $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$ for $N$ trials.
Bertrand's 1889 problem of a random chord, where three natural methods give three different probabilities ($\tfrac13$, $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac14$); "at random" must be specified.
A table listing every combination of truth values (T or F) of the simple statements, with the truth value of a compound statement in each row. $n$ simple statements need $2^n$ rows.
Whether a statement is true (T) or false (F).
A statement built from simpler statements with connectives such as "not", "and", "or", "if … then" and "if and only if".
The statement "$p$ and $q$", written $p \wedge q$; true only when both parts are true.
The statement "$p$ or $q$", written $p \vee q$; true when at least one part is true (the inclusive "or").
A compound statement that is true in every row of its truth table, such as $p \vee \sim p$.
A statement that is false in every case, such as $p \wedge \sim p$; in a proof, a conclusion that violates a given fact, definition, postulate or theorem.
The rules for negating "and" and "or": $\sim(p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q$ and $\sim(p \vee q) \equiv \sim p \wedge \sim q$.
A word that tells how many objects a statement is about, such as "all", "every", "no", "some", "there is" or "at least one".
A statement about every object of some kind ("All right angles are congruent"). One counterexample disproves it.
A statement that at least one object of some kind has a property ("Some rectangle is a square"). One example proves it.
An argument whose conclusion is true in every case where all its premises are true. Validity depends on the form, not on whether the premises are actually true.
A valid argument whose premises are all true, so its conclusion must be true.
Latin for "the mode that affirms": from $p \to q$ and $p$, conclude $q$. Another name for the Law of Detachment.
Latin for "the mode that denies": from $p \to q$ and $\sim q$, conclude $\sim p$. A valid argument form, sometimes called the Law of Contrapositive.
The invalid argument "from $p \to q$ and $\sim p$, conclude $\sim q$". It treats the inverse as if it followed from the conditional.
A proof that starts from the given facts and chains forward, step by justified step, to the conclusion.
A proof of $p \to q$ that gives a direct proof of the equivalent statement $\sim q \to \sim p$ instead.
A proof that splits the situation into cases covering every possibility and proves the conclusion in each case.
A real number that cannot be written as a fraction $\tfrac{a}{b}$ of integers with $b \ne 0$, such as $\sqrt{2}$ or $\pi$.
Describes two lengths that no common unit measures a whole number of times, such as the side and diagonal of a square; their ratio is irrational.
A method of proving a statement $P(n)$ for every whole number $n \ge n_0$: prove the base case $P(n_0)$, then prove that $P(k)$ implies $P(k + 1)$ for every $k \ge n_0$.
In a proof by induction, the proof of the first case, $P(n_0)$.
In a proof by induction, the proof that for every $k \ge n_0$, if $P(k)$ is true then $P(k + 1)$ is true.
The assumption that $P(k)$ is true, made at the start of the inductive step.
Every nonempty set of whole numbers has a smallest member. It is the reason induction is valid.
An L-shaped piece that turns a square into the next larger square; around a $k$-by-$k$ square it has $2k + 1$ unit squares.
An extra line added to a figure to make a proof possible, such as a line through a point parallel to a given line. It must be fixed by one condition so that it exists and is unique.
Geometry built on Euclid's assumptions without the parallel postulate. In it, parallels through an outside point exist but need not be unique.
The point where the perpendicular from a point to a line meets the line. Its distance from the point is the distance from the point to the line.
A nonzero vector $\langle a, b \rangle$ that moves from one point of a line to another; when $a \ne 0$ the slope is $\tfrac{b}{a}$. A vertical line has direction vector $\langle 0, 1 \rangle$.

For $\vec u = \langle a_1, b_1 \rangle$ and $\vec v = \langle a_2, b_2 \rangle$, the number $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2$. It equals $|\vec u||\vec v|\cos\varphi$, so it is $0$ exactly when the vectors are perpendicular.
A nonzero vector perpendicular to a line. For $Ax + By = C$, $\langle A, B \rangle$ is a normal vector.
The non-obtuse angle (from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$) formed where two lines cross; with direction vectors $\vec u$, $\vec v$, $\cos\varphi = \tfrac{|\vec u \cdot \vec v|}{|\vec u||\vec v|}$.

If two sides and a non-included angle of one triangle are congruent to the corresponding parts of another, and the side opposite the angle is at least as long as the other given side, the triangles are congruent. (The name is this course's; some books write SsA.)
Euclid's method of proving triangles congruent by imagining one moved and laid on top of the other. Many modern axiom systems (Hilbert's, for example) avoid it by taking SAS as an axiom.
